name: Mobile Apps with Expo and React Native
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Web and TypeScript developers who need to ship and maintain a production iOS and Android app with a small team.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of choose-the-approach, read-the-code and release-and-failure questions.

domains.name: React Native and Expo foundations
domains.summary: How React Native renders native views on the New Architecture (JSI, Fabric, Turbo Modules) with Hermes V1, and how Expo development builds, prebuild and config plugins fit around it. Core components, styling differences from the web, Metro, app config, environment variables and debugging.

domains.name: Navigation, state and data
domains.summary: File-based routing with expo-router, including layouts, stacks, tabs, modals and deep links. Server state with TanStack Query, local state and persistence, forms and keyboard handling, and offline-first sync with queued mutations.

domains.name: Native capabilities and platform integration
domains.summary: Asking for permissions at the right moment, push notifications through Expo or APNs and FCM, camera, media, location and background work within platform policy. Secure storage, biometrics, OAuth with PKCE in the system browser, and writing a small native module or config plugin.

domains.name: Performance and user experience
domains.summary: The JS and UI threads and the frame budget, fast lists with FlashList and FlatList, Reanimated and Gesture Handler on the UI thread, and startup time and bundle size. Accessibility with VoiceOver and TalkBack, roles, labels, touch targets and reduced motion.

domains.name: Build, release and over-the-air updates
domains.summary: EAS Build profiles, credentials and signing, EAS Update with runtime versions, channels and rollbacks, and what store rules allow an OTA update to change. TestFlight and Play testing tracks, store review, privacy manifests and data safety, and CI for mobile.

domains.name: Quality, security and operations
domains.summary: A mobile testing pyramid from Jest and React Native Testing Library to end-to-end tests, and OWASP MASVS security such as keeping secrets out of the bundle and pinning carefully. Crash and release-health monitoring, supporting old app versions, and choosing between a native app, a PWA and a responsive site.

scenarios.title: Turning a web product into a mobile app
scenarios.description: Bring a React and TypeScript web product to iOS and Android with Expo: share types and validation, map web routes to expo-router screens, and replace browser-only APIs with native modules, secure storage and push notifications.

scenarios.title: Shipping a fix to users without a store review
scenarios.description: A production bug needs fixing today. Decide whether it is a JavaScript-only change that EAS Update can deliver on the right channel and runtime version, roll it out gradually, and know how to roll back, or whether it needs a new store build.

scenarios.title: Debugging a slow list or janky animation
scenarios.description: A feed stutters while scrolling and a header animation drops frames. Profile the JS and UI threads, tune FlashList, move animation work to the UI thread with Reanimated, and check that the release build behaves like the profile.

scenarios.title: Getting through App Store and Google Play review
scenarios.description: Prepare a first submission and later updates: signing and credentials, TestFlight and Play testing tracks, privacy manifests and data safety forms, account deletion, target API and SDK deadlines, and staged rollouts.

scenarios.title: Handling offline use and flaky networks
scenarios.description: Keep the app usable on a train or in a basement: cache server state, persist it safely, queue mutations with idempotency keys, resolve conflicts and sync when the connection returns, and tell the user what is pending.

lessons.title: How React Native renders: the New Architecture
lessons.summary: React Native now runs only on the New Architecture: JavaScript talks to native code through JSI instead of an asynchronous bridge, which enables synchronous layout reads, concurrent React features and faster native modules. Hermes V1 is the default engine.

sections.heading: From the bridge to JSI
sections.body:
In the old (Legacy) architecture, JavaScript and native code lived on opposite sides of an **asynchronous bridge**. Every call was serialized, queued and answered later, so JavaScript could never get a native answer *right now*.

The React Native docs describe the change plainly: the New Architecture "removes the asynchronous bridge between JavaScript and native and replaces it with JavaScript Interface (JSI)". JSI lets JavaScript hold a reference to a C++ object, and the other way round, so calls can be direct and, where it matters, synchronous.

Two subsystems sit on top of JSI:

- **The new renderer (Fabric)** turns your React tree into native views (a `View` becomes a native view on iOS and Android).
- **Turbo Modules** are the native module system. Modules are loaded when first used and called through JSI.

sections.heading: What you get as an app developer
sections.body:
- **Synchronous layout.** You can measure a view in `useLayoutEffect` and update state in the same commit, so a tooltip or popover is placed correctly on its first visible frame instead of jumping.
- **Concurrent React.** Suspense, Transitions and automatic batching work as they do in React on the web.
- **Faster native calls.** No JSON serialization round trip for every call.

You rarely touch JSI directly. You feel it through libraries and through layout code that no longer needs timers or "wait a frame" hacks.

sections.heading: Timeline: the Legacy Architecture is gone
sections.body:
| Release | What changed |
|---|---|
| RN 0.68 | New Architecture opt-in |
| RN 0.76 | New Architecture on by default |
| RN 0.82 | First release running *entirely* on the New Architecture; `newArchEnabled=false` is ignored |
| RN 0.84 | Legacy code removed from iOS builds by default; Hermes V1 becomes the default engine |
| Expo SDK 55 | Legacy support dropped and `newArchEnabled` removed from app.json (SDK 54 was the last with it) |
| Expo SDK 56 | Hermes V1 is the Expo default |

Interop layers that let many older libraries keep working remain "for the foreseeable future". The practical rule for an upgrade: a library that truly cannot run on the New Architecture must be updated or replaced. There is no switch to turn the old architecture back on.

sections.heading: Expo Modules vs Turbo Modules
sections.body:
When you need your own native code, you have two first-class options. Both use JSI and both support the New Architecture.

- **Expo Modules API**: write the module in Swift and Kotlin. Expo says it has "comparable performance characteristics to React Native's Turbo Modules API".
- **Turbo Modules**: React Native's own API. Choose it when you need to write **C++** (for example, shared cross-platform C++ code).

For a typical wrapper around an iOS or Android SDK, the Expo Modules API is usually the shorter path in an Expo project.

keyPoints: JSI replaced the asynchronous bridge; JavaScript can hold references to C++ objects and call them directly.
Fabric is the renderer and Turbo Modules are the native module system, both built on JSI.
The New Architecture is the only architecture from RN 0.82 and Expo SDK 55; newArchEnabled no longer exists.
Measure in useLayoutEffect and update in the same commit to avoid a one-frame layout jump.
Hermes V1 is the default JavaScript engine (RN 0.84, Expo SDK 56).
Use the Expo Modules API (Swift/Kotlin) for most native wrappers; use Turbo Modules when you need C++.

gotchas.trap: Setting newArchEnabled: false to keep an incompatible library working after an upgrade.
gotchas.correct: The flag is gone (Expo SDK 55) or ignored (RN 0.82+). Update or replace the library; interop layers cover many older ones.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Expo Modules are slower than Turbo Modules because they are "not core".
gotchas.correct: Both run on JSI; Expo documents comparable performance. Pick Turbo Modules for C++, not for speed.

gotchas.trap: Using a timer to "wait for layout" before positioning an overlay.
gotchas.correct: Read layout synchronously in useLayoutEffect and set state in the same commit.

lessons.lab: In a new Expo project, render a button and a tooltip. First position the tooltip by measuring in useEffect and note any one-frame jump on a slow device, then move the measurement into useLayoutEffect and compare. Finally, search your package.json dependencies for any library whose README says it needs the Legacy Architecture.

lessons.title: Expo workflows: Expo Go, development builds, prebuild and config plugins
lessons.summary: Expo Go is a sandbox with a fixed set of native modules. Real projects use development builds, generate native projects with Continuous Native Generation (prebuild), and change native configuration through app config and config plugins instead of hand-editing ios/ and android/.

sections.heading: Expo Go is a sandbox, not a product
sections.body:
Expo Go is a prebuilt app with a fixed set of native modules. It is great for learning and quick experiments, but:

- It "only supports the latest SDK version".
- It cannot load native code that is not already inside it, so any library with its own native code fails there.
- Some features are unavailable in it; for example, push notifications on Android throw an error in Expo Go since SDK 55.
- Recent iOS versions of Expo Go require signing in; development builds do not.

Treat Expo Go as a learning tool. Your team's day-to-day app should be a development build.

sections.heading: Development builds
sections.body:
A development build is "your own version of Expo Go": a debug build of *your* app that includes `expo-dev-client` and lets you use "any native libraries and change any native configuration".

JavaScript changes still reload instantly. You **rebuild** the development build when you:

1. add or upgrade a library that contains native code,
2. change native app config (for example, an iOS permission string in `ios.infoPlist`, or a config plugin), or
3. upgrade the Expo SDK.

The same boundary decides what an over-the-air update can ship: JS, styling and images can change without a new binary; native code, native dependencies and permissions cannot.

sections.heading: Continuous Native Generation (prebuild)
sections.body:
With **Continuous Native Generation (CNG)**, the `android/` and `ios/` directories are generated from your app config and package.json "only when needed" by `npx expo prebuild`. New projects gitignore them by default.

Important behaviours:

- If the native directories already exist in the project, EAS Build **will not run prebuild**. Changes you make to app.json plugins or icons will then not reach the build unless you regenerate or edit the native projects by hand.
- From SDK 57 the changelog says `expo prebuild` clears and regenerates by default (`--no-clean` keeps existing directories).
- Prebuild is not meant for **brownfield** apps (existing native apps that embed React Native screens). Those keep hand-maintained native projects.

The benefit of CNG is that native configuration lives in reviewable config, so SDK upgrades regenerate clean native projects instead of merging Xcode and Gradle diffs.

sections.heading: Config plugins
sections.body:
Config plugins are "functions that perform modifications on native projects during prebuild". They are how a library (or you) changes Info.plist, AndroidManifest.xml, Gradle files and so on, without committing native folders.

Conventions from the docs:

- Name them `with<Feature>` (for example, `withCustomScheme`).
- Keep them **synchronous**.
- Use mods such as `withInfoPlist` and `withAndroidManifest` from `expo/config-plugins`. Mods "are only evaluated during the syncing phase of npx expo prebuild".
- Pass options as the optional second item in the `plugins` array entry: `["my-plugin", { "option": true }]`.

Because plugins run at prebuild, changing one never affects an already-installed binary. You need a new build.

keyPoints: Expo Go only supports the latest SDK and only the native modules it ships with.
A development build is your own Expo Go that includes expo-dev-client and any native libraries you add.
Rebuild after adding native libraries, changing native config or upgrading the SDK; JS changes just reload.
CNG generates ios/ and android/ from config; they are gitignored by default in new projects.
EAS Build skips prebuild when native directories already exist in the project.
Config plugins are synchronous with<Feature> functions whose mods run only during prebuild.

gotchas.trap: Adding a library with native code and testing it in Expo Go.
gotchas.correct: Create a development build; Expo Go cannot load native code it does not already contain.

gotchas.trap: Committing generated ios/ and android/ folders, then wondering why app.json plugin changes are ignored by EAS Build.
gotchas.correct: With native folders present EAS Build does not run prebuild. Remove and gitignore them, or maintain them by hand.

gotchas.trap: Writing an async config plugin that fetches remote settings.
gotchas.correct: Plugins should be synchronous and deterministic; they run at prebuild, not at app runtime.

lessons.lab: Create a project, add a library that requires native code, and observe the failure in Expo Go. Build a development build with expo-dev-client, then write a tiny synchronous withInfoPlist plugin that sets a custom key, run npx expo prebuild, and confirm the key in the generated Info.plist.

lessons.title: Core components, styling and platform-specific code
lessons.summary: React Native renders real native views from a small set of core components. Text must live inside Text, layout uses Flexbox with mobile defaults that differ from the web, and platform differences are handled with Platform or platform file extensions.

sections.heading: The core building blocks
sections.body:
- **View** is the basic container. It maps to a native view and lays out children with Flexbox.
- **Text** is the only component that renders strings. A raw string inside a `View` is an error. Nested `Text` inherits style from its parent `Text`; a `View` does not pass text styles down.
- **Image** shows local or remote images. For network and data images you must give explicit dimensions (width and height); a bare `{ uri }` with no size renders nothing visible.
- **Pressable** is the modern touch primitive. Its `style` and `children` can be functions of `{ pressed }`, and `hitSlop` extends the touch area beyond the visual bounds.

The Expo SDK 58 changelog lists the legacy `Touchable` root export as removed. The `TouchableOpacity`-style components still exist, but the React Native docs recommend `Pressable` as the more extensive, future-proof touch API, so use it in new code.

sections.heading: Flexbox defaults that differ from the web
sections.body:
React Native's Flexbox looks like CSS but the defaults differ. From the docs: "`flexDirection` defaulting to `column` instead of `row`, `alignContent` defaulting to `flex-start` instead of `stretch`, `flexShrink` defaulting to `0` instead of `1`, the `flex` parameter only supporting a single number."

What that means in practice:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Children stack vertically | `flexDirection: 'column'` default | `flexDirection: 'row'` |
| Long text pushes siblings off screen | `flexShrink: 0` default | `flexShrink: 1` (or `flex: 1`) on the text's container |
| `flex: '1 1 auto'` does nothing useful | `flex` takes one number | Use `flex: 1`, or set `flexGrow`/`flexShrink`/`flexBasis` separately |

Every element is also `position: 'relative'` by default, so `absolute` children are positioned against their parent.

sections.heading: Platform-specific code
sections.body:
Two tools, chosen by how much code differs:

1. **Small differences**: `Platform.OS` (`'ios'`, `'android'`, `'web'`) or `Platform.select({ ios, android, native, default })`.
2. **Large differences**: platform file extensions. Create `DatePicker.ios.tsx` and `DatePicker.android.tsx` (or `.native.tsx` for "not web") and import `./DatePicker`. The bundler picks the right file automatically.

Watch out for `Platform.Version`: on Android it is the API level (a **number**), on iOS it is a **string**. Guard numeric comparisons with `Platform.OS === 'android'`.

keyPoints: All strings must be rendered inside Text; View does not inherit text styles.
Network images need explicit width and height.
Use Pressable with a style function of { pressed } and hitSlop for touch feedback and target size.
flexDirection defaults to column, flexShrink to 0, alignContent to flex-start, and flex takes a single number.
Use Platform.select for small differences and .ios/.android/.native file extensions for large ones.
Platform.Version is a number on Android and a string on iOS.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a row layout because that is the CSS default.
gotchas.correct: React Native defaults flexDirection to column; set row explicitly.

gotchas.trap: Importing ./Picker.ios directly to "force" the iOS file.
gotchas.correct: Import ./Picker without the extension and let the bundler resolve the platform file.

gotchas.trap: Comparing Platform.Version >= 33 without checking the platform.
gotchas.correct: Check Platform.OS === "android" first; on iOS Version is a string such as "17.4".

lessons.title: Project setup: TypeScript, Metro, app config and environment variables
lessons.summary: An Expo project is configured through app.json or app.config.ts, bundled by Metro, type-checked with TypeScript against React Native's strict public API, and fed build-time values with EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables and EAS environments. None of these places is safe for secrets.

sections.heading: TypeScript and Metro
sections.body:
Expo projects are TypeScript-first. Two current facts matter:

- **Strict TypeScript API is the default** (RN 0.87, adopted in Expo SDK 58). Deep imports such as `react-native/Libraries/...` are type errors; import from the public `react-native` entry point.
- **Metro** is the bundler. It resolves imports (including `.ios.tsx` / `.android.tsx` platform files), transforms TypeScript and JSX, and inlines `EXPO_PUBLIC_` variables at build time. RN 0.88 ships Metro 0.87.

Since SDK 55, `app.config.ts` itself is transpiled with the project's own TypeScript, so it can use the same compiler settings as your app code.

sections.heading: App config: app.json and app.config.ts
EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables and .env files
sections.body:
Variables prefixed `EXPO_PUBLIC_` are **inlined at build time** into the JavaScript bundle. Rules:

- They "must be statically referenced as a property of `process.env`". `process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` works; `const { EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL } = process.env` "is invalid and will not be inlined".
- They are visible in plain text in the compiled app.
- In development, files load in this order of precedence: `.env.development.local`, `.env.local`, `.env.development`, `.env`.
- **SDK 58 change:** each Expo command sets `NODE_ENV` to its own mode and replaces any value you set. `NODE_ENV=test npx expo start` loads `.env.development`, and files like `.env.staging` are no longer loaded.

sections.heading: EAS environment variables
sections.body:
EAS stores variables per environment (`development`, `preview`, `production`; custom names need higher plans). A build profile picks one with `"environment"`, and `eas update` takes `--environment`.

Each variable has a visibility: **plain text**, **sensitive**, or **secret**. Secret values are "Not readable outside of the Expo servers". That protects the value during the build (for example a `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` used to upload source maps). It does **not** protect anything you embed in the app: if a secret is exposed as an `EXPO_PUBLIC_` value or written into app config, it ships in plain text. Keep real secrets on your server.

keyPoints: Strict TypeScript API is the default in SDK 58; import from react-native, not react-native/Libraries/*.
Metro bundles the app, resolves platform extensions and inlines EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables.
app.config.ts > app.config.js > app.json; a dynamic config receives ({ config }) and returns ExpoConfig.
extra is read through Constants.expoConfig.extra and is public; never put secrets in app config.
EXPO_PUBLIC_ values must be referenced as process.env.NAME and are plain text in the binary.
EAS secret visibility protects build-time values only, not values embedded in the app.

gotchas.trap: Destructuring EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables from process.env.
gotchas.correct: Reference each as process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_NAME so Metro can inline it.

gotchas.trap: Storing an API secret as an EAS "secret" variable and reading it through EXPO_PUBLIC_.
gotchas.correct: Anything inlined into the bundle is public; call the third-party API from your backend.

gotchas.trap: Using NODE_ENV=staging to load .env.staging on SDK 58.
gotchas.correct: Expo commands overwrite NODE_ENV; select per-environment values with EAS environments or your own variable read in app.config.ts.

lessons.lab: Add an app.config.ts that switches the app name and bundle identifier on an APP_VARIANT variable. Add EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL to .env, read it both statically and by destructuring, and compare the results in a dev build. Run npx expo config --type public and list everything that would be shipped.

lessons.title: Debugging and crash reporting
lessons.summary: React Native DevTools covers JavaScript and React concerns, native tools cover native code, error boundaries catch render errors only, and a crash reporter with uploaded source maps tells you what failed in production builds and OTA updates.

sections.heading: React Native DevTools
sections.body:
React Native DevTools is the built-in debugger. Its panels include **Console**, **Sources** (breakpoints), **Memory** (heap snapshots), **React Components** and **Profiler**; **Network** and **Performance** panels arrived in RN 0.83.

Know its limits:

- It "is designed for debugging React app concerns, and not to replace native tools". A crash inside Swift, Kotlin or a native SDK is debugged in **Xcode** or **Android Studio**.
- The Network panel does not yet cover WebSocket events.
- Dev mode is much slower than release, so judge performance on release builds.

sections.heading: Logs
sections.body: `console.log` output appears in the terminal running Metro and in the DevTools Console. Logs have a cost in production: the performance docs recommend stripping `console.*` calls from release bundles with `babel-plugin-transform-remove-console`. For production diagnostics, send structured events to a crash or analytics service instead of relying on logs nobody can read.

sections.heading: Error boundaries
sections.body:
An error boundary is a component that catches errors thrown **while rendering** its children (and in lifecycle methods) and shows a fallback UI instead of a blank screen.

It does **not** catch errors in:

- event handlers such as `onPress`,
- asynchronous code (promises, timers),
- the boundary itself.

Handle those with `try/catch` (or promise `.catch`), show your own error state, and report them to your crash reporter explicitly.

sections.heading: Crash reporting with Sentry on EAS
sections.body:
Expo documents Sentry as a crash reporter:

1. Install with `npx @sentry/wizard@latest -i reactNative`.
2. Set `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` as an EAS environment variable (sensitive visibility). EAS Build then uploads source maps automatically, so production stack traces are readable.
3. For OTA updates, run `npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist` after `eas update`, since the update has its own bundle and source maps.
4. Tag events with the running update, for example `scope.setTag('expo-update-id', Updates.updateId)`, so you can tell which update a crash came from.

Do not ship source maps inside the production app, and never expose the auth token as an `EXPO_PUBLIC_` variable. Expo's own observability product also added native crash reporting in 2026, so check the current options when you choose a tool.

keyPoints: React Native DevTools: Console, Sources, Memory, React Components, Profiler, and Network/Performance since 0.83.
Debug native crashes in Xcode or Android Studio; DevTools is not a replacement for native tools.
Error boundaries catch render-time errors only, not event handler or async errors.
Strip console.* from release builds and use a crash reporter for production.
Set SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN as a sensitive EAS variable so EAS Build uploads source maps.
Upload update source maps after eas update and tag events with the update ID.

gotchas.trap: Wrapping the app in an error boundary and assuming every crash is now caught.
gotchas.correct: Boundaries miss event handler and async errors; catch and report those explicitly.

gotchas.trap: Debugging a crash inside a native SDK with only the JS debugger.
gotchas.correct: Use Xcode or Android Studio for native code.

gotchas.trap: Seeing minified stack traces only for crashes after an OTA update.
gotchas.correct: Upload the update's source maps with sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps after eas update.

lessons.lab: Throw an error during render and another in an onPress handler, wrap the screen in an error boundary, and observe which one shows the fallback. Then take two heap snapshots in the DevTools Memory panel before and after opening and closing a screen several times, and compare retained objects.

lessons.title: Routing with expo-router: files, layouts and links
lessons.summary: expo-router turns files under the app directory into screens. Layouts decide whether a folder is a stack, tabs or something else; hooks read params; protected groups gate screens by auth state; and universal links / App Links open those same routes from the web.

sections.heading: Files become routes
sections.body:
Every file in the app directory (current docs use `src/app/`) is a route, and the notation is small:

| File | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `index.tsx` | The default route of its directory |
| `[id].tsx` | A dynamic segment; `/user/42` matches `user/[id].tsx` |
| `(group)/` | Organises files and can share a layout, but adds **no** URL segment |
| `_layout.tsx` | A layout that wraps its siblings; it is not a page |
| `+not-found.tsx`, `+html.tsx`, `+native-intent.tsx`, `+middleware.ts` | Special files (the `+` prefix) |

So `src/app/(auth)/sign-in.tsx` is reachable at `/sign-in`: the group name is for you, not for the URL.

sections.heading: Layouts: stacks, tabs and modals
Navigating: navigate, push, replace
sections.body:
- `router.navigate(href)` is the usual choice: it pushes a new screen **or unwinds to the route if it is already in the stack**.
- `router.push(href)` always pushes, so calling it for a route that is already in history creates a duplicate entry.
- `router.replace(href)` swaps the current screen; `<Redirect href=... />` behaves like replace.
- `router.dismiss(n)` and `router.dismissAll()` close stacked or modal screens; `router.setParams` updates the current params.

`<Link>` wraps its children in `<Text>`. To make a custom pressable the link target, use `asChild`:

```tsx
<Link href={{ pathname: '/user/[id]', params: { id: user.id, tab: 'posts' } }} asChild>
  <Pressable><Text>{user.name}</Text></Pressable>
</Link>
```

Params that are not part of the path (`tab` above) become query params. Relative hrefs such as `./details` or `../` resolve from the current screen, and `prefetch` on a `Link` prepares the target ahead of time.

sections.heading: Reading params and focus
sections.body:
- `useLocalSearchParams()` returns the params of **this** route and only updates while the route is focused. Use it in screens.
- `useGlobalSearchParams()` "updates even when the route is not focused", so every mounted screen in a stack re-renders when any URL changes. It suits analytics, not data fetching in a screen that stays mounted below others.
- `usePathname()` returns the path without the query string; `useSegments()` returns the raw, un-normalised segments.
- `useFocusEffect(cb)` runs when the screen gains focus. Its cleanup runs when the screen **loses focus, not on unmount**.

With typed routes (`experiments.typedRoutes: true`, still described as beta and off by default, though the quick-start template sets it) the router generates a git-ignored `expo-env.d.ts`, `href` values are checked at compile time, and you can write `useLocalSearchParams<'/(search)/[profile]'>()`.

sections.heading: Protected routes and auth
sections.body:
Gate screens declaratively instead of redirecting in effects:

```tsx
const { session, isLoading } = useSession();

<Stack>
  <Stack.Protected guard={!!session}>
    <Stack.Screen name="(app)" />
  </Stack.Protected>
  <Stack.Protected guard={!session}>
    <Stack.Screen name="sign-in" />
  </Stack.Protected>
</Stack>
```

- `Protected` also works inside Tabs and Drawer.
- When a guard turns false, a user on that screen is redirected and **all of its history entries are removed**, so Back cannot return to a signed-in screen after sign-out. `redirectTo` is available from SDK 58.
- The Expo auth guide keeps the splash screen up (`SplashScreen.preventAutoHideAsync()` at module scope, `SplashScreen.hide()` once the session has loaded) so the wrong group never flashes.
- Its `useStorageState` helper keeps the token in `expo-secure-store` on native and in local storage on web.
- The docs are explicit: "Protected screens are not a replacement for server-side authentication or access control." Every API call still needs the server to check the token.

sections.heading: Deep links, universal links and App Links

keyPoints: Groups in parentheses organise files and share layouts without adding URL segments.
Prefer router.navigate; push always adds an entry and replace swaps the current one.
Use useLocalSearchParams in screens; useGlobalSearchParams re-renders unfocused screens too.
Stack.Protected removes history entries when its guard flips false, but it never replaces server-side authorization.
Universal links need applinks:<host> without a scheme and an HTTPS-served AASA; App Links need assetlinks.json with the release signing fingerprint.

gotchas.trap: Redirecting signed-out users with a useEffect in every screen.
gotchas.correct: Wrap screens in Stack.Protected (or Tabs/Drawer Protected) with a guard bound to session state, and hold the splash screen until the session has loaded.

gotchas.trap: Writing "applinks:https://example.com" in associatedDomains.
gotchas.correct: Use "applinks:example.com"; the entitlement takes a host only.

gotchas.trap: Putting the debug keystore fingerprint in assetlinks.json and expecting the Play build to verify.
gotchas.correct: Use the release or Play App Signing certificate fingerprint (eas credentials or Play Console App Signing).

lessons.title: Server state with TanStack Query on mobile
lessons.summary: TanStack Query owns data that lives on a server: it caches by key, refetches when data is stale, and gives you mutations with optimistic updates. On React Native you must wire it to app focus and network state yourself.

sections.heading: Know the defaults
sections.body:
TanStack Query's important defaults explain most "why did it refetch?" questions:

- Cached data is **stale immediately** (`staleTime: 0`).
- Stale queries refetch when a new instance **mounts**, when the window **regains focus**, and when the network **reconnects**.
- Inactive cache entries are garbage collected after **5 minutes** (`gcTime`).
- Failed queries **retry 3 times** with exponential backoff before showing an error.
- Results use **structural sharing**, so unchanged parts keep their references.

`staleTime` controls *how long data counts as fresh* (no background refetch). `gcTime` controls *how long unused data stays in memory*. Raising `gcTime` does not reduce refetches; raising `staleTime` does.

sections.heading: Wire focus and network for React Native
Keys, invalidation and mutations
Optimistic updates with rollback
Pagination and infinite lists

keyPoints: Defaults: staleTime 0, gcTime 5 minutes, refetch on mount/focus/reconnect, retry 3 with backoff.
staleTime reduces refetches; gcTime only controls how long unused data stays cached.
React Native needs focusManager wired to AppState and onlineManager wired to NetInfo or expo-network.
Optimistic updates: cancelQueries, snapshot, setQueryData, return snapshot; restore in onError; invalidate in onSettled.
Use useInfiniteQuery with getNextPageParam and guard fetchNextPage with hasNextPage and isFetchingNextPage.

gotchas.trap: Raising gcTime to stop "too many refetches".
gotchas.correct: Raise staleTime; gcTime only decides how long inactive data stays in memory.

gotchas.trap: Expecting refetchOnWindowFocus to fire when a React Native app returns from the background.
gotchas.correct: Call focusManager.setFocused from an AppState listener (skip web).

gotchas.trap: Skipping cancelQueries in onMutate.
gotchas.correct: Cancel outgoing refetches first, or a response already in flight can overwrite the optimistic value.

gotchas.trap: Copying query results into useState or a global store to "cache" them.
gotchas.correct: Read from the query; the cache is the single source of truth for server data.

lessons.title: Local state and on-device persistence
lessons.summary: Put each piece of state in the narrowest home that works: component state, context for rarely changing values, an external store with selectors for busy shared client state. Persist with the store that matches the data: AsyncStorage for small preferences, SecureStore for secrets, SQLite for structured data.

sections.heading: Choose the narrowest home for state
sections.body:
| Kind of state | Home |
|---|---|
| One screen's UI (an open panel, a draft) | `useState` / `useReducer` in that component |
| Shared by a few siblings | Lift to the nearest common parent |
| Rarely changes, read widely (theme, locale, session) | React context |
| Shared client state that changes often (cart, editor, player) | An external store read with selectors (Zustand-style) |
| Data owned by a server | The TanStack Query cache, not a store |

**Context** re-renders every consumer when its value changes. That is fine for a theme, but a single `AppContext` holding a fast-changing cart re-renders every screen that reads anything from it. Split contexts by how often they change, or move busy state into an external store.

**Zustand-style stores** live outside React. Components subscribe through `useSyncExternalStore` (directly or through the library) with a **selector**, so a component re-renders only when the slice it selected changes: `const count = useCart((s) => s.items.length)`.

Do not copy query results into a store. Two copies of server data drift apart, and you lose the cache's refetch and invalidation.

sections.heading: AsyncStorage and kv-store: small, unencrypted values
sections.body:
AsyncStorage is an asynchronous, **unencrypted** key-value store of strings. It suits preferences, onboarding flags and small caches, and anything stored there should be safe to read off a compromised device.

`expo-sqlite/kv-store` is a drop-in AsyncStorage replacement backed by SQLite, and it also offers synchronous methods.

Neither is a place for access tokens, refresh tokens or other secrets.

sections.heading: SecureStore: secrets
sections.body:
`expo-secure-store` encrypts small values with the platform's protected storage:

- **iOS:** the Keychain (`kSecClassGenericPassword`). **Android:** SharedPreferences encrypted with the Android Keystore.
- The default `keychainAccessible` is `WHEN_UNLOCKED`. The `*_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY` variants do not migrate to another device through backups.
- With `requireAuthentication`, values become inaccessible if the user's biometrics change (for example, a new fingerprint). Treat that as "sign in again", not as a crash.
- iOS data *may* survive an uninstall (not guaranteed); Android data does not. The library is excluded from Android Auto Backup automatically unless you have a custom backup configuration.
- Expo enforces no size limit, but older iOS versions reportedly rejected values over about 2048 bytes, so store tokens and keys, not documents.
- The synchronous `getItem` blocks the JS thread; prefer the async API on hot paths.
- It is not available on web; the Expo auth example falls back to local storage there.

sections.heading: SQLite: structured and queryable data

keyPoints: Context re-renders all consumers on change; use selectors in an external store for busy shared state.
Server data belongs in the query cache, not duplicated into a client store.
AsyncStorage is unencrypted: preferences yes, tokens no.
SecureStore: Keychain / Keystore, WHEN_UNLOCKED by default, THIS_DEVICE_ONLY to avoid backup migration, biometric changes invalidate requireAuthentication items.
SQLite: bind parameters, migrate with PRAGMA user_version, enable WAL, verify SQLCipher with PRAGMA cipher_version.

gotchas.trap: Storing a refresh token in AsyncStorage "because it is private to the app".
gotchas.correct: AsyncStorage is unencrypted. Keep secrets in SecureStore.

gotchas.trap: Saving a large JSON blob of records in one SecureStore or AsyncStorage key.
gotchas.correct: Use SQLite for structured or growing data; keep SecureStore for small secrets.

gotchas.trap: Assuming PRAGMA key encrypted the database.
gotchas.correct: Without SQLCipher enabled it is silently ignored; check PRAGMA cipher_version.

gotchas.trap: Wrapping every consumer in memo to stop context re-renders.
gotchas.correct: memo does not stop a component that reads a changed context from re-rendering. Split the context or use a store with selectors.

lessons.lab: Build a notes app: keep the theme in context, the editor draft in a small external store with a selector, the auth token in SecureStore and the notes in SQLite with a §user_version§ migration. Use React DevTools highlighting to confirm typing in the editor re-renders only the editor.

lessons.title: Forms and input on mobile
lessons.summary: Mobile forms live with a software keyboard that covers half the screen. Pick the right keyboard and autofill hints, keep the focused field and the submit button reachable, validate with one Zod schema, and make every field and error usable with a screen reader.

sections.heading: Ask for the right keyboard
sections.body:
`TextInput` props shape the keyboard and autofill:

```tsx
const passwordRef = useRef<ComponentRef<typeof TextInput>>(null);

<TextInput
  keyboardType="email-address"
  autoCapitalize="none"
  autoComplete="email"
  textContentType="emailAddress"   // iOS autofill hint
  returnKeyType="next"
  submitBehavior="submit"
  onSubmitEditing={() => passwordRef.current?.focus()}
/>
<TextInput ref={passwordRef} secureTextEntry autoComplete="password" textContentType="password" returnKeyType="done" />
```

- `keyboardType` picks the layout (`email-address`, `numeric`, `phone-pad` and so on). `visible-password` is Android-only and *shows* the text, so it is not a way to hide a password.
- `secureTextEntry` masks the value; `autoComplete` / `textContentType` let the OS offer saved credentials and one-time codes.
- `returnKeyType` plus `onSubmitEditing` moves focus to the next field, so users can fill the form without hunting for the next input.

sections.heading: Keep fields visible above the keyboard
sections.body:
- `KeyboardAvoidingView` shifts content by its `behavior` (`padding`, `height` or `position`). The platforms behave differently, so test both; `padding` on iOS is a common starting point.
- Inside a `ScrollView`, the default `keyboardShouldPersistTaps="never"` means the first tap outside the focused input only dismisses the keyboard, so a "Submit" tap does nothing. Set `"handled"` so taps on buttons are delivered.
- React Native 0.88 deprecated the iOS-only `InputAccessoryView` and points to `react-native-keyboard-controller` (for example its `KeyboardStickyView`) for toolbars that ride on the keyboard. That library also gives consistent keyboard-aware scrolling on both platforms.
- On Android, edge-to-edge is mandatory, so account for system-bar insets as well as the keyboard.

sections.heading: Validate with one Zod schema
Accessible inputs
sections.body:
- Give every input a visible text label and expose it as the accessible name (`accessibilityLabel`, or on Android `accessibilityLabelledBy` pointing at the label's `nativeID`). Placeholder text alone is not a label: it disappears as soon as the user types.
- Do not signal errors by colour alone. Render the message as text near the field, and put it in a container with `accessibilityLiveRegion="polite"` on Android so TalkBack announces it when it appears.
- Use `accessibilityState` (or the `aria-*` props) for states such as `disabled` and `busy` on the submit button; `role` takes precedence over `accessibilityRole` when both are set.
- Make touch targets at least 48 x 48 dp (Android guidance) and keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or more for normal-size text.

keyPoints: Use keyboardType, autoComplete/textContentType and secureTextEntry so the OS shows the right keyboard and autofill.
Chain fields with returnKeyType and onSubmitEditing focusing the next ref.
keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled" lets a button tap through while the keyboard is open.
InputAccessoryView is deprecated in RN 0.88; prefer react-native-keyboard-controller.
Validate with Zod safeParse, map issues to fields, and validate again on the server.
Label every input, announce errors as text, and do not rely on colour or placeholders.

gotchas.trap: Using keyboardType="visible-password" to protect a password.
gotchas.correct: That Android-only type shows the text. Use secureTextEntry.

gotchas.trap: Calling schema.parse in onSubmit without a try/catch.
gotchas.correct: Use safeParse and branch on result.success.

gotchas.trap: Showing a red border as the only error indicator.
gotchas.correct: Show the error text and make it announced to assistive technology.

gotchas.trap: Building a new keyboard toolbar with InputAccessoryView.
gotchas.correct: It is deprecated as of RN 0.88; use react-native-keyboard-controller.

lessons.lab: Build a sign-up form with email, password and confirm-password fields inside a ScrollView. Chain focus with the return key, validate with a Zod schema (add a §refine§ for matching passwords), show field errors on blur, and test with VoiceOver or TalkBack that every field is named and each error is read out.

lessons.title: Offline-first: queues, conflicts and sync
lessons.summary: An offline-first app keeps working without a network: it reads from local data, queues writes, replays them in order when the device reconnects, and handles the case where the server changed the same record meanwhile.

sections.heading: Paused and persisted mutations
Make replays safe
sections.body:
On flaky networks a request can reach the server while the response is lost. The client retries and, without protection, creates the record twice.

- Generate an **idempotency key** (a UUID) once, when the user acts, and store it with the queued mutation. Send it on every attempt so the server can return the original result instead of repeating the side effect.
- Prefer client-generated IDs for new records, so a retried create is the same record.
- Retry with exponential backoff (TanStack's default for queries) rather than a tight loop that drains the battery.

sections.heading: Detect and resolve conflicts
sections.body:
Two devices edit the same note offline. Whoever syncs last silently overwrites the other if the server accepts blind writes ("last write wins").

A safer protocol uses optimistic concurrency:

1. Each record carries a version (or an `ETag`).
2. The client sends the version it based the edit on, for example in an `If-Match` header.
3. If the server's version has moved on, it rejects the write with **412 Precondition Failed** instead of overwriting.
4. The client fetches the current record and resolves: merge non-overlapping fields automatically, or show the user both versions.

Pick the policy per data type: last write wins can be fine for a "last opened" timestamp, but not for a document body.

sections.heading: Sync on reconnect
sections.body:
- Keep the UI usable offline: show cached or local data with a subtle "offline" or "pending" indicator instead of a blocking error screen.
- On reconnect, `onlineManager` lets paused mutations resume and stale queries refetch (`refetchOnReconnect` is on by default).
- Being "connected" to a network does not guarantee the server is reachable; treat request failures as the real signal and let retries handle them.
- If screens read from SQLite, write server changes into SQLite after sync, and invalidate the queries that read it.

keyPoints: Paused mutations replay in order on reconnect once onlineManager knows the network state.
Persisted mutations need setMutationDefaults (a default mutationFn) and resumePausedMutations after restore.
Use a shared scope.id to serialise writes to the same record.
Idempotency keys created once per user action make retries safe.
Use versions or ETags with If-Match and 412 to detect conflicts instead of last write wins.

gotchas.trap: Persisting the mutation cache and expecting queued writes to run after a cold start.
gotchas.correct: Register setMutationDefaults for each mutation key and call resumePausedMutations after the cache is restored.

gotchas.trap: Generating a new idempotency key on each retry.
gotchas.correct: Create it once per user action and reuse it for every attempt.

gotchas.trap: Silently overwriting the server copy on sync.
gotchas.correct: Send the base version with If-Match and resolve 412 conflicts by merging or asking the user.

lessons.lab: Extend the notes app: persist the query client, register §setMutationDefaults§ for §addNote§ and §editNote§, and give edits to the same note a shared scope id. Kill the app in airplane mode, reopen it, reconnect and confirm the queue drains in order. Then simulate a 412 from a mock server and show a merge prompt.

lessons.title: Permissions on iOS and Android: timing, denial and least access
lessons.summary: Where permission declarations live in an Expo app, when to ask, what to do after a denial, and why a system picker often beats a permission prompt.

sections.heading: Two halves of every permission
sections.body:
A permission has a **build-time declaration** and a **runtime request**.

- **iOS** needs a purpose string in Info.plist, set through `ios.infoPlist` (for example `NSCameraUsageDescription`) or through a library's config plugin props (for example the expo-media-library `photosPermission` option).
- **Android** permissions are added with `android.permissions`. To strip one that a dependency adds, list its full name in `android.blockedPermissions`, for example `android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO`.

These values end up in the native project at build time. The Expo permissions guide states that Info.plist changes "cannot be updated over-the-air", so a new or reworded purpose string needs a new store build.

sections.heading: Ask in context, not at launch
sections.body:
Request a permission at the moment the user starts the feature that needs it (tapping "Scan receipt", not the first launch screen). A short in-app explanation before the system dialog tells the user why the request matters.

Apple's guideline 5.1.1(ii) requires consent, a way to withdraw it, and purpose strings that "clearly and completely describe your use of the data". Guideline 5.1.2(i) bars apps from requiring system features such as push notifications or location in order to use unrelated functionality. Ask only when the feature needs it, and keep the rest of the app usable if the user says no.

sections.heading: Handling denial and the settings deep link
sections.body:
Expo permission methods return a response with a `status`, a `granted` flag and `canAskAgain`. Once the user has denied a prompt, the OS will not show it again (the Expo guide notes you must uninstall the app to retest the prompt). When `canAskAgain` is false:

1. Explain what the feature needs and what still works without it.
2. Offer a button that opens the app's settings page with `Linking.openSettings()`.
3. Re-check the permission when the app returns to the foreground instead of assuming the user changed it.

Never loop the request or block the whole app behind a permission the user declined.

sections.heading: Prefer pickers to broad access
sections.body:
Both stores push apps toward the smallest access that works:

- Apple 5.1.1(iii): "use the out-of-process picker or a share sheet rather than requesting full access to protected resources like Photos or Contacts".
- Google Play: apps targeting API 33+ may request `READ_MEDIA_IMAGES` or `READ_MEDIA_VIDEO` only "if system pickers (like the Android Photo Picker), are not sufficient" for core functionality, and must file a Play Console declaration.

For a profile photo or a one-off attachment, a system picker needs no library-wide media permission at all. Request full media library access only for features like a gallery or backup app whose core job is browsing the library.

keyPoints: iOS purpose strings go in ios.infoPlist or library plugin props; Android uses android.permissions and android.blockedPermissions (full names).
Permission declarations are native config: they ship in a new build, never via EAS Update.
Ask in context, explain first, and keep the app usable after a denial.
When canAskAgain is false, explain and deep link with Linking.openSettings().
Prefer system photo pickers and share sheets over broad media permissions on both stores.

gotchas.trap: Fixing a vague NSCameraUsageDescription and shipping it with eas update.
gotchas.correct: Info.plist changes cannot be updated over-the-air; ship a new build.

gotchas.trap: Calling requestPermissionsAsync again after a permanent denial and expecting a dialog.
gotchas.correct: The OS will not re-prompt; check canAskAgain and send the user to Settings.

gotchas.trap: Requesting READ_MEDIA_IMAGES just to let users pick an avatar.
gotchas.correct: Use the system photo picker; Play allows the permission only when pickers are not sufficient.

lessons.lab: In a development build, add a camera feature that asks for permission only when the user taps "Scan". Deny it (on Android you may need to deny more than once) until canAskAgain is false, then add a fallback screen with a button that calls Linking.openSettings() and re-checks status on return to the foreground.

lessons.title: Push notifications with expo-notifications and the Expo Push Service
lessons.summary: Tokens, Android channels, foreground and background handling, and how tickets and receipts tell you whether a push was actually delivered.

sections.heading: Expo push service versus APNs and FCM directly
sections.body:
expo-notifications can give you two kinds of token:

- An **Expo push token** (`ExponentPushToken[...]`) from `getExpoPushTokenAsync({ projectId })`. Your server sends to Expo's push API, which relays to APNs and FCM for you, so one request format covers both platforms.
- A **native device token** from `getDevicePushTokenAsync()`, which you use if your backend already talks to APNs and FCM directly.

Without a `projectId`, `getExpoPushTokenAsync` fails with `ERR_NOTIFICATIONS_NO_EXPERIENCE_ID`. Push does not work in Expo Go on Android (since SDK 53, and since SDK 55 it throws), so test in a development build.

sections.heading: Android channels come first
sections.body:
On Android 13 and later, the notification permission prompt "will not appear until at least one notification channel is created". Create your channel(s) with `setNotificationChannelAsync` before you request permission or fetch a token.

Channels also matter when sending: a `channelId` in the push message must already exist on the device, or the notification is not shown.

sections.heading: Foreground, tap and background handling
sections.body:
- **Foreground display:** `setNotificationHandler` decides how a notification shows while the app is open. `shouldShowAlert` is deprecated; use `shouldShowBanner` and/or `shouldShowList`. From SDK 58, foreground notifications are shown by default unless the handler says otherwise.
- **Received while open:** `addNotificationReceivedListener`.
- **User tapped it:** `addNotificationResponseReceivedListener`. For a cold start triggered by a tap, read `useLastNotificationResponse` so the tap that launched the app is not lost.
- **Background data handling:** `registerTaskAsync` with a task defined at module scope. On iOS the config plugin option `enableBackgroundRemoteNotifications` adds `remote-notification` to `UIBackgroundModes`.

Since SDK 55, the old `notification` field in app.json was removed from the schema and makes prebuild fail; configure through the expo-notifications plugin.

sections.heading: Tickets, receipts and token hygiene
sections.body:
Your server POSTs to `https://exp.host/--/api/v2/push/send` (up to 100 messages per request; the docs give a per-project rate limit). The response contains **tickets**. A ticket with status `ok` "means that the message was received by Expo's servers", not that the device got it.

About 15 minutes later, call `/getReceipts` with the ticket IDs (receipts are cleared after 24 hours). Act on errors:

- `DeviceNotRegistered`: stop sending to that token and remove it.
- `MessageTooBig`: the payload exceeded 4096 bytes.
- `MessageRateExceeded`: back off and retry later.
- `InvalidCredentials` / `MismatchSenderId`: fix your push credentials.

You can require an access token (`Authorization: Bearer`) so only your server can send to your project's tokens.

keyPoints: Expo push tokens need a projectId; native device tokens are for talking to APNs/FCM yourself.
Android 13+: create a notification channel before requesting permission or a token.
Use shouldShowBanner / shouldShowList, not the deprecated shouldShowAlert.
useLastNotificationResponse covers the cold-start tap.
A ticket ok only means Expo received it; check receipts and prune DeviceNotRegistered tokens.

gotchas.trap: Treating a ticket status of ok as delivered.
gotchas.correct: Fetch receipts later; delivery errors such as DeviceNotRegistered appear there.

gotchas.trap: Testing push in Expo Go on Android.
gotchas.correct: Use a development build; push is not supported in Expo Go on Android.

gotchas.trap: Sending with a channelId the app never created.
gotchas.correct: The channel must exist on the device or the notification is not shown.

lessons.lab: In a development build, create an Android channel, request permission, fetch an Expo push token with your projectId, and send a message with curl. Then send to an uninstalled device token, fetch receipts after a delay, and write the server logic that deletes tokens returning DeviceNotRegistered.

lessons.title: Location, media and background work within battery and policy limits
lessons.summary: Foreground versus background location, the store reviews that background access triggers, and what expo-background-task can and cannot promise.

sections.heading: Foreground first, background only if essential
sections.body:
With expo-location, foreground permission must be granted before you ask for background permission. Background location also needs platform setup:

- **iOS:** the user must grant "Always", and `UIBackgroundModes` must include `location`. If the user picked "Allow Once", a later background request "will silently fail".
- **Android:** enable `isAndroidBackgroundLocationEnabled` in the plugin config, use the `foregroundService` option for continuous tracking, and expect Play review.

Background location is not available in Expo Go. Most features (store finders, check-ins, weather) only need foreground location while the screen is open.

sections.heading: Google Play review for background location
sections.body:
Play allows background location only for a core feature with a "significant benefit to users". You need:

- A **prominent in-app disclosure** shown before the runtime prompt, which uses the word "location" and says it is used "even when the app is closed or not in use".
- A **declaration form** in the Play Console covering the feature.
- A short **video** (30 seconds or less) showing the feature and the disclosure.

Apple's guideline 2.5.4 similarly limits background modes to their intended purposes, such as VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion and local notifications.

sections.heading: Background tasks are opportunistic
sections.body:
`expo-background-task` sits on WorkManager (Android) and BGTaskScheduler (iOS). The OS decides when to run your task:

- `minimumInterval` defaults to 12 hours and cannot go below 15 minutes.
- "Tasks won't run exactly on schedule"; iOS often runs them overnight.
- Tasks are unavailable on the iOS simulator, so test on a device.
- `TaskManager.defineTask` must be called in global (module) scope, not inside a component, so the task exists when the OS wakes the app headless.

If something must happen at a precise time or right after a server event, drive it from the server (for example with a push) instead of hoping a background task fires.

sections.heading: Camera and media in practice
sections.body: Camera and media access follow the same rules as any permission: declare purpose strings at build time, ask when the user opens the feature, and prefer a system picker when the user only needs to choose existing photos. Continuous camera or location use drains the battery, so stop sessions when the screen loses focus and request the lowest location accuracy the feature needs.

keyPoints: Background location requires foreground permission first, plus iOS "Always" and UIBackgroundModes location.
Allow Once on iOS makes a later background request fail silently.
Play requires a prominent disclosure, a declaration form and a short video for background location.
Background tasks run at the OS's discretion: minimum 15 minutes, default 12 hours, often overnight on iOS.
Define tasks at module scope; test background tasks on a real iOS device.

gotchas.trap: Setting minimumInterval to 5 minutes for a near-real-time sync.
gotchas.correct: The floor is 15 minutes and timing is not guaranteed; use server-driven pushes for timely updates.

gotchas.trap: Calling TaskManager.defineTask inside a React component.
gotchas.correct: Define the task in global scope so it is registered when the app launches headless.

gotchas.trap: Requesting background location for a store locator.
gotchas.correct: Use foreground location; background access must be a core feature that passes Play review.

lessons.lab: Add expo-background-task to a development build with a task defined at module scope that records a timestamp. Install on a physical device, leave it overnight, and compare the recorded run times with the requested interval.

lessons.title: Sign-in, secure storage and biometrics
lessons.summary: OAuth and OIDC for native apps with PKCE in the system browser, where to keep tokens, and how biometric-protected values behave.

sections.heading: OAuth for native apps: system browser plus PKCE
sections.body:
RFC 8252 sets the rules for native apps:

- Apps "MUST use an external user-agent" (the system browser) and "MUST NOT use embedded user-agents" such as a WebView you control.
- Public clients "MUST implement the Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)".
- Redirects can use a private-use URI scheme, a claimed https URL, or a loopback address.
- Secrets shipped in an app "should not be treated as confidential secrets".

In Expo, `AuthSession.useAuthRequest` builds the request (with PKCE), `makeRedirectUri` produces the redirect, and calling `WebBrowser.maybeCompleteAuthSession()` lets the redirect page finish the session (it matters mainly for the web popup flow).

sections.heading: Keep secrets off the device
sections.body:
The Expo authentication guide warns: "Your client application code is not a secure place to store secrets". If a provider insists on a client secret, exchange the authorization code on your server and return your own session or tokens to the app. The same applies to `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` variables and app config: they are readable in the shipped app.

Apple 4.8 adds a store rule: if you use a third-party login for the primary account, also offer an equivalent login option that limits data to name and email, lets users keep their email private, and does not track without consent.

sections.heading: Storing tokens with expo-secure-store
sections.body:
Put access and refresh tokens in **expo-secure-store**, not AsyncStorage:

- iOS stores values in the Keychain; Android uses SharedPreferences "encrypted with Android's Keystore system".
- The default `keychainAccessible` is `WHEN_UNLOCKED`. The `*_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY` variants do not migrate via backup.
- iOS data may survive a reinstall (not guaranteed); Android data does not. Plan for both.
- The synchronous `getItem` blocks the JS thread; prefer the async methods in hot paths.
- SecureStore is not available on web, so a web build needs another strategy.

Keep access tokens short-lived and rotate refresh tokens through your server. On logout, delete them from SecureStore and revoke them server-side.

sections.heading: Biometrics as a gate on local secrets
sections.body:
Setting `requireAuthentication` on a SecureStore item makes reading it require biometric or device authentication. Values stored this way become inaccessible if the device's biometrics change (for example a new fingerprint is enrolled). Treat that as a normal path: catch the failure, clear the item, and send the user through a full sign-in again.

OWASP MASVS-AUTH-2 asks that local authentication follow platform best practices. A sound design ties the biometric check to unlocking a stored secret, as requireAuthentication does, rather than to a JavaScript flag that merely records that a check passed.

keyPoints: Native OAuth: system browser, never an embedded WebView, and PKCE for public clients (RFC 8252).
No client secrets in the app; exchange codes on your server if a secret is required.
Tokens belong in expo-secure-store (Keychain / Keystore-encrypted), not AsyncStorage.
requireAuthentication items are lost when biometrics change; handle it with re-login.
Apple 4.8: third-party primary login needs an equivalent privacy-preserving option.

gotchas.trap: Rendering the identity provider login page in a WebView to style it.
gotchas.correct: Use the system browser via AuthSession; RFC 8252 forbids embedded user-agents.

gotchas.trap: Bundling the OAuth client secret in EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables.
gotchas.correct: Anything in the client is public; do the code exchange on a server.

gotchas.trap: Assuming SecureStore values always survive an uninstall on iOS.
gotchas.correct: Survival on iOS is not guaranteed and Android data does not survive; design for both.

lessons.lab: Implement sign-in with AuthSession.useAuthRequest against a test OIDC provider using PKCE and a scheme redirect. Store the refresh token in SecureStore with a THIS_DEVICE_ONLY accessibility option, then add a logout that deletes it and calls the revocation endpoint on your server.

lessons.title: When no library exists: native modules and config plugins
lessons.summary: Choosing between a config plugin, an Expo module and a Turbo Module, and how continuous native generation decides where native changes must live.

sections.heading: Config, code, or both?
sections.body:
Start by asking what is missing:

- **Only native configuration** (an Info.plist key, a manifest entry, a Gradle setting): write a **config plugin**. Config plugins are "functions that perform modifications on native projects during prebuild".
- **Native code you call from JavaScript** (a platform API no library wraps): write a **native module**, usually with the Expo Modules API in Swift and Kotlin.
- **A library that needs both**: ship a module that also exports a config plugin.

Either way the app needs a development build. A development build is "your own version of Expo Go" that can include "any native libraries"; rebuild it whenever you add native code or change native config.

sections.heading: Writing a config plugin
sections.body:
Plugins use mods such as `withInfoPlist` and `withAndroidManifest` from `expo/config-plugins`. Mods "are only evaluated during the syncing phase of npx expo prebuild", plugins should be synchronous, and by convention they are named `with<Feature>`. Pass options as the optional second element of the entry in the `plugins` array.

With continuous native generation, `android/` and `ios/` are generated and gitignored by default, so a hand edit inside them is lost the next time they are regenerated. Put the change in a plugin so every build reproduces it. Note that if native directories are committed, "Expo Build will not run Prebuild", and your plugins will not be applied there.

sections.heading: Expo Modules API or Turbo Modules
sections.body:
Both use JSI and "all support the New Architecture". Expo documents comparable performance characteristics between Expo Modules and React Native's Turbo Modules. Pick the **Expo Modules API** for a small Swift/Kotlin wrapper in an Expo app; pick **Turbo Modules** when you need to write the module in C++.

Keep the module surface small: a few typed async functions and events, with permission requests and platform differences handled natively, and a JavaScript fallback or clear error on platforms you do not support.

keyPoints: Config-only gaps get a config plugin; missing native APIs get a native module.
Mods run only during npx expo prebuild; keep plugins synchronous and named with<Feature>.
Hand edits to generated android/ and ios/ folders do not survive regeneration.
Expo Modules API (Swift/Kotlin) for most cases; Turbo Modules when you need C++.
Any native change requires a new development build, not Expo Go.

gotchas.trap: Editing ios/Info.plist by hand in a CNG project.
gotchas.correct: Generate it from app config or a config plugin so prebuild reproduces it.

gotchas.trap: Writing an async config plugin that fetches settings from the network.
gotchas.correct: Plugins should be synchronous; pass values as plugin options instead.

lessons.lab: Write a local config plugin named withExampleKey that adds a custom Info.plist key from a plugin option, run npx expo prebuild, and confirm the key appears. Then scaffold a local Expo module that exposes one synchronous Swift/Kotlin function and call it from a development build.

lessons.title: Threads, the frame budget and where jank comes from
lessons.summary: A smooth app finishes each frame inside a fixed budget. Know which work runs on the JavaScript thread and which runs on the native UI thread, and you can explain almost every dropped frame.

sections.heading: The frame budget
sections.body:
Phones redraw the screen at least 60 times a second. The React Native performance guide puts it plainly: that gives you and the UI system **at most 16.67 ms** to produce each frame. Miss the deadline and the frame is dropped, so the UI looks stuck or stutters.

On a 120 Hz display the same arithmetic gives **about 8.33 ms** per frame (1000 / 120). Work that just fits on a 60 Hz phone can drop frames on a high-refresh device, so budget for the fastest screen you support.

A dropped frame is cumulative: a re-render that takes 200 ms costs about 12 frames at 60 Hz, and anything driven from JavaScript (for example a JS-driven animation) appears to freeze for that whole time.

sections.heading: JS thread versus UI thread
sections.body:
Two threads matter most:

| Thread | Runs | When it is blocked |
|---|---|---|
| **JavaScript thread** | your React components, business logic, API handling, touch event processing | JS-driven animations freeze, taps feel ignored |
| **Main / UI thread** | native rendering, native stack transitions, `ScrollView` scrolling | everything visibly stops |

Because native work lives on the UI thread, a `ScrollView` keeps scrolling and a native stack transition keeps animating even while the JS thread is busy. The flip side: a heavy JS task makes `Pressable`/touchable feedback late, because the JS thread cannot process the raw touch events.

sections.heading: Common causes of jank
sections.body:
- **Measuring in development mode.** The JS thread is much slower in dev mode. Always judge performance on a release build.
- **`console.*` calls in a bundled app.** They can be a big JS-thread bottleneck, including logging from libraries such as redux-logger. Strip them in production with `babel-plugin-transform-remove-console`.
- **Heavy work in the same frame as a press.** If `onPress` triggers an expensive re-render, the pressed-state feedback appears only after the handler returns. Deferring the work with `requestAnimationFrame` lets the feedback paint first.
- **Heavy JS during an animation or transition.** Move the animation off the JS thread (native driver or Reanimated) or defer the work, for example with `requestIdleCallback`.
- **Animating layout-heavy properties.** Resizing an `Image` by animating width and height re-crops and rescales every frame; animate `transform: [{ scale }]` instead.

Note that `InteractionManager` was removed in Expo SDK 58 / React Native 0.88, so do not reach for `InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions` in current code.

sections.heading: Measuring before fixing
sections.body:
Open the Dev Menu and enable **Show Perf Monitor**: it shows the JS and UI frame rates separately, which tells you which thread is dropping frames. A low JS rate with a healthy UI rate points at JavaScript work; a low UI rate points at native rendering, overdraw or expensive views.

For deeper work the React Native profiling guide recommends **Xcode Instruments** on iOS and the **Android Studio Profiler** on Android (the standalone `systrace` tool has been removed from platform-tools). Exported Android traces can be opened in Perfetto. Whatever the tool, first make sure development mode is off.

keyPoints: 60 Hz gives at most 16.67 ms per frame; 120 Hz gives about 8.33 ms.
The JS thread runs React, business logic and touch handling; scrolling and native transitions run on the UI thread.
Perf Monitor shows JS and UI frame rates separately, which tells you which thread to fix.
Profile release builds; dev mode is much slower.
Strip `console.*` in production and defer heavy work triggered by presses.

gotchas.trap: Profiling jank on the dev server and optimising whatever looks slow there.
gotchas.correct: Dev mode slows the JS thread a lot. Reproduce and measure on a release build first.

gotchas.trap: Using `InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions` to defer work after a transition.
gotchas.correct: It was removed in SDK 58 / RN 0.88. Use `requestAnimationFrame` or `requestIdleCallback`, or move the animation off the JS thread.

gotchas.trap: Assuming 16 ms of JS work per frame is fine on every device.
gotchas.correct: On a 120 Hz display the budget is about 8.33 ms, so the same work drops frames.

lessons.lab: Build a screen with a `ScrollView`, a button and an animated box. In the button's `onPress`, run a synchronous loop for about 300 ms. On a release build, turn on the Perf Monitor and press the button: note that scrolling keeps working while the JS frame rate collapses and the button feedback lags. Then wrap the loop in `requestAnimationFrame` and compare when the pressed feedback appears.

lessons.title: Fast lists: FlatList tuning, FlashList and images
lessons.summary: Long lists are where most React Native apps first drop frames. Tune FlatList with stable keys, memoised rows and getItemLayout, or switch to FlashList, which recycles row components, and cache images properly.

sections.heading: How FlatList virtualises
sections.body:
`FlatList` renders only a window of items around the viewport and fills in more in batches. The defaults from the React Native docs:

| Prop | Default | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| `initialNumToRender` | 10 | Too high delays first paint; too low shows blanks on mount |
| `maxToRenderPerBatch` | 10 | Bigger batches fill faster but block the JS thread longer |
| `updateCellsBatchingPeriod` | 50 ms | How often batches render |
| `windowSize` | 21 (10 viewports above, 10 below, 1 visible) | Smaller saves memory but risks blank areas when scrolling fast |
| `removeClippedSubviews` | `true` on Android, `false` elsewhere | Detaches off-screen views; can have bugs with some content |

Change one prop at a time and measure on a release build.

sections.heading: Row hygiene: keys, memo and getItemLayout
FlashList and recycling
sections.body:
`@shopify/flash-list` is a drop-in replacement for `FlatList` that **recycles components under the hood**: instead of unmounting off-screen rows and mounting new ones, it reuses row instances with new data. The React Native performance guide lists FlashList (and Legend List) as alternatives when a FlatList is still slow.

Recycling has two consequences you must design for:

1. **Local state can leak.** A row that keeps `useState` (an "expanded" flag, say) keeps that state when it is reused for a different item. Keep per-item state in data keyed by item id, or use the reset helper the FlashList v2 docs provide (`useRecyclingState`).
2. **Images can flash stale content.** A recycled row briefly shows the previous item's image unless the image view is told the content changed.

FlashList v2 is built for the New Architecture and no longer needs size estimates: `estimatedItemSize` is deprecated and unused, and the masonry layout became a `masonry` prop. Check the FlashList docs for the version you install.

sections.heading: Images and memory
sections.body:
Images are usually the biggest memory cost in a list. `expo-image` helps in several ways:

- **`cachePolicy`** defaults to `'disk'`. `'memory-disk'` keeps decoded images in memory with a disk fallback; `'memory'` alone may be purged quickly to avoid running out of memory.
- **`recyclingKey`** resets the view to blank or a placeholder before the new image loads, which is exactly what recycling lists like FlashList need.
- **`allowDownscaling`** defaults to `true`; turning it off can hurt performance, so serve images close to their display size.
- **`placeholder`** (for example a blurhash) gives an instant low-cost preview.

keyPoints: FlatList defaults: initialNumToRender 10, maxToRenderPerBatch 10, windowSize 21.
Use a stable `keyExtractor`, memoised rows and a `useCallback` renderItem.
`getItemLayout` skips measurement for fixed-height rows.
FlashList recycles row components, so reset per-item state and set an image `recyclingKey`.
expo-image caches to disk by default; `memory-disk` adds an in-memory layer.

gotchas.trap: Raising `windowSize` and `initialNumToRender` to "fix" blank areas on every device.
gotchas.correct: Larger windows mean more memory and more JS work per batch. Make rows cheaper first and measure on low-end hardware.

gotchas.trap: Keeping an "expanded" `useState` inside a FlashList row.
gotchas.correct: Recycled rows keep that state for a different item. Store it per item id or reset it on recycle.

gotchas.trap: Passing `estimatedItemSize` to FlashList v2.
gotchas.correct: v2 measures items itself; the prop is deprecated and unused.

lessons.lab: Render 2,000 rows with an avatar and two lines of text in a `FlatList`, then in `FlashList`. For each, measure JS frame rate while flinging on a release build. In the FlashList version, add an "expanded" toggle with `useState` and observe it leak to other items; fix it by storing the expanded ids in the parent. Switch avatars to `expo-image` with a `recyclingKey` and confirm stale images no longer flash.
