lessons.title: Animations and gestures on the UI thread
lessons.summary: Animations stay smooth when each frame is computed off the JavaScript thread. Reanimated runs animation logic as worklets on the UI thread, and Gesture Handler recognises gestures natively, so a busy JS thread no longer freezes motion.

sections.heading: Why JS-driven animation stutters
sections.body:
The core `Animated` API calculates each keyframe on the JavaScript thread unless you set `useNativeDriver: true`. Any JS work longer than a frame then freezes the animation. `LayoutAnimation` runs on Core Animation and is unaffected by JS frame drops, but it only suits fire-and-forget animations; anything interruptible needs a driven animation.

For gesture-driven, interruptible motion, the standard answer in an Expo app is **Reanimated** plus **Gesture Handler**.

sections.heading: Reanimated: shared values and worklets
Gesture Handler
sections.body:
`react-native-gesture-handler` gives you native touch and gesture recognition. Expo's reference notes its gesture logic runs entirely on the native thread, so it is deterministic and does not wait for JavaScript. Wrap the app (or the screen root) in `GestureHandlerRootView`, describe gestures, and attach them with `GestureDetector`. Pair a pan gesture with a Reanimated shared value and a drag can follow the finger at full frame rate even while the JS thread renders.

Gesture Handler 3 moved from the chained builder API to hooks and renamed some callbacks. Follow the upgrade guide for the version you install rather than copying older snippets.

sections.heading: Choosing the right tool
sections.body:
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Simple fade or slide, not interruptible | `Animated` with `useNativeDriver: true` or `LayoutAnimation` |
| Gesture-driven, interruptible, physics | Reanimated shared values + Gesture Handler |
| Zooming an image | animate `transform: [{ scale }]`, not width and height |
| Screen transitions | native stack, which animates on the UI thread |

Whatever you pick, respect the user's **reduce motion** setting (see the accessibility lesson).

keyPoints: `Animated` computes frames on the JS thread unless `useNativeDriver: true`.
Reanimated worklets run on the UI thread; shared values sync through `.value`.
Reanimated 4 needs `react-native-worklets`; `babel-preset-expo` configures the plugin.
Gesture Handler recognises gestures on the native thread.
Animate transforms and opacity rather than layout properties.

gotchas.trap: Driving a drag with `setState` in a JS touch handler.
gotchas.correct: Each move waits for the JS thread and a re-render. Use a Gesture Handler pan updating a Reanimated shared value.

gotchas.trap: Replacing `babel-preset-expo` with a custom preset list and losing the worklets plugin.
gotchas.correct: Keep `babel-preset-expo`, or add `react-native-worklets/plugin` as the last plugin.

gotchas.trap: Copying Gesture Handler 2 builder snippets into a v3 project.
gotchas.correct: v3 uses hooks and renamed callbacks; follow the v3 upgrade guide.

lessons.lab: Build a draggable card twice: once with `PanResponder` and `setState`, once with a Gesture Handler pan updating a Reanimated shared value. Add a button that blocks the JS thread for 500 ms. On a release build, drag while blocking and compare: the Reanimated version should keep following your finger.

lessons.title: Startup time and bundle size
lessons.summary: Cold start is mostly loading and evaluating your JavaScript. Hermes precompiles it to bytecode, and you keep the bundle lean by measuring it with Expo Atlas, trimming dependencies, deferring rarely used code and sizing assets.

sections.heading: Hermes and bytecode
sections.body:
Hermes is a JavaScript engine optimised for React Native and is the default; no configuration is needed. Its main startup advantage is that JavaScript is **compiled to Hermes bytecode at build time**, so the device skips parsing and compiling source at launch. The React Native docs say that for many apps this improves start-up time, lowers memory use and shrinks app size compared with JavaScriptCore.

Hermes V1 became the default in React Native 0.84 and in Expo SDK 56, where Expo described it as giving faster startup, better runtime performance and lower memory use. You can confirm Hermes is running with `global.HermesInternal`, but also confirm the precompiled `.hbc` bundle is what ships.

sections.heading: Measure the bundle with Expo Atlas
sections.body:
Before trimming, find out what is in the bundle:

```sh
EXPO_ATLAS=true npx expo export
npx expo-atlas .expo/atlas.jsonl
```

Atlas shows each module's size and who imports it, so you can trace a heavy dependency back to the single import that pulls it in. Analyse with production settings (dev mode disables optimisations), and use `--no-bytecode` when you need readable output for analysis. Treat the Atlas file like source code, and **avoid publishing source maps to production**: they cause security and performance issues.

sections.heading: Shrinking and deferring work
sections.body:
- **Audit dependencies.** The libraries you choose dominate bundle size. Replace a large utility library with the few functions you use.
- **Defer rarely used code.** React's `lazy` with `Suspense` and a dynamic `import()` defers loading and evaluating a component's module until it first renders, which keeps a heavy, rarely visited screen out of the startup path. Measure the effect on your platform rather than assuming it.
- **Do less at launch.** Avoid top-level work in modules imported by the root layout (big JSON parsing, synchronous storage reads, analytics init that blocks render).
- **Right-size assets.** Ship images near their display size, prefer modern compressed formats and let `expo-image` downscale; huge bitmaps cost decode time and memory.
- **Strip logging** with `transform-remove-console` in production.

sections.heading: Profile startup properly
sections.body: Measure cold start on a **release build** on a low-end physical device, before and after each change; the Hermes docs explicitly recommend benchmarking before and after. Use Xcode Instruments on iOS and the Android Studio Profiler on Android to see where launch time goes, and compare against your previous release rather than a single run.

keyPoints: Hermes compiles JS to bytecode at build time, which speeds startup.
Hermes V1 is the default (RN 0.84, Expo SDK 56).
`EXPO_ATLAS=true npx expo export` then `npx expo-atlas` to inspect the bundle.
Never publish source maps to production.
Defer rarely used screens with `React.lazy` and measure on release builds.

gotchas.trap: Switching to JavaScriptCore to improve startup.
gotchas.correct: Hermes precompiles bytecode and is the optimised default; investigate bundle contents and launch work instead.

gotchas.trap: Analysing bundle size from a development build.
gotchas.correct: Dev mode disables optimisations; analyse a production export.

gotchas.trap: Shipping source maps with the app so crash traces are readable.
gotchas.correct: Upload source maps to your crash reporter instead; do not publish them to production.

lessons.lab: Run `EXPO_ATLAS=true npx expo export` on your app and open it with `npx expo-atlas`. Identify the three largest dependencies and the import that pulls each in. Move one rarely used screen behind `React.lazy`, re-export, and compare cold start on a release build.

lessons.title: Accessibility on iOS and Android
lessons.summary: Screen reader users hear your app through VoiceOver and TalkBack. Give every control a role and a name, group related content, respect text scaling and reduce motion, and make touch targets large enough.

sections.heading: Roles, labels, hints and state
sections.body:
VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) read the accessibility tree React Native builds from your props:

- **`accessible`** groups a view and its children into one focusable element.
- **`accessibilityLabel`** is the spoken name; required for icon-only buttons.
- **`accessibilityHint`** explains the result of the action when it is not obvious.
- **`accessibilityRole`** (`button`, `header`, `link`, `image`, `switch`, `tab`, `adjustable` and more) tells the user what kind of element it is. The newer `role` prop takes precedence over `accessibilityRole`.
- **`accessibilityState`** reports `disabled`, `selected`, `checked`, `busy` and `expanded` (the `aria-*` props are equivalents).
- **`accessibilityActions`** with `onAccessibilityAction` expose custom actions, such as increment and decrement on an adjustable control.

```tsx
<Pressable
  accessibilityRole="button"
  accessibilityLabel="Delete message"
  accessibilityHint="Removes this message from the thread"
  onPress={remove}
>
  <TrashIcon />
</Pressable>
```

sections.heading: Grouping, hiding and announcing
sections.body:
- Make a card one element with `accessible` on the container and a combined label, so the reader does not stop on every text fragment.
- On Android, `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` hides decorative subtrees.
- `accessibilityLiveRegion` (Android, `polite` or `assertive`) announces changes to a view, such as a cart total.
- `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility()` posts a message for the screen reader on both platforms; `isScreenReaderEnabled()` tells you whether one is running.

sections.heading: Dynamic type and touch targets
sections.body:
**Text scaling.** `Text` has `allowFontScaling` **true by default**, so fonts follow the user's text size setting. Do not turn it off globally to protect a layout; use `maxFontSizeMultiplier` to cap growth on genuinely constrained elements and let containers grow or wrap.

**Touch targets.** Android's guidance is at least **48dp x 48dp** for touch targets; Apple's Human Interface Guidelines have long recommended about 44 x 44 pt. Make small icons easier to hit with padding or `hitSlop`, which extends the press area beyond the element. The press area never extends past the parent view's bounds, and overlapping siblings with a higher z-index win.

**Contrast.** Android recommends at least 4.5:1 for small text and 3:1 for large text.

sections.heading: Reduced motion

keyPoints: Every control needs a role and a spoken name; icon-only buttons need `accessibilityLabel`.
`role` takes precedence over `accessibilityRole`.
`allowFontScaling` defaults to true; cap with `maxFontSizeMultiplier` instead of disabling.
Android touch targets: at least 48dp x 48dp; `hitSlop` cannot extend past the parent.
Read `isReduceMotionEnabled()` and subscribe to `reduceMotionChanged`.

gotchas.trap: Setting `allowFontScaling={false}` app-wide because large text breaks layouts.
gotchas.correct: Keep scaling, fix layouts to grow, and cap only constrained elements with `maxFontSizeMultiplier`.

gotchas.trap: Checking reduce motion once at app start.
gotchas.correct: Subscribe to `reduceMotionChanged` so the app reacts when the setting changes.

gotchas.trap: Adding a big `hitSlop` to a small icon inside a tight parent.
gotchas.correct: The touch area never extends past the parent bounds; enlarge the parent or pad the control.

lessons.lab: Turn on VoiceOver or TalkBack and navigate one screen of your app without looking. Fix every unnamed control, group cards into single elements, set the largest text size and fix any clipped text, and make one animation respect Reduce Motion with a `reduceMotionChanged` listener.

lessons.title: EAS Build profiles, credentials and build numbers
lessons.summary: How eas.json build profiles shape each binary, who owns iOS and Android signing material, and how to keep build numbers unique without hand-editing them.

sections.heading: Build profiles in eas.json
sections.body:
`eas.json` has three top-level keys: `cli`, `build` and `submit`. Each entry under `build` is a **profile** you select with `eas build --profile <name>` (`-e`). A typical project has three:

| Profile | Typical keys | Who installs it |
|---|---|---|
| `development` | `developmentClient: true`, `distribution: "internal"` | Developers, with the dev server |
| `preview` | `distribution: "internal"`, `android.buildType: "apk"`, `channel: "preview"` | Testers, installed directly |
| `production` | `distribution: "store"` (the default), `autoIncrement: true`, `channel: "production"` | Store users |

Other keys you will meet: `extends` (inherit from another profile), `environment` (which EAS environment's variables to load), `env` (plain values; the docs say "Don't put secrets here"), `node`, `resourceClass`, `ios.simulator`, `credentialsSource` and `ios.image` / `android.image`.

`android.buildType` is `app-bundle` (what Play wants) or `apk` (what you can sideload onto a test device).

sections.heading: Secrets and environment variables
sections.body:
Values you need at build time belong in **EAS environment variables**, not in `eas.json`. Each variable has a visibility: plain text, sensitive or secret. Secret values are not readable outside Expo's servers, including on the website and in EAS CLI. A build profile picks an environment (`development`, `preview` or `production`) with its `environment` key.

One caveat applies to all of them: a secret variable protects the value on EAS, **not** a value you embed in the app. Anything inlined into the JS bundle (for example `EXPO_PUBLIC_*`) is readable by anyone who has the binary.

sections.heading: Signing credentials
sections.body:
EAS can generate and store credentials for you (`credentialsSource: "remote"`, the default) or read them from a local `credentials.json` (`"local"`).

**iOS**
- A distribution certificate belongs to the Apple **account**, not to one app, so several apps on the same team can share it.
- Provisioning profiles tie an app ID, a certificate and (for ad hoc builds) devices together. They expire after 12 months.
- Push keys don't expire, and an account can hold up to two.

**Android**
- With Play App Signing, Google holds the app signing key and you sign uploads with an **upload key**.
- If you lose the upload key, Play support can reset it. The new upload certificate takes effect 72 hours later.
- Never commit a keystore to the repository.

sections.heading: Versions and build numbers
sections.body:
There are two kinds of version:

- `version` is the user-facing version. It maps to `CFBundleShortVersionString` on iOS and `versionName` on Android. The Expo docs say "the user-facing version should be explicitly set and updated by you."
- `ios.buildNumber` and `android.versionCode` are build versions. Each binary you upload needs a new one.

Set `cli.appVersionSource` to `remote`, which the docs call the recommended behavior from EAS CLI 12. EAS then stores build numbers on its servers, and `autoIncrement: true` in a profile bumps them on every build. That avoids two developers or two CI runners uploading the same build number. `autoIncrement` with a remote source bumps build numbers only, not `version`. If you leave `appVersionSource` unset, the CLI warns and falls back to `local`.

`eas build:version:set` sets the stored value, and `eas build:version:sync` writes it back into your local project.

keyPoints: A build profile in eas.json decides distribution (internal or store), dev client, channel, environment and signing source.
Use `cli.appVersionSource: "remote"` plus `autoIncrement` so EAS issues unique build numbers.
You own the user-facing `version`; EAS manages buildNumber and versionCode.
iOS distribution certificates belong to the account; provisioning profiles expire after 12 months.
With Play App Signing, a lost upload key is reset through Play support, and the new key takes effect 72 hours later.
Keep secrets in EAS environment variables, never in eas.json `env` or the JS bundle.

gotchas.trap: Putting an API secret in the `env` block of a build profile because it is "only in CI".
gotchas.correct: eas.json is committed and the docs say not to put secrets in `env`. Use an EAS environment variable with secret visibility, and still keep real secrets out of the app bundle.

gotchas.trap: Expecting `autoIncrement` to bump the marketing version (1.4.0 to 1.5.0).
gotchas.correct: With a remote version source it bumps buildNumber and versionCode only. You change `version` yourself.

gotchas.trap: Generating a new Android keystore after losing the upload key.
gotchas.correct: Play accepts uploads only when they are signed with the registered upload key, and Google keeps the app signing key. Ask Play support to reset the upload key and register the new upload certificate.

lessons.lab: In a sample Expo project, add `development`, `preview` and `production` profiles to eas.json. Make `preview` extend nothing, use `distribution: "internal"` and `android.buildType: "apk"`. Set `cli.appVersionSource` to `remote` and `autoIncrement: true` on production. Run `eas build:version:set`, then `eas build:version:sync`, and check how the build numbers in your app config change.

lessons.title: EAS Update: runtime versions, channels, rollouts and the OTA boundary
lessons.summary: How an update finds its build, how to roll it out and roll it back, and which changes are allowed over the air under Expo's limits and the store rules.

sections.heading: How an update reaches a build
sections.body:
Every build carries three things: a **channel** (from its eas.json profile), a **runtime version** and a **platform**. You publish updates to a **branch**, and a channel points at a branch. By default a channel points at the branch with the same name.

A build accepts an update only when the platform and runtime version **match exactly**. The client downloads the update's manifest, then fetches only the assets it does not already have. Since SDK 56, Hermes bytecode diffing is on by default, so clients download binary patches instead of whole bundles.

Default client behavior, from the `expo-updates` config:
- `checkAutomatically: ON_LOAD` checks on every launch. Other values are `ON_ERROR_RECOVERY`, `WIFI_ONLY` and `NEVER`.
- `fallbackToCacheTimeout` is `0`, so launch doesn't wait. A newly downloaded update usually runs on the **next** launch.
- If nothing usable is downloaded, the app runs the **embedded** update that shipped in the binary.

For more control, use the JS API. `checkForUpdateAsync()` only checks and "does not actually download". `fetchUpdateAsync()` downloads, and `reloadAsync()` restarts into the new update. The `useUpdates()` hook exposes `isUpdateAvailable`, `isUpdatePending`, `downloadProgress` and error fields.

Since SDK 55, `eas update` requires `--environment`, so the update is bundled with the same EAS environment variables as the build.

sections.heading: Runtime versions
sections.body:
The runtime version guarantees "compatibility between a build's native code and an update". You choose a policy in app config:

| Policy | Runtime version equals | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `appVersion` | `version` | Forget to bump `version` after a native change and incompatible JS reaches old builds |
| `nativeVersion` | `version` plus buildNumber or versionCode | Same risk if you change native code without bumping |
| `fingerprint` | A hash of the native project from `@expo/fingerprint` | Changes automatically when native inputs change |
| a manual string | Whatever you type | Fully on you |

The `fingerprint` policy "works for both projects with and without custom native code". `eas fingerprint:compare` shows what changed between a build and an update. A platform-specific `runtimeVersion` (under `ios` or `android`) overrides the top-level one.

sections.heading: Rollouts and rollbacks
sections.body:
**Per-update rollout.** `eas update --rollout-percentage=10` sends the update to a share of users. Raise it with `eas update:edit`, or undo it with `eas update:revert-update-rollout`. Only one rollout can be in progress for a given branch, platform and runtime version. With EAS CLI 24.9.0+ you can end the active one while publishing with `--force-end-active-rollout`.

**Branch-based rollout.** `eas channel:rollout` splits a channel between two branches. While it is active, publish with `--branch`, not `--channel`.

**Promotion.** `eas update:republish --group <id> --destination-branch production` copies an update you already tested to another branch without rebuilding the bundle. `eas channel:edit production --branch <name>` repoints a channel.

**Rollback.** `eas update:rollback` either republishes an earlier update or tells clients to run the embedded update (`eas update:roll-back-to-embedded`). It does **not** delete the bad update. It publishes a newer instruction that clients pick up on their next check.

sections.heading: What OTA may and may not change
sections.body:
Three texts set the limits. They differ in detail, so an update must satisfy all of them.

**Expo.** Updates can change "non-native pieces (such as JS, styling, and images)". They cannot change "native code or native dependencies", "app permissions", "the Expo SDK version", or "anything that requires a new app binary version". Expo adds that "your updates need to follow the App Store and Play Store guidelines."

**Apple.** DPLA 3.3.1(B) allows downloaded interpreted code only if it does not change the app's primary purpose, does not bypass OS signing, sandbox or security features, and does not create a storefront for other apps. App Review 2.5.2 forbids downloading code that "introduces or changes features or functionality". 2.5.19 bans hidden, dormant or undocumented features. Apple's 2026-10-16 news post says this covers changing an app after approval. 2.3.1(a) says new features must be described in the Notes for Review.

**Google Play.** An app may not update itself "using any method other than Google Play's update mechanism" or download executable code such as dex, JAR or .so files. The rule "does not apply to code that runs in a virtual machine or an interpreter" with indirect API access.

In practice: ship bug fixes, copy, styling and assets OTA. Ship new features, new permissions, native modules and SDK upgrades in a reviewed binary.

keyPoints: An update applies only when channel to branch mapping, platform and runtime version all line up; runtime version and platform must match exactly.
By default an update downloads on launch and runs on the next launch; use fetchUpdateAsync plus reloadAsync to apply sooner.
The fingerprint runtime policy changes the runtime version automatically when native inputs change.
Only one rollout per branch, platform and runtime version can be in progress.
`eas update:rollback` republishes an older update or the embedded one; it does not delete anything.
OTA covers JS, styling and images; native code, permissions and SDK upgrades need a new binary, and feature changes need App Review.
Since SDK 55, `eas update` needs `--environment`.

gotchas.trap: Keeping the `appVersion` policy and adding a native module without bumping `version`.
gotchas.correct: Old builds share the runtime version and download JS that calls missing native code. Bump the version, or use the `fingerprint` policy.

gotchas.trap: Deleting a bad update and expecting clients to fall back.
gotchas.correct: Use `eas update:rollback` (or roll back to embedded) so clients receive a newer instruction.

gotchas.trap: Treating "it's only JavaScript" as proof that any OTA change is allowed.
gotchas.correct: Apple's 2.5.2 and 2.5.19 and DPLA 3.3.1(B) limit what downloaded code may change. New features go through review.

lessons.lab: Set `runtimeVersion: { policy: "fingerprint" }`, build a preview binary on channel `preview`, and publish a text change with `eas update --branch preview --environment preview -m "copy fix"`. Relaunch twice and note when it appears. Then add a native library, run `eas fingerprint:compare`, and confirm the runtime version changed.

lessons.title: Submitting to the App Store and Google Play
lessons.summary: Beta channels on both stores, gradual production releases, and the review guidelines that most often send a build back.

sections.heading: Submitting with EAS Submit
sections.body:
`eas submit` uploads a binary. Pass `--latest`, `--id` or `--path` to choose which one, or run `eas build --auto-submit` (`-s`). Submit profiles in eas.json hold store settings:

- **iOS:** `ascAppId` and `appleId`.
- **Android:** `serviceAccountKeyPath`, `track` (`internal`, `alpha`, `beta`, `production`), `releaseStatus` (`completed`, `draft`, `halted`, `inProgress`) and `rollout` (0 to 1, only with `inProgress`).

Both stores also set platform floors. Since 2026-04-28, Apple requires builds made with Xcode 26 and the iOS 26 SDK. Since 2026-08-31, Google Play requires new apps and updates to target API 36. Check the live requirement pages before each release.

sections.heading: Beta testing: TestFlight and Play tracks
sections.body:
**TestFlight**
- Internal testers: up to 100 people who hold certain roles on your App Store Connect team.
- External testers: up to 10,000, invited by email or through a public link.
- The first build you send to external testers needs TestFlight App Review approval. Later builds are "automatically sent for review once they're added to a group".

**Google Play tracks**
- Internal: up to 100 testers. Builds are available "within minutes" and "might not be subject to standard Play policy or security reviews".
- Closed: email lists of up to 2,000 people, or Google Groups.
- Open: anyone can join, or you set a limit of at least 1,000.

A **new personal developer account** (created after 2023-11-13) must run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days before it can apply for production access. Plan that into the first launch date.

sections.heading: Gradual production releases
sections.body:
**Apple phased release** spreads an update over 7 days: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, then 100%. It applies only to users with **automatic updates** on. Anyone can still download the new version manually from the App Store at any time. You can pause for up to 30 days in total.

**Google Play staged rollout** goes to the percentage you choose, and it "won't increase automatically". Halting stops new users from receiving that version, but users who already have it keep it. Resuming targets the same users. To fix a bad release, roll out a new release with a fixed bundle. You can't remove countries after a staged rollout starts.

Neither mechanism lets you take a binary back from users who have it. For a JS-only fault, EAS Update rollback is often faster; for native faults, ship a fixed build.

sections.heading: Review guidelines that commonly cause rejection
sections.body:
| Guideline | What reviewers check |
|---|---|
| 2.1(a) | Complete app. Provide a working demo account "(and turn on your back-end service!)" |
| 2.3.1(a) | New features described "with specificity in the Notes for Review" |
| 2.5.2 / 2.5.19 | No downloaded code that adds features; no hidden or dormant features |
| 3.1.1 | In-app purchase to unlock digital features |
| 4.2 | More than "a repackaged website" |
| 4.2.3(ii) | Tell users before a large download at first launch |
| 4.8 | Login service requirements when you use third-party login |
| 5.1.1(v) | In-app account deletion if you support account creation |

Cite these by section number from the live guidelines page; Apple updated it on 2026-10-16.

keyPoints: TestFlight: up to 100 internal and up to 10,000 external testers; the first external build needs TestFlight review.
Play internal testing reaches up to 100 testers within minutes; closed tracks use email lists or Google Groups.
New personal Play accounts need 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days in a closed test before production.
Apple phased release affects automatic updates only; manual downloads are always possible.
Play staged rollouts never advance on their own, and halting does not remove the version from users who have it.
A missing or broken demo account (2.1) is an avoidable rejection.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a 1% phased release means only 1% of users can get the version.
gotchas.correct: Phased release limits automatic updates. Anyone can download the update manually from the App Store.

gotchas.trap: Halting a Play staged rollout to "recall" a crashing build.
gotchas.correct: Halting only stops new users from getting it. Roll out a new release with a fixed bundle.

gotchas.trap: Planning a production launch the week a new personal Play account is created.
gotchas.correct: Budget at least 14 days of a closed test with 12 opted-in testers first.

lessons.lab: Write a release checklist for one version: the TestFlight group and Play track for beta, the Notes for Review text, a demo account with the backend running, the phased release and staged rollout percentages, and the trigger that makes you halt.

lessons.title: Store privacy requirements: manifests, labels, data safety and account deletion
lessons.summary: What Apple and Google require you to declare about data, where an Expo app declares it, and what account deletion must look like on each store.

sections.heading: Apple privacy manifests
App Store privacy details
sections.body:
The privacy "nutrition label" on your App Store page is filled in App Store Connect:

- Declare all data that you **or third-party partners** (analytics, ads, crash SDKs) collect, unless every optional-disclosure criterion applies.
- For each data type, say whether it is linked to the user and whether it is used for **tracking**. Tracking means linking your app's data with third-party data for targeted ads or ad measurement, or sharing it with a data broker.
- You can update the label without shipping a new app version.

sections.heading: Google Play data safety
sections.body:
Every published app needs a Data safety form, including apps on closed, open and production tracks. Only internal-test-only apps are exempt.

- **Collected** means transmitted off the device. Data processed only on the device is not collected.
- Transfers to a **service provider** that processes data for you are not "sharing".
- Ephemeral processing still has to be declared.
- The form asks about encryption in transit and whether users can request deletion. Automatic deletion within 90 days qualifies.
- You are responsible for what your **SDKs** collect.
- Google doesn't verify declarations before publishing, but a mismatch with app behavior can lead to enforcement.

sections.heading: Account deletion on both stores
sections.body:
**Apple (5.1.1(v))**
- If users can create an account in the app, they must be able to start deleting it **in the app**, and the option must be easy to find.
- Delete the account record and its data. "Only offering to temporarily deactivate or disable an account is insufficient."
- If you offer Sign in with Apple, revoke the user's tokens through the Sign in with Apple REST API.
- Outside highly regulated industries, don't make users phone or email you to finish.
- Tell users that subscriptions billed through Apple continue until they cancel them.

**Google Play**
- If your app lets users create an account anywhere, you need an in-app deletion path **and** a web link where users can request deletion without reinstalling. That link goes in the Data safety form.

keyPoints: Declare required-reason API usage in `ios.privacyManifests`; copy reasons from static CocoaPods dependencies when Apple misses them.
App Store privacy labels cover data collected by you and by third-party SDKs, including whether it is linked or used for tracking.
Play's Data safety form is required for every published app except internal-only ones; you answer for your SDKs.
Apple: in-app, easy-to-find, full deletion; deactivation alone is not enough; revoke Sign in with Apple tokens.
Google Play: in-app deletion plus a web deletion link listed in Data safety.

gotchas.trap: Leaving an analytics SDK out of the privacy label because your own code never reads that data.
gotchas.correct: Both Apple and Google hold you responsible for data your third-party SDKs collect.

gotchas.trap: Offering "Deactivate account" as the deletion feature.
gotchas.correct: Apple says deactivation alone is insufficient; the account and its data must be deleted.

gotchas.trap: Providing account deletion only on a website for the Play listing.
gotchas.correct: Google requires both an in-app path and a web link.

lessons.lab: Inventory every SDK in a sample app and list what each sends off the device. Draft the App Store privacy details and the Play Data safety answers from that list, then add an `ios.privacyManifests` entry for any required-reason API it uses.

lessons.title: CI for mobile with EAS Workflows
lessons.summary: Automating builds on merge, previews for pull requests, and a versioning strategy that holds up when several pipelines build at once.

sections.heading: Workflow files and triggers
sections.body:
EAS Workflows are YAML files in `.eas/workflows/`. The top-level keys are `name`, `run_name`, `on`, `jobs`, `defaults` and `concurrency`. Triggers include `on.push.branches` and `on.pull_request.branches`. Both take globs, and `!` excludes a pattern.

Jobs have a `type`. Useful ones here: `build`, `submit`, `update`, `update-rollout`, `fingerprint`, `get-build`, `testflight`, `maestro`, `github-comment` and `require-approval`. Ordering keys:

- `needs`: run after these jobs, and only if they succeeded.
- `after`: run after these jobs whatever their result.
- `if`: a condition.

A job reads earlier outputs as `needs.<job_id>.outputs.<name>`.

sections.heading: Build on merge, update when you can
sections.body:
A native build is slow, and most merges only change JavaScript. The docs suggest combining `fingerprint`, `get-build` and `update` jobs "to skip redundant native builds":

1. `fingerprint` computes `android_fingerprint_hash` and `ios_fingerprint_hash`.
2. `get-build` looks for an existing build with that `fingerprint_hash` and outputs its `build_id`.
3. If a compatible build exists, run an `update` job. If not, run `build`.

A sketch of the shape (a composition for illustration, not an Expo example; check the syntax reference for exact parameters):

```yaml
name: Main
on:
  push:
    branches: ['main']
jobs:
  build_android:
    type: build
    params:
      platform: android
      profile: production
```

The `build` job's `profile` defaults to production. An `update` job takes `branch` or `channel` (not both), plus `platform`, `message` and `rollout_percentage`.

sections.heading: Previews for pull requests
sections.body:
For a PR, testers want to see the change on a device without waiting for a store build. Two common patterns:

- **Update preview.** On `pull_request`, publish an `update` to a branch named for the PR and post how to open it with `github-comment`. Testers open it in a development or preview build with a matching runtime version. This is fast and works only for JS-level changes.
- **Preview build.** When the fingerprint changed, run a `build` with an internal-distribution profile so testers can install it directly.

Clean up PR branches when the PR closes (there is a `branch-delete` job type).

sections.heading: A versioning strategy that survives CI
sections.body:
- Set `cli.appVersionSource: "remote"` and `autoIncrement: true` on store profiles. EAS then issues build numbers, so parallel runners never collide.
- Change the user-facing `version` deliberately, in a commit, when you cut a release.
- Use the `fingerprint` runtime policy so CI never publishes an update to builds whose native code differs.
- Pass `--environment` to every `eas update` (required since SDK 55).

keyPoints: Workflows live in `.eas/workflows/*.yml` and trigger on push or pull_request branch globs.
`needs` requires success; `after` runs regardless; outputs are read as `needs.<id>.outputs.<name>`.
Combine fingerprint, get-build and update jobs to skip native builds when only JS changed.
PR previews: publish an update for JS-only changes; build an internal binary when the fingerprint changes.
Remote version source plus autoIncrement keeps build numbers unique across parallel CI runs.

gotchas.trap: Running a full native store build for every merge, including copy changes.
gotchas.correct: Check the fingerprint first and publish an update when a compatible build already exists.

gotchas.trap: Setting both `branch` and `channel` on an `update` job.
gotchas.correct: Use one or the other.

gotchas.trap: Using `after` for a submit job that should only run when the build passed.
gotchas.correct: `after` runs regardless of outcome. Use `needs`.

lessons.lab: Create `.eas/workflows/pr-preview.yml` that runs on `pull_request` to `main`, publishes an update to a PR-specific branch and posts a GitHub comment. Then sketch the main-branch workflow that uses fingerprint and get-build to choose between `update` and `build`.

lessons.title: The mobile testing pyramid: Jest, RNTL and Maestro
lessons.summary: Most confidence on mobile comes from fast Jest and React Native Testing Library tests of logic and components. A small set of end-to-end flows on a real build, run with Maestro (or Detox), guards the critical paths.

sections.heading: Why the pyramid matters more on mobile
sections.body:
End-to-end tests on mobile are expensive: every run needs a **compiled app binary**, a simulator or emulator (or a device), and time to boot and drive the UI. They are also the layer most prone to flakiness from animations, network timing and OS dialogs.

So the shape that works is the classic pyramid:

- **Many unit tests** for pure logic: formatting, validation schemas, reducers, sync and retry rules.
- **A healthy layer of component tests** with React Native Testing Library (RNTL), rendering screens and components in Jest and asserting what the user sees.
- **A few end-to-end flows** on a real build for the paths that must never break: sign-in, onboarding to the first core action, purchase or checkout.

If a bug can be caught by a Jest test, catch it there. Use E2E for what only E2E can prove: that the built app launches, navigates and talks to native modules correctly.

sections.heading: Unit and component tests with jest-expo and RNTL
End-to-end flows with Maestro or Detox
sections.body:
Maestro flows are YAML files that drive the real app:

```yaml
appId: com.example.app
---
- launchApp
- assertVisible: 'Welcome!'
```

Detox is the long-standing alternative: tests are written in JavaScript and run against a build made for testing. Either way, the test targets a **built binary**, not the Metro dev server, so E2E needs its own build profile. In Expo's E2E example the profile builds an iOS **simulator** build (`ios.simulator: true`) and an Android **APK** (`android.buildType: apk`), because store formats cannot be installed directly on an emulator.

Keep flows short and focused on user outcomes. Assert on visible text or accessibility labels, and avoid sleeping for fixed times when the tool can wait for an element.

sections.heading: Running E2E in CI with EAS Workflows
sections.body:
EAS Workflows has a `maestro` job type. It takes the `build_id` produced by an earlier build job and a `flow_path` list. A sketch based on Expo's E2E example (check the docs for exact keys):

```yaml
jobs:
  build_android_e2e:
    type: build
    params:
      platform: android
      profile: e2e-test
  maestro_android:
    needs: [build_android_e2e]
    type: maestro
    params:
      build_id: ${{ needs.build_android_e2e.outputs.build_id }}
      flow_path: ['.maestro/home.yaml']
```

A practical split: Jest and RNTL on every pull request (fast, no build), and the Maestro job on merges to the main branch or on release candidates, where paying for a build is worth it.

keyPoints: Mobile E2E needs a compiled build and a simulator or device, so keep it to a few critical flows.
Use the jest-expo preset; it mocks native Expo modules so tests run in Node.
RNTL tests query what the user sees (text, accessibility info), not component internals.
transformIgnorePatterns is a regex controlling which node_modules packages Jest skips transforming.
Maestro flows are YAML (appId, ---, launchApp, assertVisible); Detox is the JS-based alternative.
Expo's E2E profile uses ios.simulator: true and android.buildType: apk.
EAS Workflows runs Maestro with a maestro job fed the build_id of an earlier build job.

gotchas.trap: Cover every validation branch of a form with E2E flows.
gotchas.correct: Test validation rules in Jest (unit or RNTL); keep E2E for a handful of critical user journeys.

gotchas.trap: Point E2E tests at the Metro dev server or Expo Go.
gotchas.correct: Run E2E against a dedicated test build (simulator build on iOS, APK on Android).

gotchas.trap: Assert on component state or implementation details in RNTL tests.
gotchas.correct: Query by visible text or accessibility information, the way a user finds things.

lessons.lab: In an Expo app, add the jest-expo preset and RNTL, then write one component test that renders your home screen and asserts the welcome text. Add a Maestro flow that launches the app and asserts the same text, add an e2e-test build profile with ios.simulator: true and android.buildType: apk, and wire a build job plus a maestro job in an EAS workflow that runs on pushes to main.

lessons.title: Mobile security with OWASP MASVS
lessons.summary: OWASP MASVS gives a checklist of 24 controls in 8 groups. For an Expo team the big ones are: nothing secret ships in the bundle, tokens go in SecureStore, traffic is protected and pinned only where you control the endpoint, and the server, not jailbreak detection, enforces what users may do.

sections.heading: The MASVS map
sections.body:
The OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) v2 has **8 control groups and 24 controls**:

| Group | What it asks |
|---|---|
| MASVS-STORAGE | Store sensitive data securely; prevent its leakage |
| MASVS-CRYPTO | Strong, current cryptography and proper key management |
| MASVS-AUTH | Secure auth protocols, secure local auth, extra auth for sensitive operations |
| MASVS-NETWORK | Secure all traffic; identity pinning for endpoints you control |
| MASVS-PLATFORM | Secure IPC, WebViews and UI |
| MASVS-CODE | Up-to-date platform, an update-enforcement mechanism, no vulnerable components, input validation |
| MASVS-RESILIENCE | Platform integrity, anti-tampering, anti-static and anti-dynamic analysis |
| MASVS-PRIVACY | Minimize access, prevent identification, be transparent, give user control |

Use it as a review checklist: for each group, write down what your app does and where the evidence is.

sections.heading: Secrets never ship in the bundle
sections.body:
Everything in your client code is readable by anyone who installs the app. Expo is explicit: `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` variables are inlined into the JavaScript as **plain text**, and anything in client code "should be considered public and readable to any individual that can run your app". App config (`app.json` / `app.config.ts`) must not hold secrets either, because it is embedded in the build.

Bytecode compilation or obfuscation does not change this; it only slows a determined reader down.

What to do instead:

- **Third-party API keys with real power** (payments, LLM providers, admin APIs): call them from **your backend**, which holds the key and enforces per-user auth and rate limits.
- **Build-time secrets** (for example a Sentry auth token used to upload source maps): store them as EAS environment variables with an appropriate visibility, used by the build, never read by app code.
- **Keys designed to be public** (for example a publishable or client-side key whose provider expects it to ship) are fine in `EXPO_PUBLIC_*`, as long as the provider restricts what they can do.

sections.heading: Secure storage for tokens
sections.body:
MASVS-STORAGE-1: "The app securely stores sensitive data." In Expo, refresh tokens and similar credentials belong in **expo-secure-store**, not AsyncStorage (which is unencrypted):

- iOS stores values in the **Keychain**; Android stores them in SharedPreferences "encrypted with Android's Keystore system".
- The default `keychainAccessible` is `WHEN_UNLOCKED`. The `*_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY` variants do not migrate to a new device through backup.
- Values saved with `requireAuthentication` become inaccessible if the user's biometrics change, so design a re-login path.
- On iOS data may survive an uninstall (not guaranteed); on Android it does not. Do not rely on either behavior.

MASVS-STORAGE-2 ("prevents leakage of sensitive data") is the other half: keep tokens and personal data out of logs, analytics events and crash report payloads.

sections.heading: Network security and certificate pinning
sections.body:
MASVS-NETWORK-1 asks the app to secure all traffic with current best practices (TLS everywhere, no cleartext exceptions you cannot justify). MASVS-NETWORK-2 says the app "performs identity pinning for all remote endpoints **under the developer's control**".

Pinning means the app accepts only specific certificates or public keys for your API, which blocks interception by a proxy with a user-installed CA. Its operational risk is real: if the server's key changes and the app has no matching pin, **every installed copy loses connectivity** until users install a new binary. So:

- Pin only domains you control, not third-party CDNs or SDK endpoints whose certificates you do not manage.
- Pin public keys (Android pins are SHA-256 hashes of the certificate's `SubjectPublicKeyInfo`) rather than a single leaf certificate, and include a **backup pin**: Android's docs say to "always include a backup key", otherwise "you must push out an update to the app to restore connectivity".
- Plan rotation before you ship. When pins live in native configuration (such as Android's Network Security Configuration), changing them needs a new build, not an OTA update.

sections.heading: Jailbreak and root realities
sections.body:
MASVS-RESILIENCE-1 asks the app to validate "the integrity of the platform", and the other RESILIENCE controls cover anti-tampering and anti-analysis. These are **defense in depth**. On a device the attacker controls, any client-side check (jailbreak or root detection included) can be patched, hooked or skipped.

Practical consequences:

- The **server** enforces authorization, entitlements, prices and limits. Never trust a flag the client sends ("isPremium": true).
- Detection is useful to raise cost, add friction or adjust risk scoring, not as the sole control.
- Blocking rooted users outright also blocks legitimate power users; decide based on your threat model (banking and DRM differ from a to-do app).

keyPoints: MASVS v2: 8 groups, 24 controls (STORAGE, CRYPTO, AUTH, NETWORK, PLATFORM, CODE, RESILIENCE, PRIVACY).
EXPO_PUBLIC_* values and app config are plain text in the app; treat them as public.
Powerful third-party keys live on your backend; the app calls your API.
Tokens go in expo-secure-store (Keychain / Keystore-encrypted), not AsyncStorage.
Pin identity only for endpoints you control, with a backup pin and a rotation plan.
Jailbreak/root detection is defense in depth; the server enforces entitlements.

gotchas.trap: Hermes bytecode or obfuscation makes an embedded API key safe.
gotchas.correct: Anything in the bundle is readable; move privileged keys behind your own backend.

gotchas.trap: Store the refresh token in AsyncStorage because it is simpler.
gotchas.correct: Use expo-secure-store; AsyncStorage is unencrypted.

gotchas.trap: Pin the certificates of every host the app talks to, including third-party SDKs.
gotchas.correct: MASVS-NETWORK-2 scopes pinning to endpoints under your control.

gotchas.trap: Gate premium features with a client-side jailbreak check.
gotchas.correct: Enforce entitlements on the server; client checks are bypassable.

lessons.title: Crash monitoring, release health and staged rollouts
lessons.summary: Ship to a small slice first, watch crash and error signals tagged by release and update, and know the exact stop button for each channel: Apple phased release, Google Play staged rollout and EAS Update percentage rollouts.

sections.heading: Crash reporting that points at real code
sections.body:
A crash report is only useful if the stack trace maps back to your source. With Sentry in an Expo app:

- Set it up with `npx @sentry/wizard@latest -i reactNative`.
- **EAS Build** uploads source maps automatically when `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` is set (store it as a sensitive EAS environment variable).
- **EAS Update** bundles need their own upload: run `npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist` after `eas update`. Skip this and errors from OTA updates show minified frames.
- Tag events with the running update: `scope.setTag('expo-update-id', Updates.updateId)`. Then a spike can be traced to one OTA update, not just to a store version.

Other analytics can carry the same key; the SDK 58 changelog notes PostHog events can include `eas/update_id`. Expo also announced its own observability features in 2026; check the changelog for current status.

sections.heading: Three release layers, three rollout controls
sections.body:
| Channel | How the rollout works | How to stop |
|---|---|---|
| **Apple phased release** | Automatic updates go to 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% over 7 days | Pause (up to 30 days in total). Applies to **automatic updates only**: anyone can manually download the new version from the App Store at any time |
| **Google Play staged rollout** | You choose the percentage; it **won't increase automatically** | Halt: new users stop getting it, but users who already have it **keep it**. For a bad release, roll out a new release with a fixed bundle |
| **EAS Update rollout** | `eas update --rollout-percentage=10`, raise with `eas update:edit` | `eas update:revert-update-rollout`; or `eas update:rollback` to republish an earlier update or send clients back to the embedded one |

Notes that catch people out:

- On Play, countries cannot be removed once a staged rollout starts.
- For EAS Update, "only one rollout can be in progress for a given branch, platform, and runtime version".
- `eas update:rollback` does **not delete** the bad update; it publishes an instruction that supersedes it.
- An OTA update normally applies on the **next** launch (`fallbackToCacheTimeout` defaults to 0), so watch metrics over a day of launches, not minutes.

sections.heading: A release-health routine
sections.body:
1. Release to a small slice (phased, staged or rollout percentage).
2. Watch crash and error rates **for that release or update ID** against the previous one, plus the key business events (sign-in success, checkout completion).
3. Decide with a pre-agreed threshold: expand, hold, or stop.
4. To stop: pause or halt the store rollout, or revert the OTA rollout. Remember that a store halt does not remove the build from users who already have it, so the fix is a new release (or an OTA fix if the bug is in JavaScript and within OTA rules).

The OTA layer is the fastest fix path for JavaScript bugs, but it can only change "non-native pieces (such as JS, styling, and images)", and updates must still follow the store guidelines.

keyPoints: Upload source maps for both EAS Build (SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN) and EAS Update (sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps after eas update).
Tag crash events with Updates.updateId so problems map to one OTA update.
Apple phased release: 7 days, 1% to 100%, automatic updates only, pausable.
Play staged rollout: manual percentage; halting does not remove the release from users who have it.
EAS Update: --rollout-percentage, update:edit, revert-update-rollout; one active rollout per branch, platform and runtime version.
eas update:rollback does not delete the bad update.

gotchas.trap: Halting a Play staged rollout rolls affected users back to the previous version.
gotchas.correct: Halting only stops new users getting it; ship a fixed release to the affected users.

gotchas.trap: Apple's phased release keeps the new version away from everyone outside the current percentage.
gotchas.correct: It only paces automatic updates; anyone can download it manually.

gotchas.trap: Source maps from the store build also symbolicate OTA update crashes.
gotchas.correct: Each EAS Update bundle needs its own source map upload.

lessons.lab: Add Sentry to an Expo app with the wizard, set SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN as an EAS environment variable, and tag events with expo-update-id. Publish an update with --rollout-percentage=10, throw a test error from it, confirm the event is tagged with the new update ID and symbolicated, then revert the rollout with eas update:revert-update-rollout.

lessons.title: Supporting old versions and choosing app, PWA or web
lessons.summary: Mobile users stay on old binaries for months, so APIs must stay backward compatible, the app needs a way to enforce a minimum version, and feature flags must respect store review rules. Before any of this, decide whether you need a native app at all.

sections.heading: Old binaries never fully go away
sections.body:
Unlike a website, you cannot redeploy every client. Users skip updates, turn off automatic updates, or sit on old OS versions. Design for it:

- **Additive API changes by default.** Add fields and endpoints; do not rename or remove fields old clients read. When a breaking change is unavoidable, version the endpoint (for example a new path or version header) and keep the old version until usage drops.
- **Send the app version with every request** (and the OTA update ID) so the backend can measure who is on what and make version-aware decisions.
- **Retire on data, not dates.** Remove an old API version once monitoring shows its traffic is negligible, or after you have enforced a newer minimum version.

sections.heading: Forced-update mechanisms
Feature flags and kill switches
sections.body:
Remote flags let you turn a feature on for a percentage of users, or off instantly if it misbehaves, without a new binary. They pair well with staged rollouts.

There is a store-policy boundary. Apple's App Review Guidelines prohibit "hidden, dormant, or undocumented features" (2.5.19, clarified in the 2026-10-16 update to include changing features after approval), and 2.3.1(a) says new features must be described in the Notes for Review. So:

- **Fine:** gradual exposure or a kill switch for a feature that was in the reviewed build and described to App Review.
- **Not fine:** shipping a dormant feature hidden behind a flag to switch on after approval.

The same reasoning applies to OTA updates, which also must follow store guidelines.

sections.heading: App, PWA or responsive web?
sections.body:
For a small team, every platform you ship is ongoing cost. Ask what the product truly needs:

- **Responsive web app:** content, dashboards, forms and occasional use. One codebase, instant deploys, no review.
- **PWA:** a web app that can be installed and work offline. Know the iOS limits from web.dev: there is **no install prompt** (users must use Share > Add to Home Screen), iOS PWAs "lack support for capabilities such as badging and app shortcuts", each installation has **isolated storage**, and install criteria vary by browser.
- **Native app (Expo):** reliable push notifications, background work, camera, location, biometrics and secure storage, store discovery, or in-app purchases.

If you do go native, it must be more than a wrapped website: App Review 4.2 rejects apps that are only "a repackaged website". Expo can also target the web from the same codebase, which narrows the cost gap.

keyPoints: Prefer additive API changes; version endpoints for unavoidable breaking changes.
Send the app version and update ID with requests so you can measure old-version traffic.
MASVS-CODE-2: have a way to enforce updates.
Android: Play In-App Updates (flexible or immediate). iOS: your own minimum-version check against your backend.
Feature flags may gate reviewed features; dormant hidden features violate App Review 2.5.19.
iOS PWAs: no install prompt, no badging or app shortcuts, isolated storage per installation.
App Review 4.2 rejects apps that are only a repackaged website.

gotchas.trap: Rename an API field and ship the matching app update the same day.
gotchas.correct: Old binaries keep calling the API for months; add the new field and keep the old one.

gotchas.trap: Use an OTA update to force users onto a build with a new native module.
gotchas.correct: Native changes need a new binary; enforce it with a minimum-version check or Play In-App Updates.

gotchas.trap: Ship an unreviewed feature dormant behind a flag and enable it after approval.
gotchas.correct: Describe features to App Review; use flags for gradual exposure and kill switches.

gotchas.trap: Expect iOS to show an install banner for your PWA.
gotchas.correct: iOS has no install prompt; users add it via Share > Add to Home Screen.

lessons.lab: Add a /app-config endpoint to your backend that returns minSupportedVersion. In the app, compare it with the running version on launch, show a blocking screen with a store link when below, and fail open on network errors. On Android, wire the immediate Play In-App Updates flow for the same condition. Then list every API field your current app reads and mark which ones a planned backend change would break.

flashcards.front: What did JSI replace in React Native's New Architecture?
flashcards.back: The asynchronous bridge. JSI lets JavaScript hold references to C++ objects (and vice versa) and call them directly.

flashcards.front: What are Fabric and Turbo Modules?
flashcards.back: Fabric is the New Architecture renderer that turns the React tree into native views; Turbo Modules are the native module system. Both are built on JSI.

flashcards.front: From which React Native version is the New Architecture the only architecture?
flashcards.back: RN 0.82. Setting newArchEnabled=false is ignored there. Expo SDK 55 removed newArchEnabled from app.json.

flashcards.front: Which JavaScript engine is the default in current React Native and Expo?
flashcards.back: Hermes V1 (default in RN 0.84 and Expo SDK 56).

flashcards.front: How do you avoid a one-frame jump when positioning an overlay based on a measured view?
flashcards.back: Measure in useLayoutEffect and update state in the same commit; the New Architecture supports synchronous layout reads.

flashcards.front: Expo Modules API or Turbo Modules: when do you pick Turbo Modules?
flashcards.back: When you need C++. Both use JSI and Expo documents comparable performance.

flashcards.front: What is a development build?
flashcards.back: "Your own version of Expo Go": a debug build of your app with expo-dev-client that can include any native libraries and native configuration.

flashcards.front: Name three changes that require rebuilding a development build.
flashcards.back: Adding or upgrading a library with native code, changing native app config (permissions, plugins), and upgrading the Expo SDK.

flashcards.front: Which Expo SDK versions does Expo Go support?
flashcards.back: Only the latest SDK version.

flashcards.front: What is Continuous Native Generation (CNG)?
flashcards.back: Generating the ios/ and android/ projects from app config and package.json with npx expo prebuild, only when needed; the folders are gitignored by default.

flashcards.front: When does EAS Build skip prebuild?
flashcards.back: When the native directories (ios/, android/) already exist in the project.

flashcards.front: What is a config plugin, and when do its mods run?
flashcards.back: A synchronous with<Feature> function that modifies native projects; its mods are evaluated only during npx expo prebuild.

flashcards.front: How do you pass options to a config plugin?
flashcards.back: As the second element of its entry in the plugins array, e.g. ["my-plugin", { "option": true }].

flashcards.front: List the React Native Flexbox defaults that differ from the web.
flashcards.back: flexDirection column (not row), alignContent flex-start (not stretch), flexShrink 0 (not 1), and flex accepts a single number only.

flashcards.front: Why does long Text push its siblings off screen in a row?
flashcards.back: flexShrink defaults to 0 in React Native, so items do not shrink. Set flexShrink: 1 (or flex: 1) on the text container.

flashcards.front: What must a remote Image have to be visible?
flashcards.back: Explicit dimensions (width and height); network and data images are not sized automatically.

flashcards.front: Where can raw strings be rendered in React Native?
flashcards.back: Only inside a Text component. Nested Text inherits styles; View does not pass text styles down.

flashcards.front: How does Pressable support pressed feedback and a larger touch area?
flashcards.back: style (and children) can be a function of { pressed }; hitSlop extends the touch area beyond the visual bounds.

flashcards.front: How do platform file extensions work?
flashcards.back: Create Name.ios.tsx and Name.android.tsx (or Name.native.tsx for non-web) and import ./Name; the bundler resolves the right file.

flashcards.front: What type is Platform.Version on each platform?
flashcards.back: A number (the API level) on Android and a string on iOS.

flashcards.front: Which app config file wins if app.json and app.config.ts both exist?
flashcards.back: app.config.ts (then app.config.js, then app.json). A dynamic config receives ({ config }) and returns an ExpoConfig.

flashcards.front: How is the extra field of app config read at runtime, and is it private?
flashcards.back: Through Constants.expoConfig.extra. It is public; never put secrets in app config. npx expo config --type public shows what is embedded.

flashcards.front: Why does const { EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL } = process.env not work?
flashcards.back: EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined only when statically referenced as process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL.

flashcards.front: What does EAS "secret" visibility protect?
flashcards.back: The value is not readable outside Expo's servers during builds. It does not protect values you embed in the app bundle.

flashcards.front: What changed about NODE_ENV in Expo SDK 58?
flashcards.back: Each command sets NODE_ENV to its own mode and replaces your value; NODE_ENV=test npx expo start loads .env.development, and files like .env.staging are not loaded.

flashcards.front: What does the Strict TypeScript API (default in SDK 58) reject?
flashcards.back: Deep imports from react-native/Libraries/*; import from the public react-native entry point instead.

flashcards.front: What do error boundaries not catch?
flashcards.back: Errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (promises, timers) and the boundary itself; only rendering errors are caught.

flashcards.front: Which tool debugs a crash inside native Swift or Kotlin code?
flashcards.back: Xcode or Android Studio. React Native DevTools targets React app concerns and does not replace native tools.

flashcards.front: How do you get readable Sentry stack traces for an EAS Update?
flashcards.back: Run npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist after eas update, and tag events with Updates.updateId.

flashcards.front: expo-router: what does a folder named (auth) do to the URL?
flashcards.back: Nothing. Parenthesised groups organise files and can share a layout but add no URL segment, so (auth)/sign-in.tsx is /sign-in.

flashcards.front: expo-router: what is _layout.tsx?
flashcards.back: A layout that wraps the routes beside it (for example a Stack or Tabs navigator). It is not a page itself.

flashcards.front: router.navigate vs router.push vs router.replace
flashcards.back: navigate pushes or unwinds to the route if it is already in the stack (the usual choice); push always adds an entry; replace swaps the current screen.

flashcards.front: How do you make a custom Pressable act as an expo-router Link?
flashcards.back: Wrap it in <Link href=... asChild>. Without asChild, Link wraps its children in <Text>.

flashcards.front: useLocalSearchParams vs useGlobalSearchParams
flashcards.back: Local updates only for the focused route; global updates even when the route is not focused, re-rendering background screens. Use global for things like analytics.

flashcards.front: When does a useFocusEffect cleanup run?
flashcards.back: When the screen loses focus, not when it unmounts.

flashcards.front: What happens when a Stack.Protected guard becomes false?
flashcards.back: Users on those screens are redirected and the screens' history entries are removed, so Back cannot return to them.

flashcards.front: Do protected routes secure your API?
flashcards.back: No. The docs say protected screens are not a replacement for server-side authentication or access control.

flashcards.front: How do you present a route as a sheet with detents?
flashcards.back: presentation: 'formSheet' with sheetAllowedDetents (ascending fractions 0 to 1, or 'fitToContents') and optionally sheetInitialDetentIndex.

flashcards.front: Correct form of an iOS associatedDomains entry
flashcards.back: "applinks:example.com", with no https:// scheme. The AASA file is served over HTTPS at /.well-known/apple-app-site-association.

flashcards.front: Which fingerprint goes in assetlinks.json for an EAS / Play build?
flashcards.back: The release signing certificate's SHA-256: from eas credentials -p android, or Play Console App Signing "Digital Asset Links JSON".

flashcards.front: TanStack Query default staleTime and gcTime
flashcards.back: staleTime 0 (stale immediately); gcTime 5 minutes for inactive cache entries.

flashcards.front: When do stale TanStack queries refetch by default?
flashcards.back: On mount of a new instance, on window focus and on network reconnect. Failed queries retry 3 times with exponential backoff.

flashcards.front: How does TanStack Query learn about app focus in React Native?
flashcards.back: Call focusManager.setFocused(status === 'active') from an AppState change listener (skip on web).

flashcards.front: How does TanStack Query learn about connectivity in React Native?
flashcards.back: onlineManager.setEventListener wired to NetInfo (or expo-network), calling setOnline with the connection state.

flashcards.front: Four steps of an optimistic update in onMutate
flashcards.back: cancelQueries for the key, snapshot with getQueryData, write with setQueryData, return the snapshot. Restore it in onError; invalidate in onSettled.

flashcards.front: useInfiniteQuery: how do you signal there are no more pages?
flashcards.back: Return undefined (or null) from getNextPageParam; hasNextPage becomes false.

flashcards.front: Is AsyncStorage encrypted?
flashcards.back: No. It is an unencrypted async key-value store, fine for preferences, not for tokens or secrets.

flashcards.front: SecureStore backing stores and default accessibility
flashcards.back: iOS Keychain; Android SharedPreferences encrypted with the Keystore. Default keychainAccessible is WHEN_UNLOCKED; *_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY prevents migration via backup.

flashcards.front: What happens to a requireAuthentication SecureStore item after the user enrols a new fingerprint?
flashcards.back: It becomes inaccessible. Handle it by falling back to a full sign-in and storing a fresh value.

flashcards.front: expo-sqlite: how do you track schema migrations?
flashcards.back: Read and set PRAGMA user_version and run migrations in order (for example in SQLiteProvider onInit).

flashcards.front: expo-sqlite: is withTransactionAsync exclusive?
flashcards.back: No; other queries can interleave. withExclusiveTransactionAsync uses a separate connection, so PRAGMA foreign_keys does not apply inside it.

flashcards.front: How do you confirm SQLCipher encryption is active in expo-sqlite?
flashcards.back: Query PRAGMA cipher_version. Without SQLCipher enabled (useSQLCipher), PRAGMA key silently does nothing.

flashcards.front: What does keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled" fix?
flashcards.back: With the default "never", a tap outside the focused input inside a ScrollView only dismisses the keyboard; "handled" lets taps on buttons go through.

flashcards.front: What replaces InputAccessoryView as of React Native 0.88?
flashcards.back: It is deprecated; RN points to react-native-keyboard-controller (for example KeyboardStickyView).

flashcards.front: Zod: parse vs safeParse
flashcards.back: parse throws on invalid input; safeParse returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error }. z.flattenError(error).fieldErrors maps issues to fields.

flashcards.front: How do you resume persisted TanStack mutations after an app restart?
flashcards.back: Register setMutationDefaults with a mutationFn per mutation key, restore the cache, then call resumePausedMutations.

flashcards.front: TanStack mutation scope.id
flashcards.back: Mutations sharing the same scope id run in serial, one after another.

flashcards.front: How does If-Match prevent lost updates?
flashcards.back: The client sends the version (ETag) it edited; if the server copy has changed, the server responds 412 Precondition Failed instead of overwriting.

flashcards.front: Why attach an idempotency key to a queued create?
flashcards.back: If the request reached the server but the response was lost, the retry carries the same key, so the server returns the first result instead of creating a duplicate.

flashcards.front: Where does an iOS permission purpose string go in an Expo app?
flashcards.back: In ios.infoPlist (for example NSCameraUsageDescription) or through a library config plugin prop such as expo-media-library photosPermission.

flashcards.front: How do you remove an Android permission that a dependency adds?
flashcards.back: List its full name in android.blockedPermissions, for example android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO.

flashcards.front: Can a changed permission purpose string ship via EAS Update?
flashcards.back: No. Info.plist changes cannot be updated over-the-air; you need a new build.

flashcards.front: What should the app do when a permission response has canAskAgain false?
flashcards.back: Explain the impact, offer Linking.openSettings(), and re-check the status when the app returns to the foreground.

flashcards.front: When may an Android app targeting API 33+ request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES on Google Play?
flashcards.back: Only if system pickers such as the Android Photo Picker are not sufficient for core functionality, with a Play Console declaration.

flashcards.front: What does Apple 5.1.1(iii) say about Photos or Contacts access?
flashcards.back: Use the out-of-process picker or a share sheet rather than requesting full access where possible (data minimization).

flashcards.front: Android 13+: why might the notification permission prompt never appear?
flashcards.back: It does not appear until at least one notification channel has been created.

flashcards.front: What error do you get calling getExpoPushTokenAsync without a projectId?
flashcards.back: ERR_NOTIFICATIONS_NO_EXPERIENCE_ID.

flashcards.front: What does a push ticket with status ok mean?
flashcards.back: Only that Expo's servers received the message. Check receipts later for delivery errors.

flashcards.front: What should a server do on a DeviceNotRegistered receipt?
flashcards.back: Stop sending to that push token and remove it.

flashcards.front: What replaces the deprecated shouldShowAlert in setNotificationHandler?
flashcards.back: shouldShowBanner and/or shouldShowList.

flashcards.front: Which API handles a notification tap that cold-started the app?
flashcards.back: useLastNotificationResponse.

flashcards.front: Where can you test push notifications on Android?
flashcards.back: In a development build. Push is not supported in Expo Go on Android (SDK 53+, and it throws from SDK 55).

flashcards.front: What happens to an iOS background location request if the user chose "Allow Once"?
flashcards.back: It silently fails.

flashcards.front: What does Google Play require for background location access?
flashcards.back: A core feature with significant user benefit, a prominent in-app disclosure before the prompt, a declaration form, and a short video.

flashcards.front: expo-background-task: default and minimum minimumInterval?
flashcards.back: Default 12 hours; minimum 15 minutes. Runs are not exact and iOS often runs them overnight.

flashcards.front: Where must TaskManager.defineTask be called?
flashcards.back: In global (module) scope, not inside a component.

flashcards.front: RFC 8252: which user-agent and which extension must native OAuth clients use?
flashcards.back: An external user-agent (the system browser), never an embedded one, and PKCE for public clients.

flashcards.front: What happens to a SecureStore value saved with requireAuthentication when biometrics change?
flashcards.back: It becomes inaccessible; the app should clear it and ask the user to sign in again.

flashcards.front: When are config plugin mods such as withInfoPlist evaluated?
flashcards.back: Only during the syncing phase of npx expo prebuild.

flashcards.front: When should you choose a Turbo Module over the Expo Modules API?
flashcards.back: When you need to write the module in C++. Otherwise both use JSI with comparable performance.

flashcards.front: Frame budget at 60 Hz and at 120 Hz?
flashcards.back: About 16.67 ms per frame at 60 Hz and about 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Miss it and the frame is dropped.

flashcards.front: What runs on the React Native JavaScript thread?
flashcards.back: Your React components, business logic, API handling and touch event processing. When it is blocked, JS-driven animations freeze and taps feel ignored.

flashcards.front: Why can a ScrollView keep scrolling while the JS thread is blocked?
flashcards.back: Scrolling (and native stack transitions) run on the native main/UI thread, not the JS thread.

flashcards.front: How do you tell whether the JS or the UI thread is dropping frames?
flashcards.back: Enable Show Perf Monitor from the Dev Menu; it shows the JS and UI frame rates separately.

flashcards.front: Why must you profile a release build?
flashcards.back: JavaScript thread performance suffers greatly in dev mode, so dev measurements are misleading.

flashcards.front: How do you stop `console.*` calls slowing a production bundle?
flashcards.back: Add `babel-plugin-transform-remove-console` for the production environment; it also strips calls from third-party libraries.

flashcards.front: FlatList defaults for `initialNumToRender`, `maxToRenderPerBatch` and `windowSize`?
flashcards.back: 10, 10 and 21 (10 viewports above, 10 below, and the visible one).

flashcards.front: What does `getItemLayout` give FlatList?
flashcards.back: Row length and offset without measuring rendered items, for fixed-height rows. Faster rendering and accurate `scrollToIndex`.

flashcards.front: What does FlashList do differently from FlatList?
flashcards.back: It recycles row components: off-screen rows are reused with new data instead of unmounted and remounted.

flashcards.front: FlashList v2 and `estimatedItemSize`?
flashcards.back: Deprecated and no longer used; v2 measures items itself and is built for the New Architecture.

flashcards.front: Which expo-image prop prevents a recycled row from flashing the previous image?
flashcards.back: `recyclingKey`: changing it resets the view to blank or the placeholder before the new image loads.

flashcards.front: expo-image `cachePolicy` default, and what `memory-disk` adds?
flashcards.back: Default is `disk`. `memory-disk` caches in memory with a disk fallback; `memory` alone may be purged quickly.

flashcards.front: What is a Reanimated worklet?
flashcards.back: A short-running JavaScript function that can run on the UI thread, so animation frames do not wait for the JS thread.

flashcards.front: What extra package and Babel plugin does Reanimated 4 need?
flashcards.back: `react-native-worklets`, with `react-native-worklets/plugin` listed last. `babel-preset-expo` configures it automatically.

flashcards.front: Where does Gesture Handler recognise gestures?
flashcards.back: On the native thread, so recognition is deterministic and does not wait for JavaScript. Wrap the tree in `GestureHandlerRootView`.

flashcards.front: When does core `Animated` compute keyframes on the JS thread?
flashcards.back: Always, unless you set `useNativeDriver: true`.

flashcards.front: Why does Hermes improve startup?
flashcards.back: It compiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time, so the device skips parsing and compiling at launch.

flashcards.front: How do you inspect an Expo app bundle's contents?
flashcards.back: Run `EXPO_ATLAS=true npx expo export`, then `npx expo-atlas .expo/atlas.jsonl`.

flashcards.front: Which wins if both `role` and `accessibilityRole` are set?
flashcards.back: `role` takes precedence over `accessibilityRole`.

flashcards.front: Minimum touch target size on Android (and the usual iOS figure)?
flashcards.back: Android: at least 48dp x 48dp. Apple HIG has long recommended about 44 x 44 pt.

flashcards.front: Default of `allowFontScaling` on Text, and how to limit growth?
flashcards.back: True by default. Cap growth with `maxFontSizeMultiplier` rather than disabling scaling.

flashcards.front: How do you respect Reduce Motion in React Native?
flashcards.back: Read `AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled()` and subscribe to the `reduceMotionChanged` event; remove the subscription on unmount.

flashcards.front: What limits how far `hitSlop` can extend a press area?
flashcards.back: The touch area never extends past the parent view bounds, and an overlapping sibling with higher z-index wins.

flashcards.front: What are the three top-level keys in eas.json?
flashcards.back: `cli`, `build` and `submit`.

flashcards.front: What does `cli.appVersionSource: "remote"` do?
flashcards.back: EAS stores the build numbers (buildNumber / versionCode) on its servers instead of reading them from your project. The docs recommend it from EAS CLI 12.

flashcards.front: With a remote version source, what does `autoIncrement` bump?
flashcards.back: Build numbers only (iOS buildNumber, Android versionCode). You set the user-facing `version` yourself.

flashcards.front: Which values does Expo's `version` field map to on iOS and Android?
flashcards.back: `CFBundleShortVersionString` on iOS and `versionName` on Android.

flashcards.front: Which `android.buildType` lets testers sideload the build?
flashcards.back: `apk`. The other value, `app-bundle`, is the format Google Play expects.

flashcards.front: Who owns an iOS distribution certificate?
flashcards.back: The Apple developer account, not a single app, so apps on the same team can share it.

flashcards.front: How long is an iOS provisioning profile valid?
flashcards.back: 12 months.

flashcards.front: You lost your Android upload key, and the app uses Play App Signing. What now?
flashcards.back: Ask Play support to reset the upload key. The new upload certificate takes effect 72 hours later. Google keeps the app signing key.

flashcards.front: Where should a build-time secret live instead of eas.json `env`?
flashcards.back: In an EAS environment variable with secret visibility, selected by the profile's `environment` key. It still isn't safe if you embed it in the app.

flashcards.front: Which three things must line up for a build to accept an EAS update?
flashcards.back: The channel must point at the branch the update is on, and the platform and runtime version must match exactly.

flashcards.front: By default, when does a downloaded update start running?
flashcards.back: On the next launch. `fallbackToCacheTimeout` defaults to 0, so the app doesn't wait for the download.

flashcards.front: `checkForUpdateAsync()` vs `fetchUpdateAsync()` vs `reloadAsync()`
flashcards.back: check only looks and does not download; fetch downloads; reload restarts the app into the downloaded update.

flashcards.front: What does the `fingerprint` runtime version policy do?
