flashcards.back: It computes the runtime version from a hash of the native project (`@expo/fingerprint`), so a native change produces a new runtime version automatically.

flashcards.front: Name four things EAS Update cannot change.
flashcards.back: Native code or native dependencies, app permissions, the Expo SDK version, and anything that requires a new binary.

flashcards.front: How many rollouts can be in progress at once?
flashcards.back: One per branch, platform and runtime version.

flashcards.front: Does `eas update:rollback` delete the bad update?
flashcards.back: No. It republishes an earlier update or tells clients to run the embedded update. Clients pick that up on their next check.

flashcards.front: How do you move a tested update from staging to production without rebuilding it?
flashcards.back: `eas update:republish --group <id> --destination-branch production` (or repoint the channel with `eas channel:edit`).

flashcards.front: Which flag has `eas update` required since SDK 55?
flashcards.back: `--environment`, which picks the EAS environment variables used to bundle the update.

flashcards.front: Google Play's exception that lets JS updates exist
flashcards.back: Its Device and Network Abuse rule doesn't apply to code that runs in a virtual machine or interpreter with indirect API access. Executable code such as dex, JAR or .so still can't be downloaded.

flashcards.front: Apple guideline 2.5.19 in one line
flashcards.back: No hidden, dormant or undocumented features. Apple's 2026-10-16 post says that includes changing what an app does after approval.

flashcards.front: TestFlight tester limits
flashcards.back: Up to 100 internal testers (team members with certain roles) and up to 10,000 external testers. The first external build needs TestFlight App Review.

flashcards.front: Play internal testing track in brief
flashcards.back: Up to 100 testers, available within minutes, and might not go through standard Play policy or security reviews.

flashcards.front: New personal Play account: what is required before production access?
flashcards.back: A closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days.

flashcards.front: Apple phased release schedule
flashcards.back: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% over 7 days, for automatic updates only. Manual downloads are always possible, and you can pause for up to 30 days in total.

flashcards.front: What happens when you halt a Play staged rollout?
flashcards.back: New users stop receiving that version; users who already have it keep it. Fix by rolling out a new release with a fixed bundle.

flashcards.front: Where does an Expo app declare required-reason API usage for iOS?
flashcards.back: In app config under `ios.privacyManifests` → `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes`, for example the UserDefaults category with reason `CA92.1`.

flashcards.front: In Play Data safety, what counts as "collected"?
flashcards.back: Data transmitted off the device. Transfers to a service provider acting for you are not "sharing".

flashcards.front: Apple account deletion: is deactivation enough?
flashcards.back: No. Deletion must be startable in the app and remove the account; deactivation alone is insufficient.

flashcards.front: Google Play account deletion requires which two things?
flashcards.back: An in-app deletion path and a web link to request deletion, listed in the Data safety form.

flashcards.front: `needs` vs `after` in EAS Workflows
flashcards.back: `needs` runs a job only if the listed jobs succeeded; `after` runs it once they finish, whatever the result.

flashcards.front: How do EAS Workflows skip redundant native builds?
flashcards.back: Combine `fingerprint`, `get-build` and `update` jobs: if a build with the same fingerprint exists, publish an update instead of building.

flashcards.front: Why should most mobile test coverage come from Jest rather than E2E?
flashcards.back: E2E needs a compiled build plus a simulator or device and is slower and flakier. Jest unit and RNTL component tests run in Node in seconds; keep E2E for a few critical flows.

flashcards.front: What Jest preset does Expo document, and what does it do?
flashcards.back: "preset": "jest-expo". It configures Jest for Expo projects and mocks native Expo modules so tests run in Node.

flashcards.front: What kind of value does transformIgnorePatterns take, and when do you change it?
flashcards.back: A regular expression. Widen it when a package in node_modules ships untranspiled code and Jest fails with a syntax error.

flashcards.front: How should an RNTL test find elements?
flashcards.back: The way a user would: by visible text or accessibility information (for example getByText), not by component state or internals.

flashcards.front: What does a minimal Maestro flow look like?
flashcards.back: YAML: appId: <bundle id>, a --- separator, then steps such as - launchApp and - assertVisible: 'Welcome!'.

flashcards.front: What build settings does Expo's E2E profile use?
flashcards.back: ios.simulator: true (a simulator build) and android.buildType: apk, so the binary can be installed on a simulator or emulator.

flashcards.front: How does an EAS Workflows maestro job get the app to test?
flashcards.back: Through build_id from an earlier build job (needs.<build>.outputs.build_id), plus a flow_path list of flow files.

flashcards.front: How many groups and controls does OWASP MASVS v2 have?
flashcards.back: 8 groups (STORAGE, CRYPTO, AUTH, NETWORK, PLATFORM, CODE, RESILIENCE, PRIVACY) and 24 controls.

flashcards.front: Is an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable secret?
flashcards.back: No. It is inlined into the JS bundle as plain text; Expo says anything in client code is public and readable by anyone who can run the app.

flashcards.front: Where should a privileged third-party API key live for an Expo app?
flashcards.back: On your backend. The app calls your API, which holds the key and enforces per-user auth and rate limits.

flashcards.front: Where do SecureStore values live on each platform?
flashcards.back: iOS: the Keychain. Android: SharedPreferences encrypted with the Android Keystore system.

flashcards.front: What do the *_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY keychainAccessible options change?
flashcards.back: The item does not migrate to another device through backup. The default is WHEN_UNLOCKED.

flashcards.front: What does MASVS-NETWORK-2 require, and what is its scope?
flashcards.back: Identity pinning for all remote endpoints under the developer's control, not third-party hosts you do not manage.

flashcards.front: What is the main operational risk of certificate pinning?
flashcards.back: If the server key changes and the app has no matching pin, installed copies lose connectivity until users get an app update with new pins. Pin public keys, include a backup pin and plan rotation.

flashcards.front: Why is jailbreak or root detection not a primary control?
flashcards.back: On a device the attacker controls, client checks can be patched or hooked. It is defense in depth; the server must enforce entitlements.

flashcards.front: How do you get readable stack traces for crashes in an EAS Update?
flashcards.back: Run npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist after eas update. EAS Build uploads automatically only for the build itself (with SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN).

flashcards.front: How do you tie Sentry events to a specific OTA update?
flashcards.back: Tag them: scope.setTag('expo-update-id', Updates.updateId).

flashcards.front: What is the Apple phased release schedule?
flashcards.back: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% over 7 days, for automatic updates only. It can be paused for up to 30 days in total.

flashcards.front: What happens when you halt a Google Play staged rollout?
flashcards.back: New users stop receiving the version; users who already have it keep it. Fix by rolling out a new release with a fixed bundle.

flashcards.front: Which commands run and stop an EAS Update percentage rollout?
flashcards.back: eas update --rollout-percentage=10, then eas update:edit to change it, and eas update:revert-update-rollout to back out.

flashcards.front: Does eas update:rollback delete the bad update?
flashcards.back: No. It republishes an earlier update or tells clients to run the embedded update; the bad update remains.

flashcards.front: What are the two Google Play In-App Updates flows?
flashcards.back: Flexible (downloads in the background while the app stays usable) and immediate (full-screen, blocking until installed).

flashcards.front: How do you force an update on iOS?
flashcards.back: There is no OS API. The app checks a minimum supported version from your backend and shows a blocking screen linking to the App Store.

flashcards.front: Which App Review guideline limits using feature flags to reveal features after approval?
flashcards.back: 2.5.19: no hidden, dormant or undocumented features (clarified 2026-10-16 to include changing features after approval).

flashcards.front: Name two iOS PWA limitations from web.dev.
flashcards.back: No install prompt (Share > Add to Home Screen) and no badging or app shortcuts. Each installation also has isolated storage.

questions.scenario: SDK upgrade
questions.stem: A team upgrades an Expo app from SDK 54 to SDK 58. One older library throws errors, and a developer proposes adding `newArchEnabled: false` to app.json so the app runs on the old architecture again. What should the team do?
options: Add newArchEnabled: false to app.json and rebuild the development build
Update or replace the library with one that supports the New Architecture, since the Legacy Architecture can no longer be enabled
Stay on Expo Go, which still bundles the Legacy Architecture for older libraries
Set RCT_NEW_ARCH_ENABLED=0 in the iOS build environment and newArchEnabled=false in gradle.properties
questions.explanation: Expo SDK 55 dropped Legacy Architecture support and removed newArchEnabled from app.json, and React Native 0.82+ ignores the native opt-out flags. The only fix is a library version that works on the New Architecture (many older ones run through the interop layers) or a replacement.
rationales: The option was removed in SDK 55; it no longer switches architectures.
Correct. The New Architecture is the only one, so the dependency has to change.
Expo Go runs the latest SDK only and does not provide a Legacy Architecture mode.
Since RN 0.82 these flags "will be ignored"; there is no Legacy Architecture to fall back to.

sources.title: React Native 0.82 release — React Native blog

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the New Architecture changed communication between JavaScript and native code?
options: All JavaScript now runs on the main UI thread, so no communication layer is needed
Messages are still serialized to JSON, but the bridge batches them more aggressively
JSI lets JavaScript hold references to C++ objects and call them directly, replacing the asynchronous bridge
JavaScript is compiled to native machine code at build time, removing the JavaScript runtime
questions.explanation: The React Native docs say the New Architecture removes the asynchronous bridge and replaces it with JSI, an interface that lets JavaScript hold a reference to a C++ object and vice versa. A JavaScript engine (Hermes) still runs the app code.
rationales: JavaScript does not move wholesale to the UI thread; the change is in how JS and native talk.
Batching JSON over a bridge describes the old model, which was removed.
Correct. JSI replaces the bridge with direct references between JS and C++.
Hermes still executes JavaScript; JSI is an interface, not ahead-of-time compilation to native code.

sources.title: About the New Architecture — React Native docs

questions.scenario: Tooltip flicker
questions.stem: A tooltip component measures its anchor view inside `useEffect`, stores the position in state, and renders. On slower devices users see the tooltip at the top-left corner for one frame before it jumps into place. What is the best fix on the current React Native architecture?
options: Wrap the state update in setTimeout(..., 16) so it runs after the next frame
Render the tooltip with opacity 0 and animate it in after a 100 ms delay
Defer the measurement with InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions
Measure in useLayoutEffect and set the position in the same commit, using synchronous layout access
questions.explanation: The New Architecture supports synchronous layout reads, so a component can measure in useLayoutEffect and update before the frame is painted. Timers and delays only hide the jump, and InteractionManager was removed in Expo SDK 58.
rationales: A timer still paints the wrong position first and adds a hard-coded delay.
Masking with an animation adds latency and still positions the tooltip late.
InteractionManager was removed in Expo SDK 58 (the changelog points to requestIdleCallback), and deferring work would delay rather than fix the jump.
Correct. Measuring in useLayoutEffect and updating in one commit avoids the visible jump.

sources.title: About the New Architecture — React Native docs

questions.scenario: Native SDK wrapper
questions.stem: An Expo team must wrap a vendor's iOS (Swift) and Android (Kotlin) SDK so JavaScript can call it. Nobody on the team writes C++. Which approach fits best?
options: Call the SDK through the legacy NativeModules bridge to avoid JSI
Write a Turbo Module in C++, because only C++ modules work on the New Architecture
Write the module with the Expo Modules API in Swift and Kotlin
Write a config plugin that exposes the SDK methods to JavaScript
questions.explanation: The Expo Modules API is built on JSI, supports the New Architecture, and Expo documents performance comparable to Turbo Modules. Turbo Modules are the better choice when you need C++, which this team does not.
rationales: The asynchronous bridge was removed; older bridge-style modules only keep working through interop layers, which is not how to build a new module.
Both Expo Modules and Turbo Modules support the New Architecture; C++ is only needed for C++ code.
Correct. Swift and Kotlin modules via the Expo Modules API run on JSI with comparable performance.
Config plugins change native project configuration at prebuild; they do not expose runtime APIs.

sources.title: Expo Modules API overview — Expo docs

questions.stem: Which statements about a project on Expo SDK 58 with React Native 0.88 are accurate? (Select two.)
options: The New Architecture is the only architecture available
Android builds still default to the asynchronous bridge
newArchEnabled must be set to true in app.json
Hermes V1 is the default JavaScript engine
questions.explanation: Hermes V1 became the React Native default in 0.84 and the Expo default in SDK 56. React Native 0.82 was the first release running entirely on the New Architecture, and Expo SDK 55 removed newArchEnabled from app.json.
rationales: Correct. The Legacy Architecture was removed; the New Architecture is the only one.
The bridge no longer exists on either platform.
The option was removed in SDK 55; there is nothing to enable.
Correct. Hermes V1 is the default in RN 0.84+ and Expo SDK 56+.

sources.title: React Native 0.84 release — React Native blog

questions.scenario: Native library in Expo Go
questions.stem: A developer adds a library that ships its own native iOS and Android code. In Expo Go the app fails because the native module cannot be found. What is the correct next step?
options: Downgrade Expo Go to an older SDK that bundled more libraries
Clear the Metro cache and restart Expo Go
Publish the library code with an over-the-air update so Expo Go downloads it
Create a development build that includes expo-dev-client and the library
questions.explanation: Expo Go contains a fixed set of native modules, so it cannot load new native code. A development build is your own version of Expo Go that can include any native libraries. OTA updates cannot deliver native code.
rationales: Expo Go only supports the latest SDK, and older builds would not include this library either.
The problem is missing native code, not a stale JavaScript cache.
OTA updates can change JS, styling and images only, not native code.
Correct. A development build compiles the library's native code into your own debug app.

questions.scenario: Plugin change not applied
questions.stem: A developer adds a library's config plugin to the `plugins` array in app.json to set an Android manifest entry, then presses "reload" in the installed development build. The manifest entry has no effect. Why?
options: Config plugins only apply to production builds, never development builds
The plugin must also be imported in App.tsx to run
Reloading only works for plugins listed in app.config.ts, not app.json
Config plugin mods run during prebuild, so the native app must be rebuilt
questions.explanation: Config plugins modify native projects during prebuild; their mods are only evaluated during the syncing phase of npx expo prebuild. A JavaScript reload does not regenerate or recompile the native app, so a new development build is required.
rationales: Plugins apply to every native build, development included, once prebuild runs.
Plugins are referenced in app config, not imported into app runtime code.
The config file format does not change when plugins run; both run at prebuild.
Correct. Native config changes need prebuild and a rebuild.

questions.scenario: Committed native folders
questions.stem: Months ago a developer ran `npx expo prebuild` and committed the generated `ios/` and `android/` folders. Now the team changes the app icon and adds a config plugin in app.json, runs EAS Build, and the new build shows neither change. What explains this, and what is the cleanest fix for a project with no hand-written native code?
options: EAS Build caches app.json; pass a flag to clear the build cache
Move the changes from app.json to app.config.js, which EAS Build always re-reads
EAS Build does not run prebuild when native directories exist; delete and gitignore ios/ and android/ so they are regenerated from config
Icons and plugins only update through EAS Update, so publish an update
questions.explanation: Expo's CNG docs state that if the native directories exist, the build will not run prebuild, so app config changes never reach the native projects. With no custom native edits, removing and gitignoring the folders restores Continuous Native Generation.
rationales: The config is read; it is not applied because prebuild is skipped.
Any app config file is ignored for native generation while prebuild is skipped.
Correct. Without the committed folders, prebuild regenerates the native projects from config.
Icons and native config are part of the binary and cannot be changed over the air.

questions.stem: Which config plugin follows Expo's documented conventions?
options: An async function that fetches the scheme from a remote server each time prebuild runs
A synchronous function named withCustomScheme that uses withInfoPlist to add a URL scheme
A Babel plugin that rewrites native files while Metro bundles JavaScript
A function called at app startup that edits Info.plist on the device
questions.explanation: Config plugins are functions that modify native projects during prebuild. The docs recommend naming them with<Feature>, keeping them synchronous, and using mods such as withInfoPlist from expo/config-plugins.
rationales: Plugins should be synchronous; a network call also makes prebuild non-deterministic.
Correct. Synchronous, with<Feature> naming, and a documented mod.
Metro and Babel transform JavaScript; native config changes belong in config plugins at prebuild.
Info.plist is part of the signed binary; it cannot be edited at runtime.

questions.scenario: Rebuild or reload
questions.stem: A team uses a development build day to day. Which changes require a new native build rather than a JavaScript reload? (Select two.)
options: Adding a library that contains native code
Fixing a bug in a TypeScript date-formatting helper
Changing the padding on a settings screen
Changing the camera permission purpose string in ios.infoPlist
questions.explanation: Expo says to rebuild a development build after adding a native library or changing native app config. Info.plist changes cannot be updated over the air. Styles and pure TypeScript logic are part of the JavaScript bundle and reload instantly.
rationales: Correct. New native code must be compiled into the binary.
A JS-only helper reloads without a rebuild.
Styling is JavaScript and reloads without a rebuild.
Correct. Info.plist is native configuration baked into the build.

questions.scenario: Brownfield app
questions.stem: A company has a mature native iOS and Android banking app and wants to add a few React Native screens to it. A developer suggests managing the native projects with `npx expo prebuild`. What is the right assessment?
options: Prebuild is required, because Expo libraries only work in projects generated by prebuild
Good idea: prebuild will merge the React Native screens into the existing Xcode and Gradle projects
Good idea, as long as the ios/ and android/ folders are gitignored first
Prebuild is not intended for brownfield apps; keep maintaining the existing native projects and integrate React Native into them
questions.explanation: The CNG docs note that prebuild is not for brownfield apps. Prebuild generates native projects from config, which would discard the hand-maintained native app rather than embed React Native in it.
rationales: Prebuild is optional; it is a way to generate native projects, not a requirement for using Expo libraries.
Prebuild generates projects from config; it does not merge into an existing hand-written app.
Gitignoring the existing native app's source would throw away the product.
Correct. Brownfield apps keep their native projects and add React Native into them.

questions.scenario: Web layout port
questions.stem: A web developer ports a toolbar: a container `View` with three icon buttons. On the web the equivalent `div` with `display: flex` showed the icons side by side, but on mobile they stack vertically. What change fixes it?
options: Wrap each icon in its own ScrollView
Add display: "flex" to the container style
Set flexDirection: "row" on the container
Set alignContent: "stretch" on the container
questions.explanation: In React Native every View is a flex container and flexDirection defaults to column instead of row. Setting flexDirection: "row" lays the children out horizontally.
rationales: ScrollViews do not change direction and add unnecessary complexity.
Views already use Flexbox; the issue is the default direction.
Correct. React Native defaults to column, so row must be set explicitly.
alignContent controls wrapped lines and does not change the main axis.

sources.title: Layout with Flexbox — React Native docs

questions.scenario: Overflowing title
questions.stem: A list row has an avatar, a title `Text` and a fixed-width button inside a `View` with `flexDirection: "row"`. Long titles push the button off the right edge of the screen instead of wrapping. The same markup with CSS on the web shrinks the title. What is the cause and fix?
options: Text cannot wrap inside a row; replace it with a TextInput set to read-only
flexShrink defaults to 0 in React Native; give the title (or its container) flexShrink: 1 or flex: 1
Set overflow: "hidden" on the row so the button stays visible
flex only supports a single number; set flex: "1 1 auto" on the title
questions.explanation: React Native defaults flexShrink to 0 instead of 1, so items keep their natural width and overflow. Allowing the title to shrink (flexShrink: 1 or flex: 1) lets it wrap within the remaining space.
rationales: Text wraps normally once its container is allowed to shrink.
Correct. The mobile default prevents shrinking; enabling it lets the text wrap.
Clipping hides the overflow but the button is still pushed out of view.
Because flex takes a single number, the CSS shorthand string does not work.

sources.title: Layout with Flexbox — React Native docs

questions.stem: A screen renders `<View style={styles.badge}>New</View>` and the app throws an error about text strings. What is the correct fix?
options: Add the string as an accessibilityLabel on the View
Set the fontSize style on the View so it can render text
Wrap the string in a Text component inside the View
Use a template literal {`New`} instead of plain text
questions.explanation: In React Native, strings must be rendered inside a Text component. View is a layout container and does not render or style text, so the string goes in a Text child.
rationales: An accessibility label is read by screen readers; it does not display text.
View does not accept or pass down text styles.
Correct. Only Text renders strings.
A template literal is still a raw string outside Text.

questions.scenario: Touch feedback
questions.stem: A design calls for a card that darkens while pressed and a small close icon that is easy to hit. The project is on Expo SDK 58. Which implementation fits?
options: Import TouchableOpacity from the react-native root export and set activeOpacity
Wrap the card in Text and use its onPress so the whole card is tappable
Add onClick to the View and change its style in a mouseenter handler
Use Pressable with style={({ pressed }) => [styles.card, pressed && styles.pressed]} and hitSlop on the close icon
questions.explanation: Pressable supports a style function that receives { pressed } and hitSlop to enlarge the touch area beyond the visual bounds, so it covers both the pressed state and the small close icon. The React Native docs point to Pressable as the more extensive, future-proof touch API.
rationales: TouchableOpacity fades the card rather than darkening it and does nothing for the close icon's hit area; React Native recommends Pressable as the more extensive, future-proof touch API.
Text is for strings; using it as a card container misuses the component and its layout.
React Native views have no onClick or hover events for touch input.
Correct. Pressed styling plus hitSlop meet both requirements.

questions.scenario: Divergent picker
questions.stem: A date picker needs about 200 lines of iOS-only code and a completely different Android implementation. Other screens should simply import the picker. What is the cleanest structure?
options: DatePicker.ios.tsx and DatePicker.android.tsx, imported elsewhere as ./DatePicker.ios
One file with Platform.OS checks around every block of code
DatePicker.ios.tsx and DatePicker.android.tsx, imported elsewhere as ./DatePicker
A runtime require() of a file path built from Platform.OS
questions.explanation: For large platform differences, React Native recommends platform-specific file extensions. Importing the base name lets the bundler pick the .ios or .android file automatically; Platform.OS checks suit small differences.
rationales: Importing the .ios file explicitly would ship the iOS version to Android.
Scattered checks work for small differences but become hard to read for whole implementations.
Correct. The bundler resolves the platform file from the extensionless import.
Dynamic require paths are not statically resolvable by the bundler.

questions.scenario: Version gate
questions.stem: Code shared by both platforms enables a feature with `if (Platform.Version >= 33)` to target Android 13 and later. QA reports odd behaviour on iOS. What is the problem?
options: Platform.Version reports the React Native version, not the OS version
Platform.Version is the API level (a number) on Android but a string on iOS, so the check must be guarded with Platform.OS === "android"
Platform.Version is undefined on iOS, so the check always throws
Platform.Version is only available inside .android.tsx files
questions.explanation: The React Native docs state that Platform.Version is the API level number on Android and a version string on iOS. Comparing an iOS string to 33 is meaningless, so the check needs a Platform.OS guard.
rationales: It reports the operating system version, not React Native's.
Correct. The type and meaning differ per platform, so guard by OS first.
It is defined on iOS, as a string.
Platform is available in any file.

questions.scenario: Invisible avatar
questions.stem: A profile screen renders `<Image source={{ uri: user.avatarUrl }} />`. The URL is valid and the request succeeds, but nothing appears. What is the likely cause?
options: Remote images require a width and height style to be visible
The Image must be wrapped in a Text component
Image cannot load https URLs without a config plugin
Remote images only load in release builds
questions.explanation: The React Native Image docs note that network and data images are not sized automatically, so you must specify their dimensions. Without a width and height the image has zero size.
rationales: Correct. Give network images explicit dimensions.
Image is a standalone component, not text content.
Image loads https URLs without any plugin.
Remote images load in development builds as well.

questions.scenario: Undefined API URL
questions.stem: A config module reads `const { EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL } = process.env;`. The value is set in `.env`, but in the app it is `undefined`. What fixes it?
options: Move .env into the ios/ and android/ folders
Rename the variable to API_URL without the prefix
Read it at runtime with Constants.expoConfig.extra.EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL
Reference it as process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL so it is statically inlined
questions.explanation: Expo inlines EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables at build time only when they are statically referenced as a property of process.env. The docs call destructuring from process.env invalid; it will not be inlined.
rationales: Native folders have nothing to do with how Metro reads .env files.
Without the EXPO_PUBLIC_ prefix the variable is not exposed to app code at all.
extra holds app config values; .env variables do not appear there automatically.
Correct. Static property access lets the bundler inline the value.

questions.scenario: Third-party API key
questions.stem: A team calls a paid AI API directly from the app. To "protect" the key they store it as an EAS environment variable with secret visibility and expose it to the app as `EXPO_PUBLIC_AI_KEY`. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: Safe: secret visibility means the value cannot be read outside Expo's servers
Unsafe only on Android; iOS encrypts the JavaScript bundle
Unsafe: EXPO_PUBLIC_ values are inlined in plain text into the app, so the key must stay on a server that proxies the calls
Safe as long as the app is minified with Hermes bytecode
questions.explanation: Secret visibility protects the value on EAS, but Expo notes it does not protect values you embed in the app. EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables are visible in plain text in the compiled app, so the key belongs on a backend.
rationales: That protection covers EAS storage, not a value inlined into the bundle.
Neither platform makes an embedded string secret.
Correct. Anything shipped in the app is public; proxy the call from your server.
Bytecode is not encryption; inlined strings remain extractable.

questions.scenario: Preview variant
questions.stem: A team wants preview builds to install side by side with production, with a different app name and bundle identifier chosen by an `APP_VARIANT` variable set in the build profile. Where should this logic live?
options: In App.tsx, reading APP_VARIANT at startup and changing the bundle identifier
In a dynamic app.config.ts that receives ({ config }) and returns an ExpoConfig based on process.env.APP_VARIANT
In a postinstall script that rewrites app.json in place
In an EXPO_PUBLIC_APP_VARIANT variable read by the app's root layout
questions.explanation: Name and bundle identifier are build-time app config. A dynamic app.config.ts (which takes precedence over app.json) can extend the static config and switch values on an environment variable at build time.
rationales: The bundle identifier is fixed in the signed binary; JavaScript cannot change it at runtime.
Correct. Dynamic app config computes identifiers when the native app is generated.
Mutating app.json on install is fragile and unnecessary when dynamic config exists.
A runtime JS variable cannot change native identifiers.

questions.stem: Which statements about the `extra` field in Expo app config are correct? (Select two.)
options: It is encrypted on the device with the platform keystore
App code can read it at runtime through Constants.expoConfig.extra
npx expo config --type public shows what is embedded in builds and updates, including extra
It is stripped from production builds, so it is safe for API secrets
questions.explanation: Expo documents reading extra through Constants.expoConfig.extra and using npx expo config --type public to inspect the embedded public config. The docs warn not to include sensitive information in app config.
rationales: App config is not encrypted with the keystore; it is public.
Correct. extra is exposed at runtime through expo-constants.
Correct. This command shows the public config that ships with the app.
extra ships with the app; the docs say not to put sensitive data in app config.

questions.scenario: Strict types after upgrade
questions.stem: After upgrading to Expo SDK 58, TypeScript reports errors on imports such as `import x from "react-native/Libraries/Utilities/..."`. Runtime behaviour has not changed. What is the right response?
options: Downgrade TypeScript to an older major version
Add // @ts-ignore above each deep import
Set skipLibCheck: false in tsconfig.json
Switch imports to the public react-native entry point, since the Strict TypeScript API rejects deep imports
questions.explanation: React Native's Strict TypeScript API became the default in RN 0.87 and is adopted in SDK 58. Deep imports from react-native/Libraries/* are type errors by design; the fix is to use the public API.
rationales: The errors come from React Native's type definitions, not the compiler version.
Suppressing errors hides reliance on private internals that may change.
skipLibCheck controls checking of declaration files and does not expose private paths.
Correct. Use the public react-native exports.

questions.scenario: Staging env file
questions.stem: On Expo SDK 58 a developer runs `NODE_ENV=staging npx expo start` expecting values from `.env.staging`, but the app shows development values. What is happening, and what is a better approach?
options: .env.staging must be renamed .env.staging.local to be picked up
Metro caches .env files; clearing the cache will load .env.staging
Expo commands now set NODE_ENV to their own mode, so .env.staging is not loaded; select per-environment values with EAS environments or a dedicated variable read in app config
NODE_ENV must be exported in the shell profile rather than set inline
questions.explanation: Since SDK 58 each command sets NODE_ENV to its mode and replaces any value you set, so start loads development files and .env.staging is no longer loaded. EAS environments (development, preview, production) or your own variable are the supported way to switch values.
rationales: The .local suffix changes precedence within a mode; it does not create a staging mode.
This is documented loading behaviour, not a cache problem.
Correct. NODE_ENV is overwritten, so use a different selection mechanism.
Expo replaces NODE_ENV however it is set.

questions.scenario: Uncaught press error
questions.stem: A screen is wrapped in an error boundary. A bug throws inside the `onPress` handler of a "Save" button, and the fallback UI never appears. Why, and what should the team do?
options: Error boundaries only work in release builds; test in release mode
Error boundaries catch rendering errors, not errors in event handlers; catch the error in the handler, show an error state and report it
The boundary must be placed inside the button, not around the screen
onPress errors are swallowed by React Native and need no handling
questions.explanation: React documents that error boundaries catch errors during rendering, not in event handlers or asynchronous code. Errors from handlers must be caught with try/catch and reported explicitly.
rationales: Boundaries behave the same in development and release.
Correct. Handler errors bypass boundaries and need explicit handling.
Moving the boundary does not change which errors it can catch.
Unhandled handler errors still surface and must be handled.

questions.scenario: Native SDK crash
questions.stem: The app crashes immediately when a vendor's native iOS SDK initializes. React Native DevTools shows no JavaScript error before the crash. What should the developer use next?
options: Debug the native code in Xcode, since React Native DevTools is not meant to replace native tools
Inspect the crash in the DevTools Network panel
Add more console.log calls around the JavaScript call site
Open the React Components panel to find the failing component
questions.explanation: The React Native docs say DevTools is designed for React app concerns and not to replace native tools. A crash inside native SDK code needs Xcode (or Android Studio on Android), where native stack traces and breakpoints are available.
rationales: Correct. Native crashes are diagnosed with native tooling.
Network inspection does not reveal a native initialization crash.
JS logs stop before the native crash and cannot show the native stack.
The React tree does not show native SDK failures.

sources.title: React Native DevTools — React Native docs

questions.scenario: Minified OTA crashes
questions.stem: Sentry shows readable stack traces for crashes in store builds made with EAS Build, but crashes from the latest EAS Update show only minified frames. What is the most likely missing step?
options: Disabling Hermes so stack traces are not minified
Exposing SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN to the app as EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN
Bundling source maps inside the update so the device can symbolicate
Running npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist after eas update
questions.explanation: Expo's Sentry guide says EAS Build uploads source maps automatically when SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN is set, but updates need a separate upload with npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist after eas update. Shipping tokens or source maps in the app is unsafe.
rationales: Disabling the default engine is unnecessary; uploading source maps fixes symbolication.
The token is a build-time credential and must never be embedded in the app.
Source maps should not be published to production clients.
Correct. Each update has its own bundle and needs its source maps uploaded.

questions.scenario: Growing memory
questions.stem: Memory use grows each time users open and close a chat screen. The developer suspects a JavaScript object is retained after unmount. Which tool is the best fit?
options: The Perf Monitor overlay frame-rate counters
console.log in every component's render
The DevTools Memory panel, comparing heap snapshots before and after opening the screen several times
The DevTools Network panel filtered to WebSocket traffic
questions.explanation: React Native DevTools includes a Memory panel for heap snapshots, which shows retained objects between snapshots. Frame-rate counters and logs do not reveal what is retained, and the Network panel does not cover WebSocket events.
rationales: Frame counters show rendering speed, not retained memory.
Render logging adds noise and does not reveal object retention.
Correct. Heap snapshots identify retained objects.
The Network panel does not yet cover WebSocket events and does not show retained memory.

sources.title: React Native DevTools — React Native docs

questions.stem: A team sets up Sentry for an Expo app built and updated with EAS. Which practices follow Expo's guidance? (Select two.)
options: Expose the auth token as EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN so the app can upload its own source maps
Ship source maps inside the production bundle so crashes symbolicate on the device
Store SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN as an EAS environment variable with sensitive visibility so EAS Build uploads source maps
Tag events with the running update, for example scope.setTag("expo-update-id", Updates.updateId)
questions.explanation: Expo's Sentry guide uses a sensitive SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN for automatic source map uploads on EAS Build and tags events with the update ID. EXPO_PUBLIC_ values are plain text in the app, and Expo advises against publishing source maps to production.
rationales: This would leak the token in plain text inside the app.
Source maps should stay off production clients.
Correct. The token stays a build-time credential.
Correct. Tagging links each crash to the update that produced it.

questions.scenario: A team is reorganising src/app so that sign-in, sign-up and forgot-password share one layout with a plain header. Product insists the URLs stay /sign-in, /sign-up and /forgot-password.
questions.stem: How should they structure the files?
options: Move the three screens into src/app/(auth)/ with a _layout.tsx in that folder
Move them into src/app/auth/ and add an index.tsx that redirects
Prefix each file with an underscore, such as _sign-in.tsx, to hide the folder from the URL
Move them into src/app/+auth/ so the folder is treated as special
questions.explanation: A group folder in parentheses can hold a shared _layout.tsx without adding a URL segment, so (auth)/sign-in.tsx stays at /sign-in. A plain folder adds a segment, and the underscore and plus prefixes have other meanings.
rationales: Correct. Groups add no URL segment and can share a layout.
A plain auth/ folder would move the screens to /auth/sign-in.
The underscore prefix marks _layout files; it does not create pathless routes.
The + prefix is reserved for special files such as +not-found.tsx; it is not a way to group screens.

questions.scenario: A checkout flow is Cart > Shipping > Payment. On Payment, a "Back to cart" button calls router.push('/cart'). Testers report that after a few round trips, pressing the hardware back button walks through several copies of Cart and Payment.
questions.stem: Which change best fixes this?
options: Call router.replace('/cart') so Payment is swapped for a new Cart screen
Keep router.push('/cart') but call it inside a setTimeout so the stack settles first
Call router.setParams({ screen: 'cart' }) on the Payment route
Call router.navigate('/cart') so the router unwinds to the Cart entry already in the stack
questions.explanation: router.navigate pushes or unwinds to an existing route, so returning to a Cart that is already in history pops back to it. router.push always adds a new entry, which causes the duplicates. replace would still leave a stale Shipping entry beneath a new Cart.
rationales: replace swaps only the current screen; Cart and Shipping stay underneath, so history is still wrong.
Delaying push still pushes a new Cart entry each time; timing is not the cause of the duplicates.
setParams changes the current route's params; it does not navigate to Cart.
Correct. navigate unwinds to the existing route instead of stacking another copy.

sources.title: Navigate between pages — Expo Router docs

questions.scenario: A product detail screen at src/app/product/[id].tsx calls useGlobalSearchParams() and fetches the product whenever id changes. From product 1 the user opens a related product 2, which is pushed on top. The analytics team notices product 1's screen, now in the background, also refetches with id 2.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Read params with useLocalSearchParams(), which only updates for the focused route
Keep useGlobalSearchParams() and add a useFocusEffect cleanup that cancels the fetch on unmount
Use router.replace when opening related products so only one detail screen exists
Read the id from usePathname() and parse it manually
questions.explanation: useGlobalSearchParams updates even when a route is not focused, so every mounted detail screen sees the newest id. useLocalSearchParams returns this route's own params and only updates while it is focused, which is what a screen-level fetch needs.
rationales: Correct. Local params belong to the screen that owns them.
The useFocusEffect cleanup runs when the screen loses focus, not on unmount, and the global hook would still deliver the wrong id.
This hides the symptom by destroying back navigation to the first product.
usePathname returns the current global path, so a background screen would still see the new product's path.

sources.title: Hooks API reference — Expo Router docs

questions.scenario: An app gates its main tabs with <Stack.Protected guard={!!session}>. A reviewer asks what this protection does and does not guarantee.
questions.stem: Which two statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: When the guard becomes false, users on the protected screens are redirected and those screens' history entries are removed
Because the screens cannot render without a session, the API can skip token checks for requests made from them
The API must still authenticate and authorise every request, because protected screens are not a replacement for server-side access control
Stack.Protected only works in Stack layouts; tabs must redirect in a useEffect
questions.explanation: The docs say a guard turning false redirects users and removes all of the protected screens' history entries. They are equally clear that protected screens are not a replacement for server-side authentication or access control. Protected also works for Tabs and Drawer.
rationales: Correct. Redirect plus history removal is the documented behaviour.
Client-side gating is UX only; anyone can call the API directly.
Correct. The server must still verify every request.
Protected is also available for Tabs and Drawer layouts.

questions.scenario: Universal links to https://example.com/orders/123 open Safari instead of the app. The app config contains "associatedDomains": ["applinks:https://example.com"], and the AASA file is served over HTTPS at /.well-known/apple-app-site-association with the correct TEAMID.BUNDLEID appID.
questions.stem: What should the team change first?
options: Change the entry to "applinks:example.com" and rebuild the app
Add an android.intentFilters entry with autoVerify: true
Serve the AASA file over plain HTTP so iOS can fetch it during install
Set the app config scheme to "https"
questions.explanation: The associatedDomains entitlement takes applinks: followed by the host only, without https. Because the entitlement is native configuration, the app must be rebuilt (and reinstalled, since iOS fetches the AASA at install and update).
rationales: Correct. Remove the scheme from the entitlement value.
intentFilters configure Android App Links; they do nothing on iOS.
The AASA must be served over HTTPS.
The scheme field sets a custom deep-link scheme; https cannot be claimed that way and is not the problem.

questions.scenario: Android App Links verify on a developer's locally built APK but not on the build installed from Google Play, which uses Play App Signing. assetlinks.json lists one SHA-256 fingerprint, taken from the developer's local keystore, and is served as application/json.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Add the app signing certificate fingerprint from Play Console > App Signing ("Digital Asset Links JSON") to assetlinks.json
Remove autoVerify from the intent filter so Android stops checking
Change the Content-Type of assetlinks.json to text/plain
Add the BROWSABLE category to a custom-scheme intent filter instead
questions.explanation: Play App Signing re-signs the app with Google's app signing key, so the Play build's certificate differs from the local one. assetlinks.json must contain the fingerprint of the certificate that actually signs the installed build, which Play Console shows under App Signing.
rationales: Correct. The fingerprint must match the certificate that signs the store build.
Without autoVerify the links are not verified App Links at all; users get a chooser instead.
The file must be served as application/json.
A custom scheme is not an App Link and does not open https URLs directly.

questions.scenario: A compose screen is presented with presentation: 'modal'. Its close button calls router.back(). On the web build, users who open /compose from a bookmark click Close and nothing happens.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Switch to presentation: 'formSheet' so the web build renders a native sheet
Wrap router.back() in a setTimeout so history is ready
Check router.canGoBack() and, when it is false, navigate to a fallback route such as the home screen
Remove the route from the web build with a +not-found.tsx file
questions.explanation: On web a modal is a separate route that can be opened directly, so there may be no history to go back to. The modals guide recommends handling dismissal with router.canGoBack() and a fallback.
rationales: formSheet changes native presentation; the web route still has no history entry to return to.
A delay does not create a history entry.
Correct. Handle the no-history case explicitly.
+not-found.tsx handles unmatched URLs; it does not remove a route or fix dismissal.

questions.scenario: A news app uses TanStack Query with default options. Users switch between tabs often, and each time a tab's list mounts it fires a request even though the data is seconds old. The backend team asks to cut traffic while keeping data at most about a minute old.
questions.stem: Which change best matches the goal?
options: Increase gcTime to 30 minutes
Set staleTime to about 60 seconds for those queries
Set retry to 0
Set refetchOnMount and refetchOnReconnect to false globally
questions.explanation: By default data is stale immediately, so every new mount refetches. staleTime defines how long data counts as fresh, which suppresses refetches inside that window. gcTime only controls how long inactive data stays in memory.
rationales: gcTime keeps unused data cached longer but does not make it fresh; mounts would still refetch.
Correct. staleTime directly controls background refetching of fresh data.
Retries only follow failures; they are not causing the traffic.
This stops refetches forever, so data could get much older than a minute.

questions.scenario: A React Native app relies on refetchOnWindowFocus to refresh balances when the user returns to the app. It works in the web build, but on iOS and Android the balance stays stale after coming back from the background.
questions.stem: What should the team add?
options: An AppState change listener that calls focusManager.setFocused(status === 'active') on native platforms
refetchInterval: 1000 on every balance query
A NetInfo listener passed to onlineManager.setEventListener
A useFocusEffect in the root layout that calls queryClient.clear()
questions.explanation: React Native has no window focus events, so TanStack Query cannot detect app foregrounding by itself. The React Native guide wires AppState to focusManager.setFocused, skipping web. onlineManager handles connectivity, which is a different trigger.
rationales: Correct. This maps app foregrounding to Query's focus concept.
Polling every second wastes battery and network and does not fix the missing focus signal.
onlineManager drives refetch on reconnect, not on app focus.
Clearing the cache throws away all data and causes loading states everywhere.

questions.scenario: A field-service app enables refetchOnReconnect, but after a technician drives out of a dead zone nothing refetches until they pull to refresh. Mutations made offline also fail immediately instead of waiting.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: onlineManager was never connected to the device's network state, for example via NetInfo or expo-network
staleTime is too short
gcTime evicted the queries while offline
The app uses useInfiniteQuery instead of useQuery
questions.explanation: TanStack Query only knows the device is offline or back online if onlineManager is wired to a network source on React Native. Without it, reconnect refetches do not fire and mutations are not paused while offline.
rationales: Correct. Wire onlineManager.setEventListener to NetInfo or expo-network.
A short staleTime makes refetches more likely, not less.
Even after eviction, a mounted query refetches; the missing piece is the reconnect signal.
Infinite queries follow the same online rules.

questions.scenario: A like button uses an optimistic mutation. In onMutate the code calls setQueryData to flip liked, then returns nothing. Occasionally the heart flips back a moment after the tap even though the request succeeds, and when the request fails the heart stays wrongly liked.
questions.stem: Which onMutate implementation fixes both problems?
options: Await cancelQueries for the post key, snapshot the current data with getQueryData, call setQueryData, and return the snapshot for onError to restore
Call invalidateQueries for the post key before setQueryData so the cache is fresh
Move setQueryData into onSuccess so the UI only changes after the server confirms
Set staleTime: Infinity on the post query so it never refetches
questions.explanation: An in-flight refetch can land after the optimistic write and overwrite it, which is why cancelQueries comes first. Returning a snapshot from onMutate lets onError roll back when the request fails. onSettled should then invalidate to re-sync.
rationales: Correct. Cancel, snapshot, write, return the snapshot.
Invalidating starts a refetch that can overwrite the optimistic value, the exact bug being fixed.
This removes the optimistic behaviour instead of fixing it.
This hides the race by never refreshing the post, and still gives no rollback.

questions.scenario: A feed screen uses FlashList with onEndReached. The current code keeps page in useState, calls useQuery(['feed', page]) and appends each result to an items array in state. Pull-to-refresh shows stale pages, and fast scrolling sometimes loads the same page twice.
questions.stem: Which approach should replace it?
options: Keep the useState array but debounce onEndReached by 500 ms
Fetch all pages up front in one request and set gcTime to Infinity
useInfiniteQuery with initialPageParam and getNextPageParam, rendering data.pages.flatMap(...) and calling fetchNextPage only when hasNextPage and not isFetchingNextPage
Store loaded pages in a global store so other screens can reuse them
questions.explanation: useInfiniteQuery keeps every page in the query cache under one key, so refetch and invalidation cover the whole list. Guarding fetchNextPage with hasNextPage and isFetchingNextPage prevents duplicate page loads from repeated end-reached events.
rationales: A debounce reduces duplicates but leaves the hand-built list outside the cache, so refresh stays broken.
Loading everything at once does not scale for feeds and gcTime does not affect freshness.
Correct. Pages live in the cache and fetches are guarded.
Duplicating server data in a client store loses refetch and invalidation.

questions.scenario: An app has five tabs, each with live queries. Profiling shows background tabs re-rendering whenever their cached data updates, and users want a tab's data refreshed when they return to it.
questions.stem: Which two techniques follow the TanStack Query React Native guidance? (Select two.)
options: Set gcTime: 0 so unfocused tabs drop their data
Give each tab navigator a new key on every focus to force a remount
Pass subscribed: false to useQuery when useIsFocused() is false, so unfocused screens stop re-rendering on cache updates
Refetch in a useFocusEffect callback when the screen regains focus, skipping the first call that happens on mount
questions.explanation: The React Native guide shows subscribed with useIsFocused to pause off-screen observers, and useFocusEffect to refetch when a screen comes back into focus, skipping the initial mount call. Dropping the cache or remounting throws away data and causes loading flashes.
rationales: gcTime 0 discards cached data, causing spinners on every return.
Forced remounts lose state and refetch everything.
Correct. Unsubscribed observers do not re-render on cache updates.
Correct. Screen focus is the mobile equivalent of window focus for a single screen.

questions.scenario: A security review of a React Native app finds the OAuth refresh token stored with AsyncStorage.setItem('refresh', token). The developer argues that app storage is private to the app.
questions.stem: What should the team do?
options: Base64-encode the token before writing it to AsyncStorage
Move the token to expo-secure-store, which uses the iOS Keychain and Keystore-encrypted storage on Android
Put the token in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ environment variable
Write the token to a plain SQLite table with a random name
questions.explanation: AsyncStorage is unencrypted, so a token there can be read from a compromised or backed-up device. SecureStore keeps values in the iOS Keychain and in SharedPreferences encrypted with the Android Keystore, which is where secrets belong.
rationales: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.
Correct. Secrets belong in SecureStore.
EXPO_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the bundle in plain text; they are not even per-user.
An unencrypted SQLite table is no safer than AsyncStorage; obscure naming is not protection.

questions.scenario: An inspection app must store about 5,000 checklist records offline, filter them by site and status, sort by due date, and update single records frequently. The prototype keeps them as one JSON string in AsyncStorage.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate storage?
options: expo-secure-store, one key per record
A React context holding the array, saved to AsyncStorage on every change
expo-sqlite with indexed tables and parameterised queries
A single expo-sqlite/kv-store key holding the JSON array
questions.explanation: Structured data that is filtered, sorted and updated record by record is what SQLite is for. Rewriting one big JSON value on every edit is slow and fragile, and SecureStore is meant for small secrets.
rationales: SecureStore is for small secret values; older iOS versions reportedly rejected large values, and it has no querying.
This still serialises the whole dataset on every change and keeps it all in memory.
Correct. SQLite gives queries, indexes and single-row updates.
kv-store uses SQLite underneath but exposes key-value access, so this is the same single-blob problem.

questions.scenario: A shopping app keeps user, theme and cart in one AppContext. Changing a cart quantity makes React DevTools highlight nearly every screen. A developer proposes wrapping all screens in memo.
questions.stem: What is the most effective fix?
options: Wrap every screen in memo so unchanged props skip rendering
Move the cart into an external store and have components subscribe with selectors to only the slice they read, keeping theme and user in context
Replace useState with useReducer inside the AppContext provider
Copy the cart into each screen's local state on mount
questions.explanation: Every consumer of a context re-renders when its value changes, and memo does not stop that. An external store read through selectors (as with useSyncExternalStore) re-renders only components whose selected slice changed. Rarely changing values like theme can stay in context.
rationales: memo skips renders on equal props, but a component that reads a changed context still re-renders.
Correct. Selectors limit re-renders to the components that need the new value.
useReducer changes how state updates, not who re-renders.
Local copies drift out of sync with the real cart.

sources.title: Passing data deeply with context — React Learn

questions.scenario: A team fetches orders with useQuery, then in onSuccess-style effects copies the result into a global Zustand-style store that every screen reads. After a user edits an order on another screen, the list shows the old values until restart.
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Write the edited order into both the store and the query cache by hand
Persist the store to AsyncStorage so it survives restarts
Read orders directly from the query, invalidate the orders key after the edit, and keep the store for client-only UI state
Set staleTime to 0 on the orders query
questions.explanation: Server data should have one home, the query cache, where invalidation and refetch keep it current. Copying it into a client store creates a second copy that nothing refreshes. Stores are for client state such as filters or UI toggles.
rationales: Keeping two copies in sync by hand is the anti-pattern that caused the bug.
Persisting a stale copy makes it survive restarts, which is worse.
Correct. One source of truth for server data.
staleTime is already 0 by default; the store copy is never refreshed regardless.

questions.scenario: A developer is reviewing an expo-sqlite data layer before release.
questions.stem: Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: If SQLCipher is not enabled, PRAGMA key throws an error, so a missing setup is caught at startup
Building SQL with string concatenation is safe because expo-sqlite escapes every value it executes
withTransactionAsync is not exclusive, so other queries can interleave with the transaction
Tracking the schema version with PRAGMA user_version is a documented way to run migrations in order
questions.explanation: The expo-sqlite docs say withTransactionAsync is not exclusive and recommend PRAGMA user_version for migrations. PRAGMA key silently does nothing without SQLCipher, so check PRAGMA cipher_version. Only bound parameters in prepared statements are escaped.
rationales: It fails silently, which is why the docs recommend checking PRAGMA cipher_version.
Escaping applies to bound parameters, not to strings you concatenate into SQL.
Correct. Use withExclusiveTransactionAsync when you need exclusivity.
Correct. user_version tracks the schema version.

questions.scenario: A banking app stores a device key in SecureStore with requireAuthentication: true. After a user adds a new fingerprint in system settings, reading the key fails and the app crashes on launch.
questions.stem: How should the app handle this?
options: Treat the failure as expected invalidation: catch it, delete the item, send the user through full sign-in and store a fresh key
Switch the key to AsyncStorage so biometric changes cannot affect it
Retry getItemAsync in a loop until biometrics succeed
Set keychainAccessible to ALWAYS so the key is readable without unlocking
questions.explanation: The SecureStore docs state that values saved with requireAuthentication become inaccessible when biometrics change. That is a security feature, so the app should recover by re-authenticating the user and creating a new value rather than crashing.
rationales: Correct. Recover with a full sign-in and re-store.
This gives up encryption for a secret.
The old value will never become readable again; a loop only hangs the app.
Accessibility settings do not bring back an item invalidated by a biometric change, and weakening them lowers protection.

questions.scenario: A login screen wraps its fields and a Sign in button in a ScrollView. With the keyboard open, users tap Sign in and the keyboard closes, but nothing is submitted; a second tap works.
questions.stem: Which change fixes this?
options: Call Keyboard.dismiss() in the button's onPress
Wrap the button in an InputAccessoryView
Set blurOnSubmit on every TextInput
Set keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled" on the ScrollView
questions.explanation: With the default keyboardShouldPersistTaps="never", a tap outside the focused input dismisses the keyboard and the child never receives it. "handled" lets taps on children that handle them, such as buttons, go through.
rationales: onPress never runs on the first tap, so this changes nothing.
InputAccessoryView is iOS-only and deprecated as of RN 0.88; it also does not change tap handling.
Return-key behaviour does not affect taps on a button.
Correct. Taps reach the button while the keyboard is open.

questions.scenario: A sign-up handler calls SignUp.parse(values) and then submits. When the email is invalid, the app shows a red error screen in development and nothing helpful to users in production.
questions.stem: What should the handler do instead?
options: Call SignUp.safeParse(values), and if success is false map the error to per-field messages; otherwise submit result.data
Wrap the whole screen in an error boundary that shows "Invalid form"
Validate with a regular expression in each onChangeText instead of Zod
Disable the Sign up button permanently until all fields are filled
questions.explanation: parse throws on invalid input, while safeParse returns a result object with success and either data or error. Branching on it lets the form show field errors, for example from z.flattenError(error).fieldErrors, without exceptions.
rationales: Correct. Invalid input becomes a normal branch.
Error boundaries catch render errors, not exceptions thrown in event handlers, and they give no field-level feedback.
This duplicates rules outside the schema and loses the inferred type.
Filled is not the same as valid, and users still get no explanation.

questions.scenario: An accessibility audit of a checkout form finds that fields only have placeholder text, invalid fields get a red border, and TalkBack users do not learn why submission failed.
questions.stem: Which change best addresses the findings?
options: Add visible labels exposed as each field's accessible name, and render each error as text in a container with accessibilityLiveRegion="polite" so it is announced
Make the red border thicker and add a shake animation
Set accessible={false} on the inputs so TalkBack skips the confusing fields
Put the error text in the placeholder of the invalid field
questions.explanation: Placeholders disappear when typing and are not a reliable label, and colour alone does not convey an error to screen reader users. A labelled field plus error text in a polite live region gives TalkBack users the name and the reason for failure.
rationales: Correct. Named fields and announced error text.
Still colour and motion only; nothing is announced.
Hiding inputs from assistive technology makes the form unusable.
Placeholder text vanishes when the user types and is still not announced as an error.

questions.scenario: A login form has an email field and a password field. The team wants the right keyboard, password autofill and a masked password.
questions.stem: Which two configurations should they use? (Select two.)
options: On the email field: keyboardType="email-address", autoCapitalize="none" and autoComplete="email"
On the password field: secureTextEntry with autoComplete="password"
On the password field: keyboardType="visible-password" to hide the characters
A new InputAccessoryView toolbar, the recommended way to add a Next button in RN 0.88
questions.explanation: keyboardType, autoCapitalize and autoComplete give the email field the right keyboard and autofill. secureTextEntry masks the password and autoComplete lets the OS offer saved credentials. visible-password is an Android keyboard type that shows the text.
rationales: Correct. Right keyboard, no auto-capitalisation, autofill hint.
Correct. Masked input plus credential autofill.
visible-password shows the password; it is the opposite of masking.
InputAccessoryView is deprecated in RN 0.88 in favour of react-native-keyboard-controller.

questions.scenario: A notes app persists its TanStack Query cache. A user creates three notes in airplane mode, force-quits the app, reopens it and reconnects. The notes never reach the server; the restored mutations stay paused.
questions.stem: What is missing?
options: setMutationDefaults registering a mutationFn for the note mutation key, followed by resumePausedMutations once the cache is restored
A longer gcTime so the mutations are not garbage collected
retry: Infinity on the mutation
Calling invalidateQueries(['notes']) after launch
questions.explanation: Functions cannot be serialised, so a restored mutation has no mutationFn. The mutations guide says to register defaults with setMutationDefaults so persisted mutations can resume, then call resumePausedMutations.
rationales: Correct. Restored mutations need a default mutationFn and an explicit resume.
The mutations were restored; they cannot run because they have no function.
Retries do not help a mutation with nothing to execute.
Invalidation refetches queries; it does not replay paused mutations.

questions.scenario: While offline, a user renames a task, then marks it done, then renames it again. On reconnect the server sometimes ends with the first name, because requests overtake each other.
questions.stem: What is the most direct fix in TanStack Query?
options: Call cancelQueries before each mutation
Raise retry so failed requests try again sooner
Give these mutations the same scope id (for example scope: { id: 'task-' + taskId }) so they run in serial
Merge all edits into a single mutation by debouncing the UI for 30 seconds
questions.explanation: Mutations that share a scope id run in serial, so later edits wait for earlier ones. That guarantees the server applies the rename, completion and second rename in the order the user made them.
rationales: cancelQueries affects query refetches, not mutation ordering.
Retries do not order independent requests.
Correct. Scoped mutations run one at a time.
Debouncing delays writes and still does not guarantee order across retries.

questions.scenario: Two technicians edit the same work order offline: one changes the notes, the other the parts list. When both sync, the second upload silently overwrites the first technician's notes.
questions.stem: Which design best prevents the lost update?
options: Send the record version the edit was based on in an If-Match header; the server rejects stale writes with 412 Precondition Failed and the client merges or asks the user
Upload the whole record with a client timestamp and let the latest timestamp win
Disable editing while offline
Retry the upload until it succeeds
questions.explanation: Conditional requests make the server compare the version the client edited with its current version and refuse the write with 412 if they differ. The client then resolves the conflict, for example by merging the non-overlapping fields, instead of overwriting.
rationales: Correct. Optimistic concurrency detects the conflict instead of hiding it.
Last write wins by timestamp is exactly what loses the notes; device clocks also differ.
This breaks the offline-first requirement.
Retrying a blind write still overwrites.

questions.scenario: A queued "place order" request times out on a train. The order was actually created, but the response was lost. On reconnect the queue replays the request and the customer is charged twice.
questions.stem: What should the team add?
options: A new random idempotency key on each retry so the server can tell attempts apart
A shorter request timeout
An idempotency key generated once when the user places the order, stored with the queued request and sent on every retry
A rule that drops queued requests older than one minute
questions.explanation: An idempotency key lets the server recognise a repeated request and return the original result instead of performing the operation again. It only works if the same key is reused for every attempt of the same user action.
rationales: New keys make each retry look like a new order, which is the bug.
Shorter timeouts make lost responses more likely, not less.
Correct. One key per action, reused on retries.
Dropping old requests loses legitimate orders and does not prevent duplicates.

questions.scenario: A team is designing reconnect behaviour for an offline-capable field app.
questions.stem: Which two choices fit an offline-first design? (Select two.)
options: Show a full-screen blocking "No connection" modal until the device is online
Clear the persisted mutation queue on every launch to avoid stale writes
Wire onlineManager to network state so paused mutations resume and stale queries refetch when the device reconnects
Retry failed sync requests with exponential backoff instead of a tight loop
questions.explanation: With onlineManager wired up, TanStack Query pauses work while offline and resumes it in order when the device reconnects. Exponential backoff, the library's default for queries, avoids hammering a flaky network. Blocking the UI or discarding the queue defeats offline-first.
rationales: Offline-first means the app stays usable offline.
Clearing the queue loses user work made while offline.
Correct. This is the reconnect trigger for queries and paused mutations.
Correct. Backoff spaces out retries on unreliable networks.

questions.scenario: A receipt-tracking app requests camera, location and notification permissions on the first launch screen. Many users deny all three, and the scan feature later fails with no explanation.
questions.stem: Which change best addresses the problem?
options: Request the camera permission when the user taps "Scan receipt", after a short in-app explanation, and keep other features usable if it is denied.
Keep the launch-time prompts but block the app until all three permissions are granted.
Request all three permissions again on every launch until the user grants them.
Remove the camera purpose string so iOS grants camera access automatically.
questions.explanation: Asking in context, with an explanation, gives the user a reason to grant access and matches Apple guidance on consent. Apple 5.1.2(i) bars requiring unrelated system features to use the app, and the OS will not re-prompt after a denial anyway.
rationales: Correct: contextual requests with an explanation, plus graceful degradation, are the expected pattern.
Blocking the app on unrelated permissions conflicts with Apple 5.1.2(i).
The OS will not show the dialog again after a denial, so repeated requests do nothing.
iOS requires a purpose string to request camera access; removing it breaks the feature.

questions.scenario: A user denied the camera permission months ago. Now they tap "Scan" and requestCameraPermissionsAsync returns status denied with canAskAgain false.
questions.stem: What should the app do?
options: Call the request method in a loop until the dialog appears.
Explain why the camera is needed and offer a button that calls Linking.openSettings(), then re-check the status when the app returns to the foreground.
Ship an EAS Update with a new purpose string so the dialog shows again.
Silently fall back to reading the media library without asking.
questions.explanation: After a denial the OS will not re-prompt, so the only path is the app settings page. Linking.openSettings() opens it, and the app should re-check the permission when it comes back to the foreground.
rationales: The system dialog will not reappear after a permanent denial.
Correct: explain, deep link to settings, and re-check on return.
Info.plist changes cannot ship over-the-air, and a new string would not reset a denial.
Accessing another protected resource without consent is not an acceptable workaround.

questions.scenario: App Review rejects a build because the NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription text is too vague. The team edits ios.infoPlist in app.config.ts.
questions.stem: How should the corrected purpose string reach users?
options: Publish it with eas update to the production channel.
Change it at runtime by calling a permissions API with the new text.
Create a new native build that includes the updated Info.plist and submit it for review.
Store the text in EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables so it can change without a build.
questions.explanation: Purpose strings live in Info.plist, which is part of the native binary. The Expo permissions guide states that Info.plist changes cannot be updated over-the-air, so a new build is required.
rationales: EAS Update delivers JavaScript and assets, not Info.plist changes.
There is no runtime API that rewrites the system purpose string.
Correct: native configuration changes require a new build.
Environment variables are inlined into JavaScript and do not affect Info.plist.

questions.scenario: An Android app targeting API 36 lets users choose one profile photo. The team plans to request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES so it can show its own grid of the user's photos.
questions.stem: What is the best approach under Google Play policy?
options: Request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES; any app that touches photos may use it.
Use the system photo picker and do not request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES.
Request READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE instead to avoid the declaration.
Request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES but only after the user taps the avatar.
questions.explanation: Google Play allows READ_MEDIA_IMAGES for apps targeting API 33+ only if system pickers are not sufficient for core functionality, with a Console declaration. Choosing one profile photo is exactly what the system picker covers.
rationales: Play restricts these permissions to apps whose core function needs broad access.
Correct: the system picker covers one-off selection with no broad permission.
Swapping in a broader legacy storage permission works against the policy's goal of minimal access and does not remove the need to justify broad media access.
Good timing does not change whether the permission is allowed at all.
