questions.scenario: A team adds a video library and discovers the Android build now declares RECORD_AUDIO, which their app never uses.
questions.stem: How should they remove it in an Expo project using continuous native generation?
options: Delete the line from android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml by hand.
Add "RECORD_AUDIO" to android.permissions.
Add "android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO" to android.blockedPermissions in app config.
Leave it; unused permissions are stripped automatically by the Play Store.
questions.explanation: android.blockedPermissions removes permissions that dependencies add, and it needs the full permission name. A hand edit to generated native files is lost when the project is regenerated.
rationales: In a CNG project the android folder is regenerated, so hand edits do not persist.
android.permissions adds permissions; it does not remove them.
Correct: blockedPermissions with the full name removes the merged permission.
The store does not strip declared permissions for you.

questions.scenario: On Android 14 devices, a development build calls requestPermissionsAsync for notifications on first launch, but no dialog ever appears. iOS works. The channel is created later, after login.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Add the notification field to app.json.
Switch to Expo Go to test notifications on Android.
Create the notification channel with setNotificationChannelAsync before requesting permission and fetching the token.
Set priority to high in every push message.
questions.explanation: On Android 13 and later, the notification permission prompt will not appear until at least one channel exists. Creating the channel first lets the prompt show.
rationales: The notification field was removed from the app.json schema in SDK 55 and makes prebuild fail.
Push does not work in Expo Go on Android.
Correct: the channel must exist before the Android 13+ prompt appears.
Message priority affects delivery, not whether the permission dialog appears.

questions.scenario: A new project calls getExpoPushTokenAsync() with no arguments in a development build and gets ERR_NOTIFICATIONS_NO_EXPERIENCE_ID.
questions.stem: What should the developer change?
options: Call getDevicePushTokenAsync and send that token to Expo's push API.
Pass the EAS projectId, for example getExpoPushTokenAsync({ projectId }).
Retry the call after a delay; the error is transient.
Request notification permission again.
questions.explanation: getExpoPushTokenAsync fails with ERR_NOTIFICATIONS_NO_EXPERIENCE_ID when it has no projectId. Passing the EAS project ID resolves it.
rationales: A native device token is for sending through APNs/FCM directly, not Expo's push API.
Correct: the Expo push token needs the projectId.
The error is deterministic, not transient.
The error concerns the missing project ID, not permission.

questions.scenario: A backend sends pushes through the Expo push API and logs success because every ticket has status ok. Users of reinstalled apps never receive messages, and the backend keeps sending to their old tokens.
questions.stem: Which two changes should the backend make? (Select two.)
options: Fetch push receipts for the ticket IDs some minutes later instead of treating tickets as delivery confirmation.
Stop sending to and delete tokens whose receipt reports DeviceNotRegistered.
Resend every message three times to make delivery more likely.
Raise the payload above 4096 bytes so APNs prioritizes it.
questions.explanation: A ticket ok only means Expo's servers received the message; delivery errors show up in receipts fetched later. DeviceNotRegistered means the token is dead and should no longer be used.
rationales: Correct: receipts reveal delivery errors that tickets cannot.
Correct: DeviceNotRegistered tokens must be pruned.
Blind resends waste rate limit and can trigger MessageRateExceeded.
Payloads over 4096 bytes fail with MessageTooBig.

questions.scenario: A chat app on SDK 58 wants foreground notifications for other conversations to appear as a banner and in Notification Center, but not for the conversation currently open.
questions.stem: How should it configure foreground behavior?
options: Return shouldShowAlert: true from setNotificationHandler for all notifications.
In setNotificationHandler, return shouldShowBanner and shouldShowList as false for the open conversation and true otherwise.
Do nothing; notifications are never shown while the app is in the foreground.
Remove the addNotificationReceivedListener so the OS decides.
questions.explanation: setNotificationHandler controls foreground presentation, and shouldShowBanner and shouldShowList replace the deprecated shouldShowAlert. Since SDK 58, foreground notifications show by default unless the handler says otherwise, so the handler must suppress the open conversation.
rationales: shouldShowAlert is deprecated, and showing everything ignores the requirement.
Correct: decide per notification with the current flags.
From SDK 58, foreground notifications are shown by default.
The received listener observes notifications; it does not control presentation.

questions.scenario: Tapping a push while the app is running opens the right order screen. Tapping one when the app was fully closed just opens the home screen. The app only uses addNotificationResponseReceivedListener registered in a screen effect.
questions.stem: What should be added?
options: Read useLastNotificationResponse at startup and navigate based on it.
Add addNotificationReceivedListener to the root layout.
Increase the push priority to high so the listener fires sooner.
Register a background task to open the screen.
questions.explanation: When a tap cold-starts the app, the response can arrive before the screen listener is registered. useLastNotificationResponse exposes the tap that launched the app so routing can use it.
rationales: Correct: it covers the cold-start tap case.
The received listener fires for notifications arriving in the foreground, not taps.
Priority does not change when JavaScript registers its listener.
Background tasks process data; they do not handle the user's tap navigation.

questions.stem: A developer on SDK 58 wants to test push notifications on an Android phone. Where should they run the app?
options: In Expo Go from the Play Store.
In a development build of the app.
In the Android emulator inside Expo Go only.
In a web build opened in Chrome on the phone.
questions.explanation: Push notifications are not supported in Expo Go on Android since SDK 53, and since SDK 55 the call throws. A development build includes the native notification setup.
rationales: Expo Go on Android does not support push.
Correct: use a development build.
The emulator still runs Expo Go, which lacks Android push support.
A web build does not exercise the native push path.

questions.scenario: A company already runs a notification service that sends directly to APNs and FCM for its native apps. It is moving one app to Expo and does not want a second delivery pipeline.
questions.stem: Which token should the Expo app register with that service?
options: The Expo push token from getExpoPushTokenAsync.
The native device token from getDevicePushTokenAsync.
The EAS project ID.
An access token for the Expo push API.
questions.explanation: expo-notifications exposes the native device token for apps that send through APNs and FCM themselves. Expo push tokens only work with Expo's push service, which relays to APNs and FCM.
rationales: Expo push tokens are addressed through Expo's push API, not APNs or FCM directly.
Correct: the native token works with the existing APNs/FCM service.
The project ID identifies the project; it is not a device address.
An Expo access token secures sending through Expo, which this team is not using.

questions.scenario: A run-tracking app requests foreground location, then background location. On some iPhones tracking stops when the screen locks, and no error is shown. UIBackgroundModes includes location.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: The app forgot to set isAndroidBackgroundLocationEnabled.
expo-location does not support background tracking on iOS.
The minimumInterval of the background task is too long.
Those users chose "Allow Once" for foreground access, so the background request silently failed.
questions.explanation: The Expo location docs note that if the user chose "Allow Once", a later background request will silently fail. Background tracking on iOS needs the "Always" grant plus the location background mode.
rationales: That option configures Android, not iOS.
Background location works on iOS with "Always" and UIBackgroundModes location.
Location updates are not driven by expo-background-task intervals.
Correct: Allow Once causes the background request to fail silently.

questions.scenario: A delivery-driver app needs background location on Android as its core feature and is preparing a Play submission.
questions.stem: Which two items does Google Play require? (Select two.)
options: A privacy policy link in the app's splash screen only.
Requesting background location in the same dialog as foreground location on first launch.
A prominent in-app disclosure before the runtime prompt that mentions location and use even when the app is closed or not in use.
A declaration form in the Play Console plus a short video showing the feature.
questions.explanation: Google Play requires a prominent disclosure shown before the prompt using the specified wording, and a declaration form with a short video. Expo also requires foreground permission before background permission.
rationales: A splash-screen link does not satisfy the prominent disclosure requirement.
Foreground permission must come first, and asking at launch lacks context.
Correct: the prominent disclosure is required before the prompt.
Correct: the declaration form and video are part of the review.

sources.title: Background location access — Google Play Console Help

questions.scenario: A team sets expo-background-task minimumInterval to 5 minutes so prices refresh every 5 minutes. On iOS, logs show runs hours apart, mostly at night.
questions.stem: What is the right conclusion?
options: The task is misconfigured; iOS runs background tasks exactly at minimumInterval.
Background tasks are scheduled by the OS with a 15-minute floor and no exact timing; time-sensitive updates should be server-driven, for example by push.
Lowering minimumInterval to 1 minute will make runs regular.
Test on the iOS simulator to get accurate scheduling.
questions.explanation: expo-background-task uses BGTaskScheduler and WorkManager, has a 15-minute minimum, and tasks do not run exactly on schedule; iOS often runs them overnight. Timely updates need a server-driven mechanism.
rationales: The docs say tasks will not run exactly on schedule.
Correct: OS-scheduled with a floor, so use the server for timely events.
The minimum is 15 minutes, so lower values do not help.
Background tasks are unavailable on the iOS simulator.

questions.scenario: A background sync task never runs after the app is killed. The code calls TaskManager.defineTask inside a useEffect in the Settings screen.
questions.stem: What should change?
options: Move TaskManager.defineTask to global (module) scope so it is defined whenever the JavaScript bundle loads.
Call defineTask again on every render.
Raise minimumInterval to 24 hours.
Move the call into the root layout's useEffect.
questions.explanation: When the OS wakes the app to run a task, no screen is mounted, so a task defined inside a component does not exist. The docs require defineTask in global scope.
rationales: Correct: module scope ensures the task is defined in headless launches.
Defining it on render still depends on the screen being mounted.
The interval is not the problem.
An effect in any component still requires UI to mount.

questions.scenario: A team implements Google sign-in by loading the provider's login page in a react-native-webview and keeps the OAuth client secret in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable to exchange the code in the app.
questions.stem: Which two changes align with RFC 8252 and Expo guidance? (Select two.)
options: Use the system browser through AuthSession with PKCE instead of an embedded WebView.
Exchange the authorization code on a server if a client secret is required, and keep the secret off the device.
Obfuscate the client secret in the JavaScript bundle.
Inject JavaScript into the WebView to autofill the password.
questions.explanation: RFC 8252 says native apps must use an external user-agent and public clients must use PKCE. Expo warns that client code is not a secure place for secrets, so a required secret belongs on a server.
rationales: Correct: system browser plus PKCE is required for native apps.
Correct: move any secret exchange to the server.
Obfuscated secrets in the app are still extractable and not confidential.
Controlling the login page in an embedded WebView is what RFC 8252 forbids.

questions.scenario: A banking app stores the OAuth refresh token in AsyncStorage. A security review flags it.
questions.stem: Which storage approach is most appropriate?
options: Keep AsyncStorage but base64-encode the token.
Store it in expo-secure-store, optionally with a THIS_DEVICE_ONLY accessibility option so it does not migrate via backup.
Put it in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ environment variable.
Store it in app config extra so it is available at startup.
questions.explanation: expo-secure-store uses the iOS Keychain and Keystore-encrypted storage on Android, which suits tokens. The THIS_DEVICE_ONLY variants keep the value from migrating via backup.
rationales: Encoding is not encryption; AsyncStorage stays unencrypted.
Correct: SecureStore is designed for secrets like tokens.
Environment variables are inlined at build time and readable in the app.
App config is embedded in builds and must not hold sensitive data.

questions.scenario: An app stores a refresh token in SecureStore with requireAuthentication: true. After a user enrolls a new fingerprint, reading the item fails every time.
questions.stem: How should the app handle this?
options: Catch the failure, delete the stored item, and send the user through a full sign-in to create a new one.
Retry the read in a loop until it succeeds.
Store a second unprotected copy of the token as a fallback.
Disable requireAuthentication for all users.
questions.explanation: SecureStore values saved with requireAuthentication become inaccessible when biometrics change. That is a designed security property, so the app should recover with a fresh sign-in.
rationales: Correct: treat it as an expected path and re-authenticate.
The value will not become readable again.
An unprotected copy defeats the purpose of the biometric gate.
Removing the protection for everyone weakens security for an edge case with a clear recovery path.

questions.scenario: An Expo app needs one platform API that no library wraps. The team needs two small async functions in Swift and Kotlin and no C++.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Write a config plugin that adds the native code during prebuild.
Write a local module with the Expo Modules API and run it in a development build.
Call the platform API from JavaScript through fetch.
Write a Turbo Module in C++ and test it in Expo Go.
questions.explanation: The Expo Modules API is the usual way to wrap Swift and Kotlin code in an Expo app, with performance comparable to Turbo Modules. Native code needs a development build rather than Expo Go.
rationales: Config plugins modify native configuration; they are not the place for module logic.
Correct: an Expo module in a development build fits this case.
fetch cannot reach native platform APIs.
C++ is not needed, and Expo Go cannot load custom native code.

questions.scenario: A team using continuous native generation adds a custom key to ios/MyApp/Info.plist by hand. The key disappears from later builds.
questions.stem: What is the durable fix?
options: Commit the ios folder and keep editing it by hand while still relying on prebuild.
Add the key through ios.infoPlist or a config plugin using withInfoPlist so prebuild generates it every time.
Ship the key with eas update.
Set the key at runtime from JavaScript on app start.
questions.explanation: With CNG the native folders are generated and gitignored, so hand edits are lost when they are regenerated. App config or a config plugin, whose mods run during prebuild, makes the change reproducible.
rationales: Committing native folders means EAS Build will not run prebuild, so plugins stop applying, and mixing both is fragile.
Correct: put the change in config or a plugin.
Info.plist changes cannot ship over-the-air.
Info.plist is read from the binary; JavaScript cannot add keys at runtime.

questions.stem: A team must expose an existing C++ image library to JavaScript in a React Native app on the New Architecture. Which approach does the Expo modules overview point to?
options: The Expo Modules API, because it is required for New Architecture support.
A Turbo Module, because you need C++.
A config plugin, because it can link C++ sources.
The legacy bridge, because it supports C++.
questions.explanation: Expo's overview says both Expo Modules and Turbo Modules use JSI and support the New Architecture with comparable performance, and recommends Turbo Modules if you need C++. The Legacy Architecture no longer exists in current React Native.
rationales: Both options support the New Architecture; the Expo API is not required.
Correct: C++ is the stated reason to choose Turbo Modules.
Config plugins change native configuration, not module code.
The legacy bridge has been removed from React Native.

questions.scenario: An iOS app lets users create their primary account only by signing in with a third-party social login.
questions.stem: What does App Review Guideline 4.8 require?
options: Nothing; any third-party login is acceptable on its own.
Also offer an equivalent login option that limits data to name and email, allows a private email, and does not track without consent.
Remove third-party login and use only email and password.
Require users to enable tracking before signing in.
questions.explanation: Guideline 4.8 says apps using third-party login for the primary account must offer an equivalent option with those privacy properties. Third-party login can stay alongside it.
rationales: Guideline 4.8 adds a requirement for primary-account third-party login.
Correct: an equivalent privacy-preserving option is required.
Third-party login is allowed; the rule adds an option rather than banning it.
Requiring tracking conflicts with Apple's privacy guidelines.

questions.scenario: A news app is preparing for App Review. The product team proposes several onboarding changes.
questions.stem: Which two proposals comply with Apple's App Review Guidelines on permissions? (Select two.)
options: Block the article list until the user grants location so local news can be shown.
Use a purpose string that just says "Needed for app features".
Let users read articles without granting notification permission, and offer alerts later from a settings toggle.
Use the system share sheet to let users share an article instead of requesting Contacts access.
questions.explanation: Apple 5.1.2(i) bars requiring system features such as push or location to use the app, and 5.1.1(iii) prefers share sheets and pickers over full access to protected resources. Purpose strings must clearly and completely describe the use of data, which a generic string does not.
rationales: Requiring location to read articles conflicts with 5.1.2(i).
5.1.1(ii) requires purpose strings that clearly and completely describe the use.
Correct: functionality stays available without the permission.
Correct: a share sheet avoids requesting Contacts access.

questions.scenario: Tapping "Apply filters" re-renders a large results screen. Users report that the button shows no pressed feedback for about 300 ms, then everything updates at once.
questions.stem: Which change most directly lets the pressed feedback appear immediately?
options: Increase the button's `hitSlop` so the press registers sooner
Wrap the expensive state update in `requestAnimationFrame` so the feedback can paint first
Defer the work with `InteractionManager.runAfterInteractions`
Move the button into a `ScrollView` so it renders on the UI thread
questions.explanation: When `onPress` triggers heavy work in the same frame, the opacity or highlight change only appears after the handler returns. The React Native performance guide recommends wrapping the expensive action in `requestAnimationFrame`. `InteractionManager` was removed in SDK 58 / RN 0.88.
rationales: `hitSlop` widens the touch area; it does nothing about a blocked JS thread.
Correct. Deferring the work one frame lets the pressed state render before the re-render.
`InteractionManager` has been removed from current React Native, so this is not a valid fix.
Only scrolling itself runs natively; the button's press handling is still JavaScript.

questions.scenario: A trace on a 120 Hz phone shows the list screen spending about 12 ms of JavaScript work per frame while scrolling. The same build looked smooth on a 60 Hz test device.
questions.stem: What best explains the stutter on the 120 Hz phone?
options: High-refresh devices run React Native in dev mode by default
120 Hz displays move scrolling onto the JS thread
The trace is wrong because frames above 60 Hz are not measured
12 ms exceeds the roughly 8.33 ms per-frame budget at 120 Hz, though it fits the 16.67 ms budget at 60 Hz
questions.explanation: At 60 Hz each frame has at most 16.67 ms; at 120 Hz the arithmetic gives about 8.33 ms. Work that fits one budget can blow the other, so per-frame JS work must shrink for high-refresh screens.
rationales: Dev mode depends on the build, not the display.
Scrolling stays on the UI thread regardless of refresh rate.
Nothing suggests the trace is invalid; the budget arithmetic explains it.
Correct. The frame budget halves at 120 Hz.

questions.scenario: A tester records severe jank on a feed screen while running the app from `npx expo start` in development mode and files a ticket to rewrite the feed.
questions.stem: What should the team do first?
options: Rewrite the feed with FlashList immediately
Reproduce and measure on a release build before changing code
Increase `windowSize` to 51
Disable Hermes to get clearer stack traces
questions.explanation: JavaScript thread performance suffers greatly in development mode, so dev measurements overstate jank. The React Native docs say to test performance in release builds, and the profiling guide says to make sure development mode is off before profiling.
rationales: Might help later, but rewriting before measuring a release build risks fixing the wrong thing.
Correct. Measure in a release build first.
A larger window adds memory and JS work and is not a diagnostic step.
Disabling Hermes changes the engine and does not address dev-mode distortion.

questions.scenario: A production build feels sluggish on older Android phones. The codebase has many `console.log` calls, and the state layer uses a logging middleware that prints every action.
questions.stem: Which change addresses this cause most completely?
options: Wrap each log in `if (__DEV__)` by hand
Add `babel-plugin-transform-remove-console` to the production Babel environment
Replace `console.log` with `console.warn`
Turn on `removeClippedSubviews`
questions.explanation: In a bundled app `console.*` statements can be a big bottleneck on the JS thread, including those from libraries such as redux-logger. The Babel plugin removes all of them in production, including calls you did not write.
rationales: Helps for your own calls but misses third-party library logging and is easy to forget.
Correct. It strips every `console.*` call from the production bundle.
`console.warn` is still a console call with the same cost.
That affects off-screen list views, not logging.

questions.scenario: Perf Monitor shows the UI thread at 60 fps but the JS thread dropping to 15 fps whenever a data refresh runs. During those refreshes a header collapse animation built with core `Animated` (no options set), which moves the header with `translateY` and fades it with `opacity`, freezes.
questions.stem: Which two changes would keep the animation smooth during refreshes? (Select two.)
options: Set `useNativeDriver: true` on the `Animated` animation (supported because it animates only non-layout properties such as transform and opacity)
Rebuild the animation with Reanimated shared values and `useAnimatedStyle`
Throttle the animation with `setTimeout` calls of 16 ms
Raise `maxToRenderPerBatch` on the feed list
questions.explanation: Core `Animated` calculates each keyframe on the JS thread unless `useNativeDriver: true` is set, so a busy JS thread freezes it. Moving the animation to the native driver or to Reanimated worklets, which run on the UI thread, decouples it from the refresh work.
rationales: Correct. The native driver computes frames off the JS thread.
Correct. Reanimated runs animation worklets on the UI thread.
`setTimeout` still runs on the blocked JS thread.
Bigger batches add more JS work per batch.

questions.scenario: A contacts list uses `FlatList` with rows that are always 64 points tall. Jumping to a letter with `scrollToIndex` is slow and sometimes lands in the wrong place.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Provide `getItemLayout` returning length 64 and offset 64 x index
Set `initialNumToRender` to the full contact count
Switch `keyExtractor` to use the index
Wrap the list in a `ScrollView`
questions.explanation: For fixed-height rows, `getItemLayout` lets FlatList compute offsets without measuring rendered items. That speeds rendering and makes index-based scrolling exact.
rationales: Correct. Known heights remove the need to measure.
Rendering every row defeats virtualisation and hurts startup and memory.
Index keys lose identity on insert or delete and do not help offsets.
Nesting a virtualised list in a ScrollView breaks virtualisation.

sources.title: Optimizing FlatList configuration — React Native docs

questions.scenario: An image-heavy FlatList runs out of memory on low-end Android devices. Rows are already memoised and use cached images. Scrolling speed is moderate.
questions.stem: Which FlatList change trades a little blank-area risk for lower memory use?
options: Lower `windowSize` from its default of 21
Raise `initialNumToRender` to 50
Raise `updateCellsBatchingPeriod` to 500 ms and `maxToRenderPerBatch` to 100
Set `removeClippedSubviews` to false
questions.explanation: `windowSize` sets how many viewports of content stay rendered; the default 21 keeps 10 above and 10 below. Lowering it reduces memory, at the cost of possible blank areas when the user scrolls fast.
rationales: Correct. A smaller window keeps fewer rows mounted.
More initial rows means more memory, not less.
Huge batches block the JS thread longer and do not reduce what stays mounted.
On Android it already defaults to true; turning it off keeps more views attached.

sources.title: Optimizing FlatList configuration — React Native docs

questions.scenario: A chat screen passes `renderItem={({ item }) => <Message item={item} />}` inline to a `FlatList`. Typing in the composer updates parent state, and profiling shows every visible `Message` re-rendering on each keystroke.
questions.stem: Which two changes stop the unnecessary row re-renders? (Select two.)
options: Use the array index as the key
Increase `windowSize`
Wrap `Message` in `memo`
Define `renderItem` with `useCallback` so its identity is stable
questions.explanation: A memoised row skips rendering when its props are unchanged, and a stable `renderItem` keeps the list from treating every render as new. The React Native list guide recommends both. Keys and window sizes do not stop parent-driven re-renders.
rationales: Index keys hurt identity on insert and delete and do not prevent re-renders.
A larger window renders more rows, not fewer.
Correct. `memo` skips re-renders with equal props.
Correct. A stable callback avoids re-rendering rows because a new function was passed.

sources.title: Optimizing FlatList configuration — React Native docs

questions.scenario: After moving a product grid to FlashList, users scrolling quickly briefly see the previous product's photo in a cell before the correct one loads. Images use `expo-image`.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Set `cachePolicy="none"`
Go back to `FlatList`
Set `allowDownscaling={false}`
Set `recyclingKey` on the image to the product id
questions.explanation: FlashList recycles row components, so an image view is reused for a different product. Changing expo-image's `recyclingKey` resets the view to blank or the placeholder before the new image loads, which is the documented fix for recycling lists.
rationales: Disabling the cache makes loads slower and the stale frame longer.
Works but throws away recycling's performance benefit for a one-prop fix.
Turning off downscaling only raises memory use.
Correct. A new key clears stale content on recycle.

questions.scenario: Each row in a FlashList has a "Show details" toggle stored in `useState` inside the row. After expanding row 3 and scrolling, row 27 appears already expanded.
questions.stem: What is happening, and what is the most appropriate fix?
options: FlashList recycles row components, so state stays with the reused instance; store expanded state per item id (or reset it on recycle)
The `keyExtractor` is missing; adding one makes FlashList unmount rows
FlashList is batching renders; lower its batch size
The toggle must use a ref instead of state
questions.explanation: FlashList reuses row components with new data instead of mounting fresh ones, so local state from one item survives into another. Keep per-item UI state keyed by id in the parent or a store, or use FlashList v2's reset helper for item-local state.
rationales: Correct. Recycling carries local state across items.
Recycling still reuses instances; keys alone do not make it unmount rows.
Batching does not move state between items.
A ref is also instance-local and leaks the same way.

questions.scenario: A feed shows the same small avatars on most rows. Using `expo-image` with default settings, the avatars flicker as they are decoded again when rows scroll back into view.
questions.stem: Which setting best reduces the flicker while keeping memory safe?
options: `cachePolicy="memory"`
`cachePolicy="none"`
`priority="low"`
`cachePolicy="memory-disk"`
questions.explanation: The default `cachePolicy` is `disk`. `memory-disk` keeps images in memory with a disk fallback, so frequently reused avatars come from memory. `memory` alone may be purged quickly to avoid out-of-memory errors, losing the disk fallback.
rationales: No disk fallback once memory is purged.
No caching at all, so every appearance reloads.
Priority orders loads; it does not cache.
Correct. Memory for speed, disk as fallback.

questions.scenario: Tapping a thumbnail animates it to full screen by animating its `width` and `height`. On iOS the animation stutters.
questions.stem: What does the React Native performance guide recommend?
options: Animate `transform: [{ scale }]` instead of width and height
Animate `flex` instead
Enable `shouldRasterizeIOS` on every image permanently
Use `LayoutAnimation` for an interruptible drag-to-dismiss
questions.explanation: Resizing an `Image` on iOS re-crops and scales the original image each frame, which is expensive. Animating a scale transform avoids that work. Rasterisation must be used sparingly because it can greatly increase memory.
rationales: Correct. Transforms avoid re-cropping each frame.
Still a layout change that resizes the image.
Overusing rasterisation can make memory use go through the roof.
`LayoutAnimation` only suits fire-and-forget, non-interruptible animations.

questions.scenario: A swipe-to-dismiss card uses a JavaScript touch responder that calls `setState` with the finger position on every move. When a background sync runs, the card lags behind the finger.
questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Debounce `setState` to every 50 ms
Move the sync into the touch handler so it finishes sooner
Switch the card to core `Animated` without the native driver
Recognise the pan with Gesture Handler and drive a Reanimated shared value used in `useAnimatedStyle`
questions.explanation: Gesture Handler recognises gestures on the native thread, and Reanimated computes animated styles in worklets on the UI thread. Together the card follows the finger without waiting for the busy JS thread.
rationales: Debouncing makes tracking choppier and still waits on JS.
Adds more work to the blocked thread.
Without the native driver `Animated` still computes frames on the JS thread.
Correct. Both recognition and animation stay off the JS thread.

questions.scenario: An Expo app replaced `babel-preset-expo` in `babel.config.js` with a hand-picked list of presets and plugins. After upgrading to Reanimated 4, animated styles crash with errors about functions not being workletized.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Reanimated 4 requires the Legacy Architecture; set `newArchEnabled: false`
Reanimated cannot run with Hermes; switch to JavaScriptCore
The worklets Babel plugin is missing; restore `babel-preset-expo` (which configures it) or add `react-native-worklets/plugin` as the last plugin
Reanimated must be installed globally with npm
questions.explanation: Reanimated 4 relies on the `react-native-worklets` Babel plugin to turn functions into worklets, and it must be listed last. In Expo, `babel-preset-expo` sets it up automatically, so a custom config that drops the preset loses it.
rationales: Reanimated 4 runs only on the New Architecture, and `newArchEnabled` was removed in SDK 55.
Reanimated runs on Hermes, the default engine; the engine has nothing to do with missing worklet transforms.
Correct. The plugin transforms worklets at build time.
Libraries are installed per project with `npx expo install`.

questions.scenario: A lead proposes switching the JavaScript engine from Hermes to JavaScriptCore "to see if cold start improves".
questions.stem: What is the strongest reason this is unlikely to help?
options: JavaScriptCore is no longer able to run React Native at all
Hermes caches the whole app in memory between launches
Hermes compiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time, so the device skips parsing and compiling source at launch
Cold start is unaffected by the JavaScript engine
questions.explanation: The React Native docs say Hermes compiles JavaScript to bytecode during the build, improving startup speed, and for many apps lowers memory and app size compared with JavaScriptCore. It is the default for that reason, so effort is better spent on bundle contents and launch work.
rationales: React Native still supports JavaScriptCore through a community package.
Hermes does not keep the app in memory between launches.
Correct. Precompiled bytecode is the startup advantage.
Parsing and compiling JS is a real part of cold start, which is why bytecode helps.

questions.scenario: The production JavaScript bundle grew sharply over two releases and nobody knows which change caused it.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate way to find the cause in an Expo project?
options: Run `EXPO_ATLAS=true npx expo export` and inspect it with `npx expo-atlas` to see module sizes and who imports them
Publish source maps with the production app and inspect them on a device
Measure the bundle from the development server with dev mode on
Delete `node_modules` and reinstall
questions.explanation: Expo Atlas visualises the bundle, including each module's size and its importers, so you can trace a heavy dependency to the import that pulled it in. Expo advises against publishing source maps to production because of security and performance issues.
rationales: Correct. Atlas is Expo's bundle analysis tool.
Expo explicitly says to avoid publishing source maps to production.
Dev mode disables optimisations, so sizes do not match production.
Reinstalling does not show what is in the bundle.

questions.scenario: A rarely visited "Reports" screen imports a large charting library. Because the root layout imports the screen component directly, the chart library is evaluated on every cold start.
questions.stem: Which change most directly removes this cost from startup, and how should it be validated?
options: Load the screen with `React.lazy(() => import(...))` and `Suspense` so its module is evaluated on first render, then compare cold start on a release build
Move the import to the bottom of the root file
Wrap the chart in `memo`
Increase the splash screen duration so users do not notice
questions.explanation: React's `lazy` with a dynamic `import()` defers loading and evaluating a component's module until it is first rendered, which keeps a heavy, rarely used screen out of the startup path. Hermes docs recommend benchmarking before and after on a release build to confirm the gain.
rationales: Correct. Defer the code and measure on a release build.
Static imports are evaluated regardless of their position in the file.
`memo` skips re-renders; it does not delay loading code.
Hides the problem instead of removing the work.

questions.scenario: VoiceOver reads a trash-can icon button as just "button", and TalkBack reads it as "unlabelled, button".
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Add `accessibilityLabel="Delete message"` and a button role to the pressable
Add `accessibilityHint="Trash"` only
Set `accessible={false}` on the icon
Render the word "Delete" in white text on a white background
questions.explanation: Icon-only controls have no text for the screen reader to speak, so they need an `accessibilityLabel` that names the action, plus a role that says it is a button. Hints describe the result of an action and do not replace a label.
rationales: Correct. Label names it; role says what it is.
A hint is supplementary; the element still has no name.
Hides the control from assistive tech entirely.
Hidden text is a hack and breaks with contrast and text-size settings.

questions.scenario: A 24 x 24 point close icon sits in a toolbar row that is 56 points tall. Users with motor impairments often miss it. Design does not want the icon to look bigger.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Add `hitSlop` (or padding) so the touchable area is at least 48dp x 48dp, staying inside the toolbar's bounds
Add a large `hitSlop` of 40 on every side
Increase the icon graphic to 48 x 48
Add `pressRetentionOffset` only
questions.explanation: Android recommends touch targets of at least 48dp x 48dp, and `hitSlop` extends the press area without changing the visible size. The press area never extends past the parent bounds, so a slop larger than the toolbar allows has no effect beyond it.
rationales: Correct. Meets the target size invisibly within the parent.
Slop beyond the parent bounds is ignored, and oversized slop can steal taps from neighbours.
Works for size but ignores the design constraint.
That only controls how far a finger can move away before the press is cancelled.

sources.title: Make apps more accessible — Android Developers

questions.scenario: At the largest system text size several cards clip their titles. A developer proposes setting `allowFontScaling={false}` on every `Text` component.
questions.stem: What is the better approach?
options: Keep font scaling, let containers grow or wrap, and cap only genuinely constrained text with `maxFontSizeMultiplier`
Disable font scaling app-wide as proposed
Set `minimumFontScale` on all text
Use fixed pixel heights on all cards
questions.explanation: `allowFontScaling` defaults to true so text respects the user's text size setting. Turning it off removes that accessibility feature; `maxFontSizeMultiplier` limits growth where layout truly cannot flex.
rationales: Correct. Preserve scaling and limit it only where needed.
Ignores the user's accessibility setting.
Only applies when `adjustsFontSizeToFit` is on, and shrinks text.
Fixed heights cause the clipping in the first place.

questions.scenario: An onboarding carousel uses large parallax movement. Some users turn on Reduce Motion in system settings while the app is open.
questions.stem: Which two steps correctly respect the setting? (Select two.)
options: Read `AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled()` when the screen mounts
Subscribe to the `reduceMotionChanged` event and remove the subscription on unmount
Read the value once at app launch and cache it for the session
Use `isScreenReaderEnabled()` as a proxy for reduced motion
questions.explanation: `isReduceMotionEnabled()` gives the current value and the `reduceMotionChanged` event reports changes, so the screen can swap parallax for fades as soon as the user flips the setting. A screen reader is a different setting.
rationales: Correct. Get the current value.
Correct. React to changes while the app runs.
Misses changes made during the session.
Screen reader use and reduce motion are separate preferences.

questions.scenario: A product card shows a title, price, rating and an "Add" label. TalkBack stops on each text fragment separately, so it takes four swipes to get through one card.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Set `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` on the card
Set `accessible` on the card container with a combined `accessibilityLabel` and an appropriate role
Add `accessibilityHint` to each text
Set `accessibilityLiveRegion="assertive"` on the card
questions.explanation: `accessible` groups a view and its children into one focusable element, and a combined label lets the screen reader announce the card in one stop. Hiding descendants would remove the content entirely, and a live region is for announcing changes.
rationales: Hides the card's content from assistive tech.
Correct. Group into one element with a clear label.
Adds more speech without reducing stops.
Live regions announce updates; they do not group content.

questions.scenario: A design-system button sets `accessibilityRole="link"` for legacy reasons. A newer wrapper also passes `role="button"` to the same element.
questions.stem: What will assistive technology be told?
options: Button, because `role` takes precedence over `accessibilityRole`
Link, because `accessibilityRole` is the native prop
Both roles, announced one after the other
No role, because the conflict cancels both
questions.explanation: The React Native accessibility docs state that `role` has precedence over `accessibilityRole`. Remove the legacy prop to avoid confusion.
rationales: Correct. `role` wins.
The docs say the opposite.
Only one role is exposed.
There is a defined precedence, not cancellation.

questions.scenario: Two CI runners build the production iOS app from different merge commits on the same day. App Store Connect rejects the second upload because its build number was already used. Each runner reads `ios.buildNumber` from app.json.
questions.stem: Which change prevents this most reliably?
options: Have each runner bump `version` in app.json before building.
Derive `ios.buildNumber` from the current timestamp in app.config.ts.
Move `ios.buildNumber` into the profile's `env` block in eas.json.
Set `cli.appVersionSource` to `remote` and `autoIncrement: true` on the production profile so EAS issues build numbers.
questions.explanation: With a remote version source, EAS keeps the build number on its servers and `autoIncrement` bumps it for every build, so parallel runners can't pick the same value. The docs call remote the recommended behavior from EAS CLI 12. Changing `version` or moving values into `env` doesn't give you a shared counter.
rationales: `version` is the user-facing version, which you set deliberately. It isn't the build number that collided.
This might avoid collisions, but it's fragile across time zones and parallel runs, and it isn't the managed mechanism the docs recommend.
`env` sets environment variables for the build process, not the app's build number, and doesn't coordinate runners.
Correct. EAS holds a single counter and increments it for each build.

questions.scenario: A developer adds `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` to the `env` block of the production profile in eas.json so source maps upload during builds. eas.json is committed to the repository.
questions.stem: What should the team do instead?
options: Rename it `EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` so Expo handles it safely.
Keep it in `env`, but make the repository private.
Store the token as an EAS environment variable with secret visibility and select that environment with the profile's `environment` key.
Put the token in app.json `extra` so it's read at runtime.
questions.explanation: The eas.json docs say not to put secrets in `env`, because the file is committed. EAS environment variables with secret visibility can't be read outside Expo's servers, and a profile selects them with `environment`. `EXPO_PUBLIC_` and app config values end up in the app, where anyone can read them.
rationales: `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` values are inlined into the JS bundle in plain text, which exposes the token to anyone with the app.
The token is still in source history and visible to everyone with repository access, and the docs advise against it.
Correct. This keeps the token on EAS and still makes it available to the build.
App config is embedded in the app and must not hold secrets.

sources.title: Environment variables in EAS — Expo docs

questions.scenario: Your Android app uses Play App Signing. The laptop holding the upload keystore was wiped, and there's no backup. A release is due.
questions.stem: What is the correct recovery path?
options: Generate a new keystore with EAS and upload the next build immediately; Play accepts any key for an existing app.
Publish the app under a new package name, because the original app can no longer be updated.
Ask Google to send back the app signing key so you can sign uploads with it.
Ask Google Play support to reset the upload key, register a new upload certificate, and plan for it taking effect about 72 hours later.
questions.explanation: With Play App Signing, Google keeps the app signing key, and you sign uploads with a separate upload key. A lost upload key can be reset through Play support, and the new certificate takes effect 72 hours later. So you lose time, not the app.
rationales: Play rejects uploads signed with an unregistered key until the reset is complete.
This is only necessary without Play App Signing. Here the app signing key is safe with Google.
Google keeps the app signing key. The fix is a new upload key, not handing over the signing key.
Correct. This matches the documented reset flow and its 72-hour delay.

questions.stem: Which statement about iOS signing credentials managed by EAS is accurate?
options: A distribution certificate belongs to the Apple account, so several apps on the same team can use it; provisioning profiles expire after 12 months.
Each app needs its own distribution certificate, and provisioning profiles never expire.
Push notification keys expire every 12 months and must be rotated with each release.
Provisioning profiles belong to the account and can sign any app ID on the team.
questions.explanation: Expo's credentials page says distribution certificates are account-level and provisioning profiles expire after 12 months. Push keys don't expire. A provisioning profile is tied to a specific app ID.
rationales: Correct. These are the account-level and expiry facts the credentials page gives.
Certificates are shared at account level, and profiles do expire.
Push keys don't expire.
A provisioning profile is specific to one app ID, so it can't sign other apps.

questions.scenario: QA wants a production-like Android build of each release candidate that they can install directly on lab phones, without the Play Store and without a development server.
questions.stem: Which two settings belong in the build profile you create for them? (Select two.)
options: `developmentClient: true`
`credentialsSource: "local"`
`distribution: "internal"`
`android.buildType: "apk"`
questions.explanation: Internal distribution produces a build you share by URL instead of through a store, and an APK can be sideloaded directly; the app-bundle format is what Play expects. A development client needs a dev server, which QA doesn't want. Where credentials come from has nothing to do with how testers install the app.
rationales: This makes a development build that loads JS from a dev server, so it isn't production-like.
This controls where EAS reads signing material, not how testers install the app.
Correct. Internal distribution is for direct installs outside the store.
Correct. APKs can be installed directly; app bundles are for Play.

questions.scenario: Release 3.2 shipped last week. The team wants to deliver several fixes this week through EAS Update instead of a store release.
questions.stem: Which two changes can be shipped as an over-the-air update? (Select two.)
options: Fixing a JavaScript bug in the checkout form's validation
Replacing an outdated onboarding image and adjusting its styles
Adding the location permission so a store finder can use GPS
Upgrading from one Expo SDK version to the next
Adding a native Bluetooth library
questions.explanation: Expo says updates can change non-native pieces such as JS, styling and images. They cannot change native code or dependencies, app permissions or the Expo SDK version. A permission, an SDK upgrade and a native library all need a new binary.
rationales: Correct. A JS bug fix is the textbook OTA change.
Correct. Images and styling are listed as updatable.
Permissions are compiled into the binary, so they can't change OTA.
The SDK version changes native code, so it needs a new build.
Native dependencies require a new binary.

questions.scenario: The app uses the `appVersion` runtime policy, and `version` stayed at 2.4.0. A developer added a native haptics module, rebuilt, and published an update to production. Users on the older 2.4.0 build began crashing when the new screen opened.
questions.stem: What is the root cause, and which change prevents a repeat?
options: The update was too large for old clients; enable bytecode diffing so clients download smaller patches.
The production channel pointed at the wrong branch; repoint it with `eas channel:edit`.
`checkAutomatically` was set to `ON_LOAD`; change it to `NEVER` so old builds stop checking.
The old and new builds share runtime version 2.4.0, so old builds accepted JS that calls missing native code; switch to the `fingerprint` policy so native changes produce a new runtime version.
questions.explanation: Runtime versions exist to keep updates on builds whose native code is compatible. With `appVersion`, the runtime version only changes when `version` does, so both binaries matched. The `fingerprint` policy hashes the native project and changes automatically when native inputs change.
rationales: Download size doesn't cause native-module crashes, and bytecode diffing is already on by default since SDK 56.
The channel worked as designed; the problem is that the runtime version didn't distinguish the builds.
That would stop all future updates, including safe ones, and doesn't address compatibility.
Correct. This identifies the mismatch and the policy that prevents it.

sources.title: How EAS Update works — Expo docs

questions.scenario: A product manager publishes an urgent copy fix with EAS Update, opens the app, and still sees the old text. After closing and reopening the app, the fix appears. The app uses default `expo-updates` settings.
questions.stem: What explains this, and how can the team make critical fixes apply in the same session?
options: By default the update downloads on launch but runs on the next launch; for critical fixes, call `fetchUpdateAsync()` and then `reloadAsync()` when an update is available.
The update failed the first time and succeeded on retry; add `--clear-cache` when publishing.
`checkForUpdateAsync()` downloads the update in the background; call it twice to apply it.
The update was published to the wrong branch, and the second launch picked up the right one.
questions.explanation: `fallbackToCacheTimeout` defaults to 0, so launch doesn't wait for a download, and the new update normally runs on the next launch. To apply sooner, download with `fetchUpdateAsync()` and restart with `reloadAsync()`. `checkForUpdateAsync()` only checks and doesn't download.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented default, and these are the APIs that apply an update sooner.
Nothing failed. This is the expected default behavior.
`checkForUpdateAsync()` does not download anything.
The fix appeared on the next launch, which matches the default timing, not a branch error.

sources.title: How EAS Update works — Expo docs

questions.scenario: Ten minutes after a production update, crash reports spike. The previous update on the branch was stable, and the store binary is fine.
questions.stem: What is the fastest correct response?
options: Delete the bad update group from the dashboard; clients will fall back automatically.
Submit a new store build with the old JS and request expedited review.
Run `eas update:rollback` to republish the previous update (or roll back to the embedded update) so clients pick it up on their next check.
Change the runtime version in app config so the bad update no longer matches.
questions.explanation: A rollback republishes an earlier update or tells clients to run the embedded one, as a newer instruction that clients pick up on their next check. It doesn't delete the bad update. A runtime change only affects new builds, and a store release is much slower.
rationales: Rollback is done by publishing something newer, not by deleting history.
This works eventually, but it's far slower than an OTA rollback for a JS-only fault.
Correct. This is the documented rollback mechanism.
Installed builds keep their embedded runtime version, so changing config doesn't affect them.

questions.scenario: Update A is at a 20% rollout on the production branch for iOS. Monitoring looks good, but a separate hotfix B now needs to go out on the same branch, platform and runtime version.
questions.stem: What constraint applies, and what is a valid way to proceed?
options: Publish B with `--rollout-percentage=20`; EAS runs the two rollouts side by side for different users.
Publish B with `--channel production` while A's rollout continues, because channel publishes bypass rollouts.
Only one rollout can be in progress per branch, platform and runtime version; finish or revert A (or publish B with `--force-end-active-rollout` on a recent EAS CLI) before rolling B out.
Delete A's rollout from the database and republish it as B.
questions.explanation: The rollouts page says only one rollout can be in progress for a given branch, platform and runtime version. You end A by editing it to 100% or reverting it, or you publish with `--force-end-active-rollout` (EAS CLI 24.9.0+). Parallel rollouts on the same key aren't supported.
rationales: Two concurrent rollouts for the same branch, platform and runtime version aren't allowed.
That flag guidance applies to branch-based rollouts, where you publish with `--branch`; it doesn't bypass a per-update rollout.
Correct. This states the documented limit and the supported ways to clear it.
There is no such delete step; rollouts are ended with edit, revert or the force flag.

questions.scenario: QA approved update group `abc123` on the `staging` branch. The team wants production users to get exactly those bundles, without re-running the bundler from a possibly newer commit.
questions.stem: Which approach does that?
options: Check out main and run `eas update --branch production` again.
Run `eas build --profile production` and submit it.
Set `checkAutomatically: NEVER` on production builds and send the update link to users.
`eas update:republish --group abc123 --destination-branch production`
questions.explanation: `eas update:republish` copies an existing update group to another branch or channel, so production receives the exact artifacts QA tested. Publishing again from a checkout rebuilds the bundle, and it might differ. A store build is unnecessary for a JS-only promotion.
rationales: This creates a new bundle from whatever is checked out, which may not be what QA approved.
A new binary is slow and unnecessary for a change that can ship as an update.
That stops production builds from checking for updates at all.
Correct. Republish promotes the tested artifacts unchanged.

questions.scenario: A fitness app was approved as a workout tracker. The team plans to use EAS Update next month to add, without a new submission, a section where third-party developers' mini-apps can be browsed and launched inside the app.
questions.stem: What is the best assessment?
options: It conflicts with Apple's rules: DPLA 3.3.1(B) bars downloaded code that creates a storefront for other apps or changes the app's purpose, and 2.5.2 bars downloaded code that adds features. Ship it in a reviewed binary with the feature described in the Notes for Review.
It is allowed because the mini-apps are JavaScript, and Apple only restricts native code.
It is allowed if the update is limited to a 10% rollout until it proves stable.
It is allowed on iOS because Google Play's interpreter exception also applies to the App Store.
questions.explanation: Apple allows downloaded interpreted code only if it doesn't change the app's primary purpose, doesn't bypass security features, and doesn't create a store for other apps. App Review 2.5.2 also bars downloaded code that adds features, and 2.3.1(a) requires new features to be described for review. Being JavaScript, or rolling out gradually, doesn't change that.
rationales: Correct. This applies the DPLA and guideline text directly.
Apple's rules cover interpreted code too, with explicit limits.
Rollout percentage doesn't affect whether a change complies.
Google's policy doesn't apply to the App Store, and Apple's own terms forbid this case.

questions.scenario: After upgrading a project to a current SDK, a CI step that ran `eas update --branch production -m "$COMMIT_MSG"` started failing. Builds still succeed.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Replace `--branch` with `--channel`, because branch publishes were removed.
Add `--skip-bundler` so CI doesn't need the project's dependencies.
Downgrade EAS CLI to a version from before the SDK upgrade.
Add `--environment production` so the update is bundled with the matching EAS environment variables.
questions.explanation: Since SDK 55, `eas update` requires `--environment`. Passing the environment makes the update bundle use the same variables as the build it targets. `--branch` remains a documented flag.

Skipping the bundler doesn't address the missing required flag and changes what gets published.
This works against current tooling rather than meeting the new requirement.

questions.scenario: A startup wants 400 customers outside the company to beta-test its iOS app before launch. The team has 6 members in App Store Connect.
questions.stem: How should they distribute the beta?
options: Add all 400 customers as internal testers so builds skip review.
Add an external TestFlight group (email invites or a public link), knowing the first build for external testers needs TestFlight App Review.
Use Apple's phased release on the App Store limited to 400 users.
Ship an ad hoc build to all 400 customers by registering their device IDs.
questions.explanation: Internal TestFlight testing is limited to 100 people with certain team roles. External testing supports up to 10,000 testers by email or public link, and the first external build must pass TestFlight App Review. Phased release is for production updates, not betas.
rationales: Internal testers must be team members with specific roles, and the cap is 100.
Correct. External groups are built for this, with a review on the first build.
Phased release rolls out a production version to automatic-update users; it isn't a beta channel.
Ad hoc distribution means managing device registration for every tester, so it doesn't scale to 400 customers. It isn't the intended beta path.

questions.scenario: A solo developer opened a new personal Google Play developer account this month and plans to launch on Android in one week. They've uploaded a build to the internal testing track and shared it with three friends.
questions.stem: What is the most important gap in this plan?
options: Internal testing builds must first pass a full policy review that takes about two weeks.
New personal accounts must run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days before applying for production access.
The app must reach an open testing track with at least 1,000 testers before production.
Production apps must start with a staged rollout below 10%.
questions.explanation: For personal accounts created after 2023-11-13, Google requires a closed test with at least 12 opted-in testers for 14 consecutive days before production access. An internal test with three people doesn't count. A one-week launch plan is too short.
rationales: Internal builds are available within minutes and might not go through standard policy review.
Correct. This is the documented requirement for new personal accounts.
1,000 is the minimum cap when you limit an open test, not a production requirement.
Staged rollout percentages are your choice, not a requirement.

questions.scenario: Version 5.1 is on a 20% Google Play staged rollout. A native crash affects some devices. The team halts the rollout.
questions.stem: Which two statements are true? (Select two.)
options: Halting automatically downgrades affected users to the previous version.
If left alone, the staged rollout would have advanced to 100% automatically after 7 days.
Users who already installed 5.1 keep it; halting only stops new users from receiving it.
The fix is to roll out a new release with a corrected bundle.
questions.explanation: Google says halting stops new users from getting the version, while existing users stay on it. A bad release is fixed by rolling out a new release with a fixed bundle. Play staged rollouts don't advance on their own; the 7-day automatic schedule is Apple's phased release.
rationales: Play doesn't roll users back to an earlier version.
Play rollouts don't increase automatically; that describes Apple's phased release.
Correct. Halting doesn't remove the version from devices.
Correct. This is Google's documented remedy.

questions.scenario: Apple rejected a B2B app under guideline 2.1. The reviewer couldn't get past the login screen. The team had provided demo credentials, but the staging backend they point to was shut down for the weekend.
questions.stem: What should they do before resubmitting?

Remove the login screen from review builds with a hidden flag.
Reply that the app is for enterprise customers only and ask for an exception.
Switch to Sign in with Apple so the reviewer can create an account.
questions.explanation: Guideline 2.1(a) asks for a demo account "(and turn on your back-end service!)", so the reviewer can use the full app. A hidden review-only path would be an undocumented feature under 2.5.19. Changing login providers doesn't fix an offline backend.
rationales: Correct. This addresses the cause of the 2.1 rejection.
A review-only hidden path is the kind of hidden behavior 2.5.19 prohibits.
Apps on the App Store must still be reviewable. Asking for an exception doesn't fix the access problem.
The reviewer still can't use the app if the backend is down.

Phased release starts at 10%, not 1%.
Phased release applies only to new installs; existing users all get 7.0 immediately.
Phased release can't be paused, so the share can't be held at 1%.
questions.explanation: Apple's phased release moves through 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50% and 100% over 7 days, for users with automatic updates on. Any user can update manually at any time, and you can pause for up to 30 days in total.
rationales: Correct. Manual downloads aren't limited by phased release.
The schedule starts at 1%.
It applies to automatic updates for existing users, not to new installs.
You can pause a phased release, for up to 30 days in total.

questions.scenario: After uploading an Expo iOS build, the team receives an email from Apple about a missing approved reason for the UserDefaults API. The call comes from a statically linked CocoaPods dependency that ships its own PrivacyInfo file.
questions.stem: What is the recommended fix in an Expo project?
options: Add an `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes` entry for the UserDefaults category with an approved reason such as `CA92.1` under `ios.privacyManifests` in app config.
Remove the dependency, because any library that calls UserDefaults is rejected.
Set the Info.plist key that disables privacy manifest checks for third-party pods.
Ignore the email; it's informational and doesn't affect review.
questions.explanation: The Expo guide explains that Apple doesn't correctly parse all PrivacyInfo files from static CocoaPods dependencies, so you copy the reasons into `ios.privacyManifests` in app config. UserDefaults is a required-reason API category, and `CA92.1` is an example reason Expo shows. Apple has required approved reasons on upload since 2024-05-01.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented Expo workaround.
Calling the API is allowed with an approved reason; removing the library isn't necessary.
No such opt-out exists in the sources.
Required-reason declarations have been mandatory for uploads since 2024-05-01.

questions.scenario: An iOS app supports account creation, Sign in with Apple, and auto-renewing subscriptions through Apple. The team is designing account deletion to meet guideline 5.1.1(v).
questions.stem: Which two design choices are required or recommended by Apple's guidance? (Select two.)
options: Let users start deletion from an easy-to-find place in the app, and delete the account record rather than only deactivating it.
Revoke the user's Sign in with Apple tokens using the Sign in with Apple REST API when the account is deleted.
Require users to email support to confirm deletion, to prevent mistakes.
Automatically cancel the user's App Store subscription as part of deletion.
questions.explanation: Apple requires deletion to start in the app, be easy to find, and remove the account, since deactivation alone is insufficient. Apps using Sign in with Apple should revoke tokens through the REST API. Outside highly regulated industries you shouldn't require email or phone steps. Apple says to tell users that billing continues through Apple, which means the app can't cancel the subscription for them.
rationales: Correct. This matches Apple's core deletion requirements.
Correct. Apple's guidance calls for token revocation through the REST API.
Apple says not to require phone or email steps unless the app is in a highly regulated industry.
Apple's guidance is to tell users that billing continues until they cancel, not to cancel automatically.

questions.scenario: An Android app sends crash logs with device identifiers to a third-party crash-reporting SDK. A teammate argues it doesn't belong on the Play Data safety form because "our code never touches it, and the SDK vendor is just a processor".
questions.stem: Which response is accurate?
options: It's exempt, because data handled by an SDK is the SDK vendor's responsibility.
It must be declared as shared with a third party, because any vendor transfer counts as sharing.
It only needs to be declared if Google's automated review detects it.
The data leaves the device, so it's collected and must be declared; you're responsible for SDK behavior. A service provider acting for you is not "sharing".
questions.explanation: Play defines "collect" as transmitting data off the device, and you're responsible for what your SDKs do. Transfers to a service provider processing data on your behalf aren't "sharing", but they're still collection. Google doesn't verify declarations before publishing, but mismatches can lead to enforcement.
rationales: Developers are responsible for the SDKs they include.
Service provider transfers are excluded from "sharing".
Declarations are the developer's duty whether or not Google detects the data.
Correct. This distinguishes collection from sharing and assigns SDK responsibility to the developer.

questions.scenario: Users of an Android app can sign up in the app or on the company website. The app has an in-app "Delete account" button.
questions.stem: What else does Google Play require?
options: A web link where users can request deletion without the app, entered in the Data safety form.
Nothing else, because the in-app button satisfies the policy.
A phone number users can call to confirm deletion.
A 30-day waiting period before any data is removed.
questions.explanation: Google's account deletion policy applies to apps that let users create an account and requires both an in-app path and a web link resource. The web link is declared in the Data safety form. Neither of the other measures is a Play requirement.
rationales: Correct. Google requires both paths.
The in-app path alone doesn't meet the requirement.
Not a Play requirement. It adds friction, too.
No such waiting period is required.

questions.scenario: Every merge to main triggers full iOS and Android production builds in EAS Workflows, even though most merges only change JavaScript. Build minutes and queue times are growing.
questions.stem: Which workflow design does Expo's documentation suggest?
options: Build only on Fridays and batch the week's merges into one binary.
Switch production builds to `--local` on CI runners to avoid the EAS queue.
Publish every merge as an update and never build again; updates can carry native changes once a build exists.
Run a `fingerprint` job, look for a compatible build with `get-build`, and run an `update` job when one exists, building only when the fingerprint is new.
questions.explanation: The Workflows docs say to combine `fingerprint`, `get-build` and `update` jobs to skip redundant native builds. `fingerprint` outputs per-platform hashes, `get-build` looks up a build for a hash, and you publish an update when a compatible binary exists. Native changes still require a new build.
rationales: Batching delays fixes and still builds when nothing native changed.
This moves where the work runs without removing unnecessary builds.
Updates can't carry native changes, so a new fingerprint still needs a build.
Correct. This is the documented pattern.

questions.scenario: Designers want to review UI changes from each pull request on their phones within minutes. Most PRs only touch screens and styles, but some add native libraries.
questions.stem: Which CI approach fits best?
options: On `pull_request`, submit every PR to TestFlight external testing.
On `pull_request`, publish every PR to the production branch at a 1% rollout.
Ask designers to run the project locally with Expo Go for every PR.
On `pull_request`, publish an EAS update to a PR-specific branch and post instructions with a `github-comment` job; when the fingerprint changed, run an internal-distribution `build` instead.
questions.explanation: An update published to a PR branch reaches designers quickly when native code hasn't changed. When the fingerprint differs, an update isn't compatible, so an internal build is needed. Production rollouts and external TestFlight are the wrong audiences, and TestFlight adds review latency.
rationales: That's slow, may need review, and targets external testers rather than designers.
This exposes unreviewed code to real users.
Expo Go supports only the latest SDK and can't load custom native libraries, and it puts the setup work on designers.
Correct. It's fast for JS changes and still handles native ones.

questions.scenario: A team wants CI to handle versioning fully. Their plan: `appVersionSource: "remote"`, `autoIncrement: true` on production, and they expect `version` to go from 1.8.0 to 1.9.0 automatically with each store build.
questions.stem: What should they change in their expectations or setup?
options: Switch to `appVersionSource: "local"`, because remote sources can't increment anything.
Remove autoIncrement and let the stores assign build numbers on upload.
Keep the remote source and autoIncrement for build numbers, but bump the user-facing `version` deliberately when they cut a release; autoIncrement with a remote source doesn't change `version`.
Set `runtimeVersion` to `nativeVersion` so EAS bumps `version` from the build number.
questions.explanation: Expo says the user-facing version should be set and updated by you. With a remote source, `autoIncrement` manages buildNumber and versionCode. Combining the two gives unique builds and intentional marketing versions.
rationales: Remote is the recommended source, and it does increment build numbers.
Neither store assigns build numbers for you; each upload must carry a new one.
Correct. This matches how Expo divides the responsibilities.
The runtime policy affects update compatibility, not the app's `version`.

questions.scenario: A three-person team has 40 Maestro flows and almost no Jest tests. The E2E suite takes 50 minutes per pull request, and about one run in five fails for reasons nobody can reproduce. Most failures are in form validation and price formatting.
questions.stem: What change gives the best return?
options: Add retries to every Maestro flow so flaky steps pass on the second attempt
Move validation and formatting coverage into Jest unit and RNTL component tests, and keep a few E2E flows for critical journeys
Replace Maestro with Detox, since a different E2E tool will remove the flakiness
Run the full E2E suite only before store submission and drop automated tests from pull requests
questions.explanation: Validation and formatting are logic that Jest and RNTL can test in seconds without a build. The pyramid keeps most coverage in fast tests and reserves E2E, which needs a built binary and a simulator, for the few flows only it can prove.
rationales: Retries hide flakiness and make the slow suite even slower; the coverage is still at the wrong layer.
Correct. Logic belongs in fast Jest tests; a small E2E set guards the critical paths.
Switching tools does not change the cost of driving a built app for logic that does not need it.
This removes fast feedback from pull requests and lets regressions pile up until release.

questions.scenario: A developer writes an RNTL test for a login screen. It reaches into the component to check that a state variable named isSubmitting becomes true after pressing the button.
questions.stem: What should the reviewer suggest?
options: Keep the test; checking internal state is the most precise assertion
Snapshot the whole component tree instead, so any change is detected
Assert what the user sees, such as the button becoming disabled or a "Signing in" text appearing, found by text or accessibility info
Delete the test and cover the login screen only with a Maestro flow
questions.explanation: React Native Testing Library is designed for testing components the way users experience them: by rendered text and accessibility information. Tests tied to internal state break on refactors that do not change behavior.
rationales: Internal state is an implementation detail; renaming it breaks the test without any user-visible change.
Whole-tree snapshots fail on any markup change and rarely express the intended behavior.
Correct. Querying visible output keeps the test meaningful and refactor-proof.
Login behavior can be covered quickly in Jest; E2E should not replace component tests.

questions.scenario: A team adds a Maestro job to its EAS workflow. The build job uses the production profile, which produces an iOS device build and an Android App Bundle (.aab). The Maestro job cannot install either artifact.
questions.stem: What should the E2E build profile change?
options: Point the Maestro job at the Metro dev server URL instead of a build
Use the production profile but add --clear-cache to the build
Run the flows in Expo Go so no build is needed
Set ios.simulator to true and android.buildType to apk
questions.explanation: Expo's E2E example uses a profile with ios.simulator: true and android.buildType: apk, because simulators need a simulator build and emulators install APKs, not App Bundles. The maestro job then takes that build's build_id.
rationales: Maestro drives an installed app; a dev server URL is not an installable artifact.
Clearing the cache does not change the artifact type.
Expo Go is a learning sandbox, not your app binary, and does not represent the shipped build.
Correct. These are the settings in Expo's E2E profile.

questions.scenario: After adding a UI library, Jest tests in an Expo project fail with "SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module", pointing into node_modules/that-library.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Remove the jest-expo preset and write a Babel config from scratch
Mock the entire library with an empty object in every test file
Switch the tests to run in Expo Go on a device
Adjust the transformIgnorePatterns regex so Jest transforms that package
questions.explanation: Some packages ship untranspiled modern syntax. transformIgnorePatterns takes a regular expression that decides which node_modules packages Jest leaves alone; widening it lets the preset transform the library.
rationales: Dropping the preset loses the native module mocks and makes the setup worse.
Blanket empty mocks hide the library and make component tests meaningless.
Jest tests run in Node, not in Expo Go.
Correct. Allow the package through transformIgnorePatterns so it is transpiled.

questions.stem: Which scenario is the best candidate for a Maestro end-to-end flow rather than a Jest test?
options: Edge cases of a currency formatting function
Launching the built app, signing in and reaching the home screen
Every error message produced by a Zod schema
The reducer that merges offline mutations
questions.explanation: E2E proves what only a built app can: launch, navigation and integration with native modules and the backend on a critical journey. Pure logic like formatting, schemas and reducers belongs in Jest.
rationales: A pure function is fastest and most precise to test in Jest.
Correct. Sign-in to home is a critical path that only a real build fully exercises.
Schema messages are pure logic; testing each through the UI is slow and brittle.
Merge logic is pure and should be unit tested with many cases.
