questions.scenario: To ship quickly, a developer puts the team's paid LLM provider key in EXPO_PUBLIC_LLM_KEY and calls the provider directly from the app. A reviewer objects. The developer replies that the release build uses Hermes bytecode, so the key is not visible.
questions.stem: What is the right response?
options: Accept it; bytecode cannot be read without the source
Move the key to app.json extra, which is not part of the JavaScript bundle
Keep the key on a backend the team controls and have the app call that backend with the user's own auth
Split the key into two EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables and join them at runtime
questions.explanation: Expo states that EXPO_PUBLIC_ values are plain text in the app and that anything in client code is public. App config must not hold secrets either. A privileged key belongs on a server that can authenticate users and limit usage.
rationales: Bytecode only slows extraction; the key is still shipped to every device.
App config is embedded in the build and must not hold secrets.
Correct. The backend keeps the key and enforces per-user auth and limits.
Splitting is obfuscation; both halves still ship in the bundle.

questions.scenario: An app stores the OAuth refresh token in AsyncStorage. A security review cites MASVS-STORAGE-1.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Base64-encode the token before saving it to AsyncStorage
Keep the refresh token in a React context so it is never written to disk
Store it in app config so it is compiled into the binary
Store the token in expo-secure-store, which uses the iOS Keychain and Keystore-encrypted storage on Android
questions.explanation: MASVS-STORAGE-1 requires sensitive data to be stored securely. AsyncStorage is unencrypted, while expo-secure-store uses the Keychain on iOS and SharedPreferences encrypted with the Android Keystore.
rationales: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.
Memory-only storage logs the user out on every restart and does not solve storage for a long-lived token.
App config is shared by every install and is readable; a per-user token cannot live there.
Correct. SecureStore uses the platform secure storage.

questions.scenario: A team is writing its guidelines for configuration values in an Expo app built with EAS.
questions.stem: Which two statements belong in the guidelines? (Select two.)
options: Private keys are safe in app.json because app config is not shipped to devices
Obfuscating the bundle makes it acceptable to embed admin API keys
Values in EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables are readable by anyone who can run the app
A build-time secret such as the Sentry auth token belongs in EAS environment variables used by the build, not in app code
questions.explanation: Expo treats anything in client code, including EXPO_PUBLIC_ values, as public, and says app config must not hold secrets. Secrets needed only during the build, such as the Sentry token used to upload source maps, live in EAS environment variables and are never read by app code.
rationales: App config is embedded in the build; Expo says not to put secrets there.
Obfuscation does not remove the key from the device.
Correct. Expo says these values are plain text and public.
Correct. Build-only secrets stay in the build environment.

questions.scenario: A streaming app unlocks premium videos when the client reports isPremium: true. After abuse is found, a product manager proposes adding a jailbreak and root detection library and blocking flagged devices as the fix.
questions.stem: What should the engineering lead recommend?
options: Adopt the library as the main control; MASVS-RESILIENCE-1 covers this case fully
Enforce entitlements on the server per authenticated user, and treat device-integrity checks as optional defense in depth
Move the isPremium flag into expo-secure-store so users cannot change it
Pin the certificate of the video CDN so the client cannot be tampered with
questions.explanation: Any client-side decision can be patched on a device the attacker controls, so detection is defense in depth in MASVS-RESILIENCE, not an authorization control. The server must decide what each user may access.
rationales: Detection can be bypassed on a compromised device and blocks legitimate users; it cannot be the main control.
Correct. Authorization belongs on the server; integrity checks only raise the cost of attacks.
Secure storage protects data at rest, but the client still decides access, which an attacker can modify.
Pinning protects traffic in transit; it does not stop a modified client claiming premium status.

questions.scenario: To satisfy MASVS-NETWORK-2, a team plans to pin the single leaf certificate of its API and also the certificates of a third-party analytics SDK and an image CDN it does not operate.
questions.stem: What is the best revision of the plan?
options: Pin all three hosts with their leaf certificates; more pins is more secure
Skip pinning and rely only on the platform trust store
Ship pins through an OTA update so they can be rotated without a new build
Pin only the API the team controls, pin public keys with a backup pin, and plan rotation before release
questions.explanation: MASVS-NETWORK-2 scopes identity pinning to endpoints under the developer's control. Android's pinning guidance says to pin public keys and always include a backup key; otherwise a key change forces an app update to restore connectivity. So pin only your own API, with a backup pin and a rotation plan.
rationales: Pinning hosts you do not control breaks the app when those providers rotate certificates.
This ignores NETWORK-2 for the endpoint the team does control.
This leaves the real problems in place: it still pins hosts the team does not control and a single leaf certificate. And when pins live in native configuration, an OTA update cannot change them.
Correct. This follows the control's scope and avoids locking out users at rotation.

questions.scenario: After an EAS Update ships, Sentry shows a spike of errors with minified stack frames. Crashes from the store build itself are symbolicated correctly.
questions.stem: What is missing?
options: SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN in the app's EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables
Source maps for the update: run npx sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps dist after eas update
A new store build, because Sentry cannot read OTA bundles
Disabling Hermes so stack traces are not minified
questions.explanation: EAS Build uploads source maps automatically when SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN is set, but an OTA update produces a new bundle whose source maps must be uploaded separately with sentry-expo-upload-sourcemaps after eas update.
rationales: The auth token is a secret for the upload step; putting it in EXPO_PUBLIC_ would leak it.
Correct. Each update bundle needs its own source map upload.
Sentry symbolicates updates fine once their source maps are uploaded.
Minification is resolved by source maps; turning off the default engine is unnecessary.

questions.scenario: A team is preparing a runbook for native store releases on both platforms.
questions.stem: Which two statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Google Play staged rollouts increase the percentage automatically over seven days
Halting a Google Play staged rollout stops new users getting the release, but users who already have it keep it
Pausing an Apple phased release removes the new version from devices that already installed it
Apple phased release paces automatic updates only; anyone can download the new version manually from the App Store
questions.explanation: Play states that a staged rollout percentage does not increase automatically and that halting only affects users who have not received it. Apple's phased release applies to automatic updates over 7 days and the version can be downloaded manually at any time.
rationales: Play says the percentage won't increase automatically; the 7-day schedule is Apple's.
Correct. This is how Play describes halting.
Pausing stops further automatic updates; it does not uninstall anything.
Correct. Phased release does not restrict manual downloads.

questions.scenario: A team published an EAS Update with --rollout-percentage=10. Two hours later, crash reports tagged with the new expo-update-id rise sharply. The previous update was healthy.
questions.stem: What is the most direct action?
options: Submit a new store build and request expedited review
Delete the update from the EAS dashboard so devices forget it
Revert the rollout with eas update:revert-update-rollout
Raise the rollout to 100% so the error data is more complete
questions.explanation: EAS Update rollouts are controlled with eas update:edit and backed out with eas update:revert-update-rollout. Tagging events with the update ID is what lets the team attribute the spike to this update.
rationales: A JS-only problem in an OTA update does not need a store build, and review adds delay.
Removing the bad update is not how EAS backs out a rollout; use the rollout or rollback commands.
Correct. This returns the rollout population to the previous update.
Expanding a failing update increases harm.

questions.scenario: A native Android release is at 20% in a Google Play staged rollout. It crashes on startup for users on one device family. The team halts the rollout.
questions.stem: What must happen next for users who already installed the bad version?
options: Nothing; halting the rollout reinstalls the previous version on their devices
Resume the halted rollout at a lower percentage
Remove the affected countries from the rollout
Roll out a new release with a fixed bundle (and a higher version code)
questions.explanation: Play says halting stops new users receiving the version while existing users keep it, and that the remedy for a bad release is rolling out a new release with a fixed bundle. Countries cannot be removed once a staged rollout starts.
rationales: Halting does not downgrade anyone.
Resuming targets the same users with the same broken build.
Play does not allow removing countries after the rollout has started, and that would not fix installed copies anyway.
Correct. Affected users need a newer fixed version.

questions.scenario: A backend team wants to rename the field total to totalCents in the order API and ship an app update the same week. Analytics show about 30% of active users are on app versions more than two months old.
questions.stem: What is the best approach?
options: Rename the field and push an OTA update so all clients switch at once
Add totalCents alongside total, migrate the app to the new field, and remove total only once old-version traffic is negligible or a minimum version is enforced
Rename the field and rely on store automatic updates to move users within a few days
Keep the old field forever and never change the API
questions.explanation: Old binaries stay in use for months, so additive changes keep them working while new versions adopt the new field. Removal waits for data showing old traffic is gone, or for a minimum-version gate, which MASVS-CODE-2 describes as an update-enforcement mechanism.
rationales: Not every client receives or applies an OTA update promptly, and builds with a different runtime version never get it.
Correct. Additive change plus data-driven retirement is the safe pattern.
Many users turn off automatic updates or delay them; this breaks them immediately.
APIs can evolve; the goal is compatibility during the transition, not freezing the schema.

questions.scenario: A security fix requires every user to move to a new native build. The app ships on both iOS and Android.
questions.stem: Which approach enforces this on both platforms?
options: Call the iOS immediate in-app update API and the Android equivalent
Publish an EAS Update that includes the native fix
Raise the minimum OS version in the next build
Have the app check a minimum supported version from the backend and block below it; on Android, use the Play immediate in-app update flow
questions.explanation: Google Play In-App Updates offers an immediate, blocking flow on Android. iOS has no equivalent OS API, so the usual design is a backend-driven minimum-version check with a blocking screen linking to the App Store, satisfying MASVS-CODE-2.
rationales: iOS has no immediate in-app update API.
OTA updates cannot change native code.
A minimum OS version does nothing to make existing installs update.
Correct. A server-driven gate works everywhere, with Play's flow on Android.

questions.scenario: A team has a social feed feature that will not be ready before the App Store submission. One engineer proposes shipping the code dormant behind a remote flag and turning it on after approval, without mentioning it to App Review.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate guidance?
options: This is fine because the code was in the binary Apple reviewed
This is fine as long as the flag is controlled by an EAS Update instead of a server
Do not ship unreviewed features hidden behind flags; use flags for gradual exposure or kill switches of features described in the Notes for Review
Encrypt the feature code so App Review cannot see it
questions.explanation: App Review Guideline 2.5.19 prohibits hidden, dormant or undocumented features, and Apple's 2026-10-16 update clarified that changing what the app does after approval is covered. 2.3.1(a) requires new features to be described in the Notes for Review.
rationales: Dormant undocumented features are exactly what 2.5.19 prohibits.
OTA updates must follow store guidelines too; the delivery channel does not change the rule.
Correct. Flags are fine for reviewed, documented features.
Hiding functionality from review is a more serious violation, not a fix.

questions.scenario: A two-person team is building a field-service tool. Technicians need reliable push notifications for new jobs, background location during shifts and photo capture, and the client wants it in both app stores.
questions.stem: Which delivery choice fits best?
options: A responsive web app only
A PWA, using Add to Home Screen on iOS
A native app built with Expo, optionally also targeting web from the same codebase
A WebView wrapper around the existing website submitted to both stores
questions.explanation: Background location, reliable push and store presence point to a native app; web.dev notes iOS PWAs lack an install prompt and capabilities such as badging. A wrapped website risks rejection under App Review 4.2, which requires more than a repackaged website.
rationales: A web app cannot do background location and has no store presence.
iOS PWAs have no install prompt and limited capabilities, which does not meet these needs.
Correct. The requirements are native ones, and Expo keeps one codebase.
Apple 4.2 rejects apps that are only a repackaged website.

questions.scenario: A small team runs a content and booking site. Analytics show users mostly visit a few times a year from search, and the product needs no device features beyond a camera-free form. The CEO asks for an app "because competitors have one".
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Build native apps for iOS and Android first, then improve the website
Invest in a fast responsive web app, and revisit a PWA or native app if repeat use or device needs appear
Wrap the site in a WebView and publish it to the stores this week
Build a PWA and tell iOS users to wait for the install banner
questions.explanation: For infrequent, search-driven use with no device APIs, a responsive web app gives the most value for a small team. A wrapped site risks App Review 4.2, and iOS shows no PWA install prompt, so users must use Share > Add to Home Screen.
rationales: Two native apps add review, release and maintenance cost without a requirement that needs them.
Correct. Match the platform to real usage and capability needs.
App Review 4.2 rejects apps that are only a repackaged website.
iOS has no PWA install prompt.

questions.scenario: A team is considering a PWA instead of a native app and wants to set iOS expectations correctly.
questions.stem: Which two statements about PWAs on iOS are supported by web.dev? (Select two.)
options: There is no install prompt; users install through Share > Add to Home Screen
Installed PWAs share storage with Safari, so a user stays logged in after installing
iOS PWAs lack support for capabilities such as badging and app shortcuts
Install criteria are identical across every browser
questions.explanation: web.dev notes iOS has no install prompt, iOS PWAs lack capabilities such as badging and app shortcuts, and each Apple installation has isolated storage. It also says install criteria vary by browser.
rationales: Correct. Users install manually from the Share menu.
Each installation has isolated storage, so users may need to sign in again.
Correct. web.dev lists these as missing.
web.dev says criteria vary by browser.
